thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrously inclusive, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

If a sentient being were to hold my name, their merit would be exactly equal and no different from that of those who hold the names of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Dharma-sons. World-Honored One!
My single name is no different from those many names. Because I have cultivated and attained true perfect penetration, this is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness.
Its blessings are complete for all sentient beings within the small thousand, middle thousand, and great thousand worlds—hence the term "trichiliocosm.

Within such a trichiliocosm, there are a total of ten billion suns and moons, collectively named one Sahā world. Guishan said: "Because the faculty of the ear is sharp for the sentient beings of this region, those who receive the Way are numerous; therefore, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation is superior, while the other faculties are dull."

Consequently, those who receive the Way are few, and thus the transformations of the various sages are inferior. This shows that although their stages of practice may be equal, they differ according to the capacity of the recipient. Even if all those beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were combined, they would only equal the single person that Avalokiteśvara opposes; therefore, the two merits of upholding the Name are truly equal.

The explanation of the fourteen fearlessnesses is hereby concluded. Someone asked: "What does one who holds the name have to fear, such that you speak of 'fearlessness'? I replied: "One who holds the name may fear that their merit is insufficient and thus harbor doubt, or they may encounter those who hold many names and fear they cannot equal them;
both of these are states from which there is no fear. Now, one who holds the name of the Bodhisattva is completely liberated from these fears.

"World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully obtain the four inconceivable and unconditioned wondrous virtues" (Wenling says: "To manifest in manifold...").

He manifests his form to convert and transform sentient beings, perfectly responding to their needs. This principle arises from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and his spiritual responses are unfathomable; thus he is named "Inconceivable and Unconditioned Sublime Virtue" (*acintyānabhisaṃskāra-guṇa*).

Now, although he previously manifested forms to respond to requests, this particular title is called "Inconceivable" because the former was a brief manifestation, whereas this is a profound clarification—such as manifesting eighty thousand heads and arms within a single body, which is truly beyond the reach of thought. Jiaoguang says: "Unconditioned Sublime Virtue" means that one examines how it is not produced by conditioned mental effort, but is rather spontaneously and freely accomplished.
First, because I initially attained the wondrous and subtle mind of hearing, the essence of the mind abandoned its hearing, and I perceived...
Because hearing, awareness, and cognition cannot be separated, they form a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and can preach boundless secret divine mantras.
Among these, I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, or ten thousand heads.
Eighty-four thousand śakara heads; two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty up to twenty-four;
and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms; two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine [eyes].

The eyes. Thus, up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, concentration or wisdom—they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty. (The "first" refers to the very beginning within the process of hearing.

Regarding the "wondrously wondrous mind of hearing": it is because when one turns the hearing back toward one's own nature, that act of turning the hearing back is *ādikṣānti* (initial awakening), while the nature of one's own nature is *mūlakṣānti* (original awakening). When initial and original awakenings merge as one, both become wondrous; hence it is so called.)

"Exquisite, exquisite is the hearing-mind. When the essence of the mind abandons hearing, that which hears and that which is heard are both exhausted. "Abandons" (yí) means to be liberated from. This is because through long practice of "hearing back" (fǎnwén), one’s singular mental essence becomes detached and exhausts the characteristics of the sense-faculties;

hence it is called "abandoning hearing. Regarding the two phrases "seeing and hearing": when the single faculty turns back to its source, the six faculties are liberated. That they are not partitioned means that seeing, hearing, and so forth are no longer restricted to their respective fundamental bases; this is the "six being liberated and the one forgotten. Their mutual penetration and interfunctioning is called "perfect integration" (yuánróng);

their lack of obstruction and hindrance is called "purity" (qīngjìng); the full sufficiency of all phenomena is called "precious awakening" (bǎojiào). This indeed demonstrates the manifestation of quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) while simultaneously clarifying the intent of perfect function and inclusive subsumption. Wēnlíng says: "The head represents the totality of the six functions; the arms symbolize the compassion of uplifting and receiving; the eyes symbolize the wisdom of illuminating and comprehending; each relies [upon these]."

The original number is expanded to eighty-four thousand to represent how, based upon the six fundamental functions and fundamental wisdom and compassion, one responds universally to the dusts of worldly toil and attains great sovereignty. This is the wondrous practice of the Equal Enlightenment stage of the eleven stages.

Now, a single body contains the ten voids, and a world-system appears at the tip of a hair; those voids and worlds are not merely like heads and arms. Those eighty-four thousand heads and arms are like the eighty-four thousand pores of a human being—they are nothing extraordinary.

The words of the Sage accord with both phenomena and principle; since they are called "inconceivable virtues," there is no way to limit them by thought or deliberation. *Śakara* translates into Chinese as "Vajra" (Diamond), meaning firm and indestructible. *Mudrā* translates as "Seal," referring here to the arm.

Each possesses its own wondrous seal. The pure jewel-eye is free from dust and united with awakening. Compassion is used to gather and transform; majesty is used to subdue; concentration is used to restore stillness; and wisdom is used to open up enlightenment. This collectively refers to the many wondrous expressions. Liaoguang says: "Compassion protects their roots of goodness;

majesty rescues those of evil nature; concentration guards against distraction; and wisdom saves those who are lost in delusion. To have attained great mastery means that one does not laboriously apply intentional effort or contrivance, but responds according to conditions without ever encountering obstruction.
Second, because one has emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing, reflection, and contemplation, it is like a sound passing through a wall—it cannot act as an obstacle. Therefore...
I am skillfully able to manifest each and every form and recite each and every mantra. Through these forms and mantras, I am able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
for this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, I am called the "Bestower of Fearlessness. (Hearing refers to the nature of hearing;

when thought enters the state of forgetting through practice, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise, and one has thus escaped the six sense objects. "Manifesting each and every form" means appearing in various bodies according to the specific capacities of beings. "Reciting each and every mantra" refers to...)

Each manifested body spoke its own mantra). Third, because I have cultivated this fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, all the worlds I visit cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures, seeking my compassionate pity (since the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment whatsoever;

thus, I cause the multitude to abandon all stinginess and clinging. "Seeking my compassionate pity" means that out of compassion I accept [their offerings], thereby performing the Buddha-work of giving). Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized ultimate perfection.
One is able to make various offerings of precious jewels to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the dharma-realm.
Those who seek a wife shall obtain a wife; those who seek children shall obtain children; those who seek samādhi shall obtain samādhi; and those who seek long life shall obtain long life.
In this way, up until seeking great *nirvāṇa* and attaining great *nirvāṇa* [the Bodhisattva] attains the Buddha-mind (which is the realization of the perfection of wisdom).

The offering of precious jewels is the perfection of merit. Because he is complete in both merit and wisdom, he extends his influence to sentient beings, causing their own aspirations to be fulfilled according to their wishes. As for the statement that the sentient beings of the six realms are also "offerers," it means that the Bodhisattva contemplates that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata, and thus gives rise toward them all with the thought that they are Buddhas.

Thus, the gift of material wealth causes them to obtain happiness; the gift of fearlessness causes them to be free from suffering; and the gift of the Dharma causes them to transform from the state of ordinary beings into the state of sainthood. Precious jewels belong to external wealth; wives, children, longevity, and one’s own life and body belong to internal wealth—all of these...

This is called the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). Great *Nirvāṇa* is the ultimate fruit of the Buddha. Among the four inconceivable powers, two types of giving include material wealth, because through the practice of generosity (*dāna*), one is able to encompass all myriad practices.

Someone asked: "What is the difference between the four inconceivable powers and the thirty-two manifestations? The answer was: "The thirty-two manifestations involve responding to specific requests or appearing in a form similar to that of the seeker to preach the Dharma. In this case [of the four inconceivable powers], there is no restriction regarding the type of request; rather, one observes what form should be used to preach mantras and provide protection, and immediately manifests it.

This is the distinction. (The explanation of the four inconceivable powers concludes above). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied: "I have attained the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination through the gateway of the ear, whereby the conditioned mind is naturally..."
"World-Honored One, by entering through the characteristic of hearing, I attained samādhi and accomplished Bodhi; this is the foremost.
That Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained the Dharma-gate of perfect penetration, and in the midst of that great assembly, he conferred upon me the name Avalokiteśvara.
Because my observation and hearing of the ten directions are perfectly luminous, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the worlds of the ten directions. (From me...)

"Below. This fully reveals the essence and function of perfect penetration. "The Samādhi of Perfect Illumination" means that when the practice of "listening inwardly" is perfected, one resolves the faculties and attains the essence; this is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). "The mind of conditions becomes sovereign" means that because one has attained perfect illumination, one responds to conditions through transformation and attains great sovereignty. "Entering the stream," etc., details the causes and effects from beginning to end.

"Because of the aspect of entering the stream, one attains samādhi" refers to the initial stage of listening inwardly and abiding in the perfectly湛 (pure and profound) and unarisen, undying nature; this constitutes the mind of the causal ground. "Accomplishing Bodhi" refers to...

Thereafter, one perfectly achieves the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition. Regarding the first point, it clarifies its excellence. That Buddha-Tathāgata is none other than Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata; that he bestows a prediction of the same name reveals the harmonious accord between teacher and disciple. From the words "By me," and so forth...

He then further explains the significance of the name: first, it indicates that the person and the dharma share the same name, such that there are no two distinct titles; second, it signifies perfect penetration and universal pervasiveness, which is why his reputation is so widespread, manifesting the excellence of this dharma-gate.

Wuxing says: "According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the past, the Buddha Ratnagarbha bestowed a prophecy upon Prince Animiṣa, naming him Avalokiteśvara. Thus, both the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* and the present sutra refer to names given to the original essence when it manifests its traces. Now that he has attained perfect penetration, he is the subsequent incarnation of that prince.
Other meanings are detailed and complete in various commentaries; they shall not be elaborated upon here."
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the householder Vīśvantara said to the youth Sudhana: "Good son, to the south of here there is a mountain named Potalaka (in the language of China, 'White Flower Tree';
this mountain abounds in these trees, and because their fragrance is perceived from afar, it is located on the seacoast of South India; formerly it was called Putuo).”
There is a bodhisattva there named Avalokiteśvara. Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path? Then he spoke in verse:
On the sea there is a mountain where many sages and worthies dwell; It is composed of various jewels and is exceedingly pure.
Flowers, fruits, and groves fill it everywhere; springs, streams, and ponds are all fully present.
O valiant hero, Avalokiteśvara, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings you dwell upon this mountain.
You should go there and inquire about all virtues; he shall show you the great skillful means.
(There is a mountain upon the sea; it is because the Great Compassionate One, in accordance with sentient beings, enters the ocean of birth and death while abiding upon the mountain of nirvāṇa.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, took his leave, and departed.

Upon reaching that mountain, he saw within the cliffs and valleys to the southwest—where springs and streams meandered in reflection, the forest trees were lush and verdant, and soft fragrant grasses were spread out, curling to the right.
On the ground, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara sat cross-legged upon a precious diamond stone (*vajramaṇi*).
Immeasurable bodhisattvas were all seated upon precious stones, respectfully surrounding him as he proclaimed the Dharma of Great Compassion, causing them to embrace all sentient beings.
Having seen this, Sudhana leaped for joy; with palms joined, he listened attentively, his eyes not blinking for a moment.
They form this thought: "A spiritual friend is the Tathāgata; a spiritual friend is the cloud of all dharmas;
a spiritual friend is the treasury of all merits; a spiritual friend is difficult to encounter; a spiritual friend is..."
The spiritual friend is the cause for the jewels of the ten powers. The spiritual friend is the inexhaustible torch of wisdom. The spiritual friend is the sprout of the roots of merit.
The spiritual friend is the gateway to all-knowledge. The spiritual friend is the guide across the ocean of wisdom. The spiritual friend is...
Having reached the requisites for the path that leads to omniscience, he then went to the place where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was.
He prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying:
"Noble One, I have already resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how..."
"I am practicing the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Holy One is skilled in providing instruction; I pray that you will speak for me. The Bodhisattva replied, "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you have already been able to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*).

I have already accomplished the liberation door of the bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). By means of this door of the practice of great compassion, I impartially transform and teach all beings."
All sentient beings continue in an uninterrupted succession. Good son, I abide in this gate of the practice of great compassion;

I am constantly present before all Tathāgatas and universally manifest before all sentient beings. (Because [this] is identical to the wondrously enlightened true mind of the Tathāgata, I am constantly present before all Tathāgatas;

because [it] shares the same essence of compassion as sentient beings, I universally manifest before all sentient beings. "Universally manifesting" refers to the manifestation through the Universal Gate. This is identical to attaining the two kinds of excellence as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Or...
They gather in sentient beings through generosity; or they gather them through kind words, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation;
or they gather them by manifesting a physical body; or they gather them by manifesting various inconceivable nets of pure light from their forms;
or they gather them through speech, or through dignified deportment, or by preaching the Dharma.

Sometimes I manifest supernatural transformations to cause their minds to awaken and attain maturity; sometimes I manifest forms identical to their own kind and dwell together with them to bring them to maturity.
Noble son, as I practice this door of the conduct of great compassion, I vow to constantly rescue and protect all sentient beings.
I vow that all sentient beings shall be freed from the fear of perilous paths and the fear of burning afflictions.
They are free from the fear of delusion; free from the fear of bondage; free from the fear of being killed; free from the fear of poverty; free from the fear of inability to subsist;
free from the fear of ill repute; free from the fear of death; free from the fear of the great assembly; free from the fear of the evil realms; and free from the fear of darkness.
They are freed from the fear of death and migration; freed from the fear of separation from loved ones; freed from the fear of encountering enemies;

freed from the fear of physical oppression; freed from the fear of mental oppression; and freed from the fear of sorrow and lamentation. (These eighteen fears comprehensively encompass the six perfections, the four means of integration, the thirty-two manifestations, the seven calamities, and the eight sufferings;

this is a concise text on the summary of saving sentient beings. Furthermore, they make this vow: "May all sentient beings, whether they think of me, invoke my name, or behold my body, all [attain liberation]."

They shall attain liberation from fear. Good son, having used these skillful means to cause all sentient beings to leave behind fear, I further instruct them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never to regress. (To think of me is the mental action; to call my name is the vocal action;

to see my body is the physical action—this means that by taking refuge in my three types of action through one's own three types of action, one can achieve liberation. Furthermore, by instructing them to advance toward the Great Mind, they are finally able to ultimately leave behind the fears of the two deaths. The *Xiyu ji* states:

In South India, in the kingdom of Malakūṭa, there is a mountain called Malaya on the southern coast of the sea. To the east of this mountain is Mount Potalaka. The mountain paths are perilous, with precipitous cliffs and steep ravines. At the summit of the mountain is a pond, its waters as clear as a mirror; from it flows a great river that circles the mountain twenty times before entering the Southern Sea.

Beside the pond is a stone celestial palace, which serves as the dwelling where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara comes and goes. Those who wish to behold the Bodhisattva disregard their own lives and bodies, braving the waters to ascend [the mountain].

The mountain was steep and perilous; those who could reach its summit were indeed few. Yet the inhabitants living at the foot of the mountain prayed with sincere hearts to see him. He would manifest himself in the form of Maheśvara or as an ash-smearing heretic (pāśupata) to console and instruct them, thereby fulfilling their wishes.
○ [Zhī] (pronounced qī; same as qī; meaning "slanted"). *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

(This sūtra teaches the dharma-gate for practicing the Pure Land. It contains sixteen sublime visualizations (*viśuddha-vipaśyanā*) that collectively clarify the adornments of the environment and the inhabitants of the Western Quarter. What is recorded here is the tenth visualization thereof.)
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Having clearly and distinctly beheld the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—(Ānanda means 'Joyous Celebration' in the language of China;

he was the Buddha’s cousin, who personally attended the Tathāgata and was foremost in erudition. Vaidehī means 'Reflection' in the language of China; she was the queen of King Bimbisāra of Magadha and the mother of King Ajātaśatru)—this concludes the ninth visualization, which teaches the contemplation of the marks and signs and the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
Herein, the primary instruction is for the visualization of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Next, one should further visualize the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. This Bodhisattva...
The Buddha’s body was eight hundred thousand *nayuta* *yojanas* in height (one *nayuta* being ten billion; one *yojana* being forty *li*). His body was the color of purple-gold.
He had a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his head, and a halo (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) above his head. Each side of his face measured one thousand *yojanas*. Within that halo...

There were five hundred transformation Buddhas, each identical to Śākyamuni. Each transformation Buddha was attended by five hundred transformation Bodhisattvas and immeasurable devas serving as attendants.
Within the light radiating from their entire bodies appeared the physical forms and characteristics of all sentient beings of the five realms of existence.
All appear therein (since the forms and appearances of sentient beings in the five realms manifest within the Bodhisattva’s light, a single invocation is immediately answered).

Upon his head is a celestial crown made of Vaiḍūrya-maṇi jewels. Within that celestial crown stands an emanation Buddha twenty-five *yojana* high. (In the past, Avalokiteśvara had already attained Buddhahood;

now, through the power of compassionate vows, he acts as a bodhisattva practicing the path of purifying a buddha-field. This represents carrying the merit of past fruition while performing present causal practices. The emanation Buddha upon the crown specifically symbolizes the carrying of fruition. [The Sanskrit for "Śākyavaiḍūrya" is...]

*Ka* (伽) means "able to overcome" in the language of China; *maṇi* (摩尼) means "as one wishes" (*yìrúì*) and is also said to mean "free from defilement. Because of this precious jewel, it can fulfill the heart's desires of sentient beings and is not stained by impurities.

The face of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is like the color of Jāmbūnada gold (*yánfútán*). [Jāmbūnada] means "supreme gold" in the language of China; its color is reddish-yellow, with a trace of purple luster. Between his eyebrows is the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa (the tuft of white hair).
He was endowed with the colors of the seven treasures (gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, agate, and conch shell). From him flowed forth eighty-four thousand kinds of light rays.
Within each light ray were immeasurable and innumerable hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddhas. Each manifested Buddha had innumerable manifested Bodhisattvas as attendants.
They manifested themselves with sovereign mastery, filling the worlds of the ten directions. His arms were the color of red lotuses.
There were eighty billion subtle and wondrous radiances that formed a necklace. Within this necklace, all manner of adornments were universally manifested.
The palms of his hands displayed the colors of five hundred billion variegated lotuses;
on the tips of his ten fingers, each finger-tip had eighty-four thousand lines, like the patterns of a seal, and within each line there were eighty-four thousand [petals].
Regarding his physical form: each and every part of his body emits eighty-four thousand rays of light. These rays are soft and supple, universally illuminating all things.

With this precious hand, he receives and guides sentient beings. When he lifts his foot, beneath his soles there appear the marks of thousand-spoked wheels, which spontaneously transform into five hundred billion towers of radiance. When he sets his foot down, vajra-maṇi flowers are scattered everywhere.

There was nothing that was not completely filled [by the vajra]. The vajra is a solid jewel; all forms and appearances manifest within it, and even stone walls cannot obstruct it. His remaining bodily features were fully endowed with the secondary marks (lakṣaṇa), no different from those of a Buddha.
Only his cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) and the mark of the invisible crown of the head did not equal those of the World-Honored One.
This is the true physical form of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. [The uṣṇīṣa is a mark; the invisible crown is a secondary excellence. These are the marks...]

"Excellent. This manifests the ultimate fruit. Since the Bodhisattva at present still dwells in the stage of the causal ground, he is not yet equal to a Buddha. This is called the Tenth Contemplation. The Buddha told Ānanda:
'If you wish to contemplate the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, you should perform this contemplation. One who performs this contemplation shall not encounter various calamities;

they shall purify their karmic obstructions and eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over incalculable kalpas. Such a Bodhisattva, by merely hearing his name, attains immeasurable [merit].'"

How much more so if one contemplates with focused attention! If there is anyone who wishes to contemplate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they should first contemplate the *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance) upon his head;

next, they should contemplate the celestial crown (*makuṭa*). As for the remaining various marks, they should likewise contemplate them in succession until all are clearly manifest, as if looking at the palm of one's hand.

(Since his physical characteristics are so numerous, it is not clear which should be contemplated first; therefore, he is taught to first contemplate the *uṣṇīṣa* and then the celestial crown. These two serve to specifically represent the virtuous marks of Avalokiteśvara. Why? Because the *uṣṇīṣa* ranks below only that of a Buddha.)

This expresses the causal practice. The presence of the transformed Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) upon the crown signifies the attainment of fruition in the past. If one becomes attached to these specific characteristics, the remaining general characteristics will be easy to understand. The practitioner contemplates the crown, the topknot, the ūrṇā-kośa, the face, the body color, and the radiance, applying the mind with focused attention to each one as they perform the visualization.

By means of this sublime contemplation, one takes the vision of the Buddha as the fundamental basis, transcending all other causes; upon reaching the Pure Land, one immediately realizes the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*);

if one contemplates otherwise, it is called false contemplation (*mithyā-darśana*). (When contemplation accords with the sutra, it is a vision in accordance with the nature of reality and is termed right contemplation; when the perceived signs contradict the sutra, it gives rise to demonic activity and is therefore termed false contemplation. — *Ekādaśamukha-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, because of this mantra, my name is noble and difficult to hear.

If there were one who recited the names of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and another who for a brief moment sincerely recited my name, the merit of these two would be exactly equal. For all those who recite..."
Those who recite my name shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression;
they shall be free from all illnesses, liberated from all obstacles and all terrors, and able to extinguish the evils of body, speech, and mind.

How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the divine mantra spoken by me, practicing according to its instructions—know that such persons are, with respect to unsurpassed bodhi, [already established].

Receiving [the merit] is as if it were held in the palm of one's hand. Reciting the names of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas and reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart for even a brief moment are equal in their merit.

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* state that the merit of upholding the names of sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is no different from upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara. While Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are still vastly inferior when compared to the merit of a single Buddha, these [sutras] now declare them to be equal;
this is truly beyond the scope of the mental capacity of ordinary beings. As stated later in the *Ratnarāja-sūtra*, it is likewise impossible to conceive of through thought.
—From the *Mahāyāna-alaṃkāra-ratnarāja-sūtra* (大乘莊嚴寶王經)

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī: "Good son, if a person were to offer celestial fine garments, as well as saffron robes, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, bedding, and so forth, to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, the merit obtained would not differ in measure from the merit of a single hair-tip of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, it is like [the merit of] the four great continents for one year..."
Within twelve months, if it were to rain heavily day and night without ceasing, I could count every single drop.
Yet, as for the merit possessed by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, I cannot fully describe its measure.
Furthermore, suppose someone were to fashion images of the Tathāgata out of celestial gold, as numerous as motes of dust, and were to make various offerings to them; the merit obtained from that—
I know the full measure of their merit; yet as for the merit possessed by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, I cannot fully describe its quantity.

Even if all the Tathāgatas of other directions were to assemble in one place, they too could not fully describe the quantity of this bodhisattva’s merit. If there is anyone who can call to mind the name of this bodhisattva, they...
When people come to distance themselves from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and saṃsāra, they will swiftly attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—
just as a king of geese flies with the wind— and there they shall behold the Tathāgata Amitāyus face-to-face and hear the sublime Dharma.
Such a person shall never again undergo the sufferings of saṃsāra. They will be free from greed, hatred, and delusion; free from old age, sickness, and death;
and free from the suffering of famine. They shall not experience the pain of birth from a womb, but by the power of the Dharma, they will be born through transformation within a lotus flower.
They dwell perpetually in that land. It is further said: This Bodhisattva can act as a bright lamp for those who are blind and in darkness;
for those scorched by the heat of a mirage, he provides cooling shade; for those parched with thirst, he manifests flowing rivers; in places of fear, he bestows fearlessness;
to those afflicted by the suffering of illness, he provides medicine; and to sentient beings undergoing torment, he acts as a parent—even unto the Avīci hell.
It causes sentient beings in the hells to see the path to nirvāṇa, and enables all sentient beings in the world to obtain these meritorious benefits and peace.

If there is anyone who can establish a four-sided maṇḍala before an image of Avalokiteśvara and constantly make offerings of incense and flowers, that person shall in the future become a Cakravartin Universal Monarch.

He is endowed with the seven treasures, namely: the precious wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who can offer even a single flower to this Bodhisattva, that person shall emit a wondrous fragrance from their body.
In whatever place they are born, they shall attain a perfect physical form. This Bodhisattva transforms—

He manifests in various forms to rescue and deliver countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, causing them to be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), where they behold the Tathāgata Amitāyus and hear the essential teachings of the Dharma; he ensures that they shall all attain the realization of Bodhi.
Although the great Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra possess inconceivable qualities, they are unable to fully comprehend this.

Knowing that this was a manifestation of Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered into the pore of this bodhisattva and traveled there for twelve years without reaching its limit; he saw that within each and every one of the pores, there was a Buddha-division.
He dwells therein; therefore, even Samantabhadra cannot perceive its boundaries or its distance.
How then could other bodhisattvas perceive it? Even the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is difficult to encounter. Why is this?
Because he is like a great parent to all sentient beings, bestowing [protection] upon all sentient beings who are terrified.
Fearless, he guides all sentient beings and acts as a great spiritual friend.
This Bodhisattva possesses a six-syllable vidyā-mantra that is difficult to encounter.

If there is anyone who can recite its name, they shall be born within his pores, never again to suffer in the depths of saṃsāra, until they eventually realize the state of parinirvāṇa. This six-syllable mantra...
Nī. This is the subtle, essential heart-mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. If there is one who knows this subtle, essential heart-mind, they immediately know liberation.
Even the infinite Tathāgatas find it difficult to know; how then could a Bodhisattva at the stage of cause (hetu-bhūmi) be able to know it?
If a person can constantly receive and uphold this dhāraṇī, then at the time of recitation, there are ninety...
An assembly of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers gathered; furthermore, an assembly of Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust gathered;

moreover, the sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also all gathered. Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings, and even countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings, came to protect this person. At that time, within the pores of the Bodhisattva’s body, there was no...
The Tathāgata measured and praised this person, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have been able to obtain this wish-fulfilling jewel;
your lineage for seven generations shall all attain liberation. As for the mantra-holder, all the worms within his belly shall attain the stage of an irreversible Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if there be another person who, with this dhāraṇī, [uses it] upon their body..."

Regarding the one who wears it upon the crown of the head: if anyone should see this person wearing it, they will see them as if seeing the body of Vajra, or as if seeing a stūpa of relics, or as if seeing the Buddha, or as if seeing one hundred million wise persons.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who can recite this dhāraṇī according to the Dharma, this is...
Such a person attains inexhaustible eloquence, attains a mass of pure wisdom, and attains great compassion.

Day by day, they attain the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās* and perfect all merits. Furthermore, even those who merely wear or carry [this teaching] shall see all men, women, and sentient beings, and they shall all swiftly attain the rank of a Bodhisattva. Such a person—
One shall forever be free from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and separation from the beloved.

If one recites this *dhāraṇī* even once, the merit obtained would be such that its quantity could not be calculated. Furthermore, suppose all men and women throughout the four great continents were to attain the stage of a Bodhisattva of the seventh ground;
the merit possessed by all those Bodhisattvas [would be surpassed by the merit of] reciting [this *dhāraṇī*] six times.

The merit of reciting the six-syllable mantra even once is no different [from other practices]. Furthermore, there are immeasurable merits; one should examine the text of that sūtra. If there are those who recite it, they must act according to the ritual rules and ensure their pronunciation is pure and correct.

Those who wear it upon themselves must also revere it as if it were the Buddha, believing in it without doubt; only then can they receive its benefits. If one harbors doubts or lacks faith, one will instead incur transgressions and faults. As for the six-syllable mantra, it may be understood as usual. Regarding the maṇḍala:
This is the altar itself.
Regarding the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to Eliminate and Subdue Poisonous Harm*:

At that time, there was the kingdom of Vaiśālī (in the language of China, "Extensive, Majestic, and Pure"). Among the more than thirty kingdoms in Central India, this is one of them. It is called "Extensive" because the country is broad and level; its cities and towns are magnificent and beautiful.

Therefore, it is named "Adorned and Pure" (Yanjing), or alternatively called "Delighting in the Way" (Haodao). This is because the people of that land delight in the True Way; they naturally cultivate benevolence and righteousness and require no sovereign ruler. Five hundred elders together practice the Dharma, and among all the people throughout the land, there are none who do not turn toward it with joy and devotion.

Therefore, the subsequent text says: "It was these five hundred elders. All the people encountered a great and malignant disease: first, their eyes became red as blood; second, pus flowed from both ears;
third, blood flowed from their nostrils; fourth, their tongues were locked and they could not speak;
fifth, whatever food they ate turned into coarse and gritty matter; and sixth, their consciousness was obstructed, like that of a drunken man. There were five yakṣas named...
Kinnakāla had a face black as ink and possessed five eyes; his canine teeth protruded upward, and he sucked the vital essence from humans. (The *Pumen shu* states:
"In the human heart there are seven drops of sweet water that nourish the spirit. If a ghost devours one drop, it causes a headache; three drops cause fainting; seven drops result in death.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Candracchattra, who, together with five hundred other elders of his kind, [set out].

They all went together to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, the people of this country have encountered a great and malignant plague. Even the skilled physician Jīvaka has exhausted his medical arts, yet he is unable to save them.

We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will rescue them from the suffering of illness and cause them to be free from affliction. (Jīvaka means "one who can bring life.")

This king was the son of King Chāyā-dṛḍha and born of Queen Nāḍī. Immediately upon emerging from the womb, he held a needle-case and a pouch of medicine in his hands and became a king of physicians for the world. Just as the Buddha is the Dharma-king, those who encounter him are healed of their ailments; therefore, he is called a "skilled physician.

Since the King of Physicians has exhausted all his arts, none others are capable [of such healing]; thus they have come together to seek refuge in the Dharma-king. At that time, the World-Honored One said to the elder:

"Not far from here, standing directly to the west, is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Amitāyus" (the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: "Passing from here through a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī").
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha; speaking in terms of buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust, it is said to be not far from here.
There are two bodhisattvas there named Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who constantly, with great compassion, take pity on all beings and rescue them from suffering and distress.

You should now prostrate yourself with your five limbs (the crown of the head, the two hands, and the two knees) toward him, burn incense, scatter flowers, and focus your mindfulness while counting your breaths.
To prevent the mind from scattering, for the duration of ten recitations, one should, for the sake of sentient beings, invoke that Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas.

"Fixing the mindfulness" means to collect the mind so it does not scatter; because the mind has no other object of reliance, one causes it to count the breaths. "Counting the breaths" means to focus the mind on the nostrils, counting either the exhalations or the inhalations from one to ten, beginning again once the cycle is complete.

Taking ten breaths as one recitation and one hundred breaths as ten recitations, one ensures the breath is harmonious—neither too slow nor too fast—so that the mind naturally becomes tranquil and settled. This serves as the expedient means for the invocation. As it is said: "When the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the moon of the Buddha appears within its reflection. For what reason, then, is this specifically enjoined?

Ten recitations: this is because it is difficult for the minds of sentient beings to maintain focus, as they quickly become distracted and agitated over a long duration. To the left of that Buddha is Avalokiteśvara, and to his right is Mahāsthāmaprāpta; thus, they are called the two Bodhisattvas.
While these words were being spoken, within the Buddha’s light, one was able to see the Buddha of Infinite Life in the West, together with the two Bodhisattvas.

Through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas both arrived in this land and went to Vaiśālī, where they stood at the threshold of the city gate. The Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas—
Sā. Together with the great assembly, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated Vaiśālī, turning it entirely golden.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī prepared willow twigs and pure water and offered them to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Out of compassion to protect and deliver all sentient beings, the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara spoke this mantra, universally instructing all sentient beings: [Mantra follows]
And they spoke these words: "You all should now with one mind recite: 'Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Sangha!
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, of great compassion and great renown, the protector and savior from suffering and distress.
Thus, recite the names of the Triple Gem three times and the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara three times, while burning various kinds of incense."

Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground toward the western direction, with single-minded concentration and regulated breath, he invoked Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to escape suffering and calamity.
Joining his ten fingers and palms together, he spoke this verse (the joining of the two sides of the palms to make one signifies that body and mind are unified;
only then does he orally recite the verse of invocation, which manifests the utmost sincerity and reverence of the three karmas).
I pray that you rescue me from suffering and distress; With great compassion, you cover all beings. Universally emitting pure light, you extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
To free us from the pain of poisonous harm, May afflictions and all manner of diseases surely come to my place;
Grant me great peace and bliss— I now prostrate myself before you in homage.
I now take refuge in the one whose name, when heard, rescues from calamity.
O Father of Compassion in the World, I pray that you will surely come, To free me from the suffering of the three poisons And bestow upon me the happiness of this life as well as Great Nirvāṇa.

(The Dharmakāya is like space: it is all-pervasive, reaching everywhere, and utterly transcends coming and going. That he now surely comes is because the water of the sentient beings' minds has become pure; thus the Buddha...)

The moon appears of its own accord; therefore, it is said that it "comes. The three poisons are greed, hatred, and delusion. These are the cause of all suffering and the source of myriad afflictions. To cause the cause to perish so that the effect is lost, and for the source to be cut off so that the branches are removed, it is said that one is "freed.

Present-world happiness is the fruit of happiness within the world, while *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of happiness that transcends the world. "Great" distinguishes this from the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, such a divine mantra is definitively auspicious; it belongs to the past, the present, and the future..."

This is the Great Compassionate Dharani Seal of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. Those who hear this mantra shall have all their sufferings forever exhausted and shall always attain peace and happiness.
They shall remain far removed from the eight difficulties and attain the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, seeing the Buddha before them.

I shall now proclaim the divine mantra for the protection and salvation of sentient beings by the Buddhas of the ten directions. (The eight difficulties are: first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghost realm; fourth, blindness, deafness, and muteness; fifth...)
Those who possess worldly wisdom and eloquence; those born six times before or after a Buddha;
those in Uttarakuru; and those in the Heaven of Non-conception). Tadyathā: mūhe mūhe dūbhe dambhe antali pantali śubhade bambhaṇarāvaśe.

Viśvāvi | Rakṣa rakṣa | Sarvasattvān svāhā. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this divine mantra is that of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time."
As it has been proclaimed: those who recite and uphold this mantra shall always be protected and sustained by all Buddhas and all great Bodhisattvas;
they shall be freed from fear, weapons, staves, poison, harm, and disease, and shall be rendered free from affliction. When these words were spoken,

The people of Vaiśālī were restored to their original state. At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and to protect all, again requested the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to preach the mantra for subduing and eliminating poisonous harms.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, with great compassion permeating his heart and sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, spoke this *dhāraṇī* for destroying evil karmic obstructions and subduing poisonous harms.
Nun’s Incantation:
Namo buddhāya. Namo dharmāya. Namo saṃghāya. Namo Avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya.
May you, out of great kindness and great compassion, take pity on me.
Protecting those in suffering and distress, and likewise protecting all sentient beings from fear, may they obtain great protection.
Tadyathā: dhauṇi | mauṇi | dūpaṇi | daṃbaṇi | apakṣimauñji | bhaṃḍāli | paṃḍāli | śubhite. (The character *vī* follows.)
Bhaṇḍāra bhasini hulu hulu bhaṇḍali durlu durlu bhaṇḍali cūlu cūlu nibhaṇḍali dhudhu dhudhu bhaṇḍāra bhasini śṛṅgi ṭiṭṭibhi nibhaṇḍali.
Cenchī! Sarva-ābhaya-kṛta! Sarva-haṃbha! Sthāgābhaya! Vīrita-vetana-svāhā!
All fears, all poisons and harms, and all evil spirits, tigers, wolves, and lions—upon hearing this mantra, [they shall be pacified].
The mouth will immediately be closed and obstructed, rendering them unable to cause harm.

Those who have violated the practice of Brahma-conduct and committed the ten unwholesome karmas will, upon hearing this mantra, be cleansed of their filth and impurities and restored to purity (the "filth and impurities" refers to the ten unwholesome karmas).

Even if one possesses karmic obstructions, turbid evils, or unwholesome states, by invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and reciting and upholding this mantra, one will immediately shatter those karmic obstructions and manifestly behold the Buddha. The Buddha told Ānanda:

It is difficult [to encounter]. If there are disciples of the fourfold assembly who uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and recite the *Dhāraṇī for Eliminating and Subduing Poisonous Harm*, those who practice this mantra shall have no afflictions of body and no ailments of mind.

Even if a great fire should come from the four directions to burn their bodies, because they recite and uphold this mantra, the Dragon King will send down rain, and they shall immediately be liberated.

[One shall be] liberated. Even if fire burns the body and every joint is in agony, if one single-mindedly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and chants this mantra three times, one will immediately be healed.
Furthermore, even if there is famine due to high grain prices, danger from kings, wild beasts, thieves, or bandits;
if one is lost on the road, imprisoned in a jail, bound by shackles, manacles, or the pillory; or if one has entered the great ocean or the black [hell],...
In the midst of whirlwinds and surging waves, amidst mountains of shifting waters, facing the perils of yakṣas and rākṣasas, poisoned drugs, swords, and blades, or when about to be executed—
due to past karmic conditions and the various evils committed in the present— one shall experience all manner of suffering and extreme terror. At such times,
one should single-mindedly invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and recite this mantra once, up to [ten times].

Seven times [this shall be done]. It will eliminate and subdue poison, harm, evil karma, evil conduct, and the accumulation of unwholesome and evil deeds, just as fire consumes wood until nothing remains.
For this reason, reciting this divine mantra spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is called "Bestowing upon All Sentient Beings the Wondrous Medicine of Ambrosia.
By it, one attains freedom from the fear of illness, the fear of untimely death, and the fear of being bound.
It is because of the fear of the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—that all in the Sahā world call the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara the Bestower of Fearlessness.
This dharani, this consecrated chapter, is the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya).
This is the ocean of great merit, certain and auspicious. Any sentient being who hears it shall obtain great and wholesome benefit. It should be recited silently.
If one wishes to recite it, one should observe the fast (*upavāsa*), refrain from drinking alcohol, and abstain from eating meat.

One should smear the body with ashes and bathe until pure. One must not eat asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) or the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). All strong-smelling, savory foods are forbidden to eat. (Asafoetida comes from foreign lands; its root resembles a radish, and its leaves resemble turnip.)

Furthermore, there are none [who may partake]. The five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garika*) are: first, onion; second, leek; third, garlic; fourth, shallot; and fifth, *hingukhāra* (asafoetida). Consuming these incurs many faults and transgressions. The noble ones and sages distance themselves from them; the devas do not protect those who eat them, and demons and malevolent spirits find an opportunity to harm them. Any mantra-dharmas one maintains or any *samādhi* one cultivates will all fail to achieve success.

What is called "foul-smelling" refers to any substance that is both pungent and malodorous. Regarding "smearing the body with ash": this means first using substances such as ash or cleansing beans (*snāna-kalka*) to rub away the filth and grease of the body, and subsequently washing it with water to make it clean, so that one may then become a fit vessel for the Way.
Women who are defiled by menstruation must not approach at all. One should constantly keep in mind the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
If one single-mindedly invokes Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and recites this dhāraṇī, one shall behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in person.
All virtuous aspirations will be fulfilled, and in a future life, one will be born before a Buddha, forever parting from suffering. (Regarding the "ten directions":

if spoken of collectively, they comprise the Buddhas of all lands throughout the dust-motes of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, who are too numerous to enumerate. If spoken of specifically, they are briefly extracted from the *Great Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Vimalamati Paying Homage to the Buddha*, and various other scriptures.)

...one should, according to whichever one [is appropriate], pay homage and recollect them. As for the Seven Buddhas: the first is Vipaśyin Buddha, and the last is our Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha; these may be understood as usual.

"To be born after the Buddhas" means that after casting off this body, one is reborn in the lands of the various Buddhas according to one's vows, completely transcending saṃsāra and reaching the stage of non-retrogression; hence it is said, "to be forever parted from suffering. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a woman possessed by an evil spirit named Caṇḍālī. That spirit, day and night, assumed the form of a man and came..."
"She was tormented by this female spirit, who possessed her body and gave birth to five hundred ghost-children. Do you remember this matter?
At that time, I instructed this woman to invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; through the continuity of her virtuous mind, she entered a state of goodness.
Ānanda, you should know that by the majestic spiritual power of such a Bodhisattva, evil spirits are subdued and one attains the vision of my own body."

Regarding "unparalleled physical form" (the Tathāgata’s body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; it is the color of purple-polished gold, radiating brilliant light, such that none in heaven or on earth can equal it; hence it is called "unparalleled physical form").

If one speaks of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is without marks and cannot be seen by ordinary beings; only Bodhisattvas of wondrous enlightenment can know it. At that time, from each and every pore of my body, there issued forth precious lotus flowers.

Upon them, countless transformation Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, praised the Great Compassionate One who bestows fearlessness, causing the woman to receive, uphold, read, and recite this mantra until she mastered it.
Through the merit of this mantra, her three obstructions will be forever exhausted, and she shall escape the fires of the prison of the triple world.

They undergo manifold sufferings. The four hundred and four diseases do not arise simultaneously. (The three obstructions are: the obstruction of afflictions, the obstruction of karma, and the obstruction of retribution. The three realms are: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.

All sentient beings are constantly scorched by the fires of the three poisons and the five desires; bound and fettered, they cannot escape. They transmigrate through the three realms, oppressed by manifold sufferings more severe than those in a prison. Regarding the four hundred and four diseases: earth, water, fire, and wind each have one hundred and ten.

By the merit of this mantra, the three obstructions are completely eliminated and one escapes from the prison of the three realms; how much more so will the various sufferings of disease be instantly extinguished? Below this is the text of the World-Honored One’s own recitation of the six-syllable divine mantra.)
[Many [details] are not recorded]. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

The one of great compassion and great renown, The person of auspiciousness, peace, and bliss, Who constantly utters auspicious words To rescue those in extreme suffering— If sentient beings hear his name, They shall leave suffering behind and attain liberation.
They also sport within the hells, taking upon themselves suffering out of great compassion;
or, dwelling among animals, they manifest in animal forms to teach them with great wisdom and cause them to resolve upon the Unsurpassed Mind.
Or, dwelling among asuras, they subdue their minds with gentle words, causing them to eliminate the habit of arrogance.
Swiftly reaching the shore of the unconditioned, he manifests his body as a hungry ghost;
for those tormented by hunger and thirst, milk of fragrant color issues from his hands, which he bestows so they may be fully satiated.
With a mind of great kindness and great compassion, he sports within the five realms of existence, constantly employing well-accumulated wisdom and unsurpassed, supreme skillful means.
Universally teaching all beings, Causing them to leave behind the suffering of birth and death, May they always attain a place of peace and bliss, Reaching the shore of Great Nirvana.

(The five paths refer to humans, animals, hells, asuras, and hungry ghosts. Heaven is not mentioned here because celestial beings are addicted to sensual pleasures and do not seek liberation from suffering; therefore, it is not mentioned.
From the *Compassionate Forest Collection of Avalokiteśvara*, Volume One.
