Part Two: Responsive Manifestations, Section One.

In the past, in the kingdom of Tsau-ku-ta (Jāguḍa) in India, there was a great merchant leader who worshipped celestial deities and sought blessings and merit through sacrifices, while holding the Buddha in contempt.
He did not believe in cause and effect. Later, leading a caravan of merchants, he traveled across the South Sea to exchange goods for profit.

He encountered a storm and lost his way; tossed by the waves and drifting on the billows, three years passed. His provisions were exhausted and he could not even sustain himself. Those on the same ship had no hope for the morrow.
United in their efforts and shared purpose, they called upon the deity they served. Their minds were weary with anxiety, and in the darkness...
Their efforts were in vain. Suddenly they saw a great mountain with lofty cliffs and steep peaks; two suns appeared together, shining with double brilliance and clarity.
At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying, "We are fortunate to have encountered this great mountain; we should halt here and find peace and security.
The leader of the merchants said, "This is not a mountain; it is a makara fish. Those lofty cliffs and steep peaks are its fins and gills."

...as well. For two days the sun shone with double brilliance; this was the light of their eyes. Before the sounds of their voices had subsided, the sails of their boats drifted away into the distance.
Thereupon, the merchant leader addressed his companions, saying: "I have heard that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is able to bestow peace and happiness upon those in peril and distress.

We should each, with utmost sincerity, invoke his name. They then immediately chanted together in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name. Once the towering mountains had vanished from sight, the two...
The sun also set. Suddenly, a śramaṇa was seen; his deportment was dignified and orderly, and he approached, his *khakkhara* staff soaring through the air to rescue those drowning.

Before long, he had arrived back in his native land. Thereupon, his faith became firm and steadfast; seeking merit without turning back, he erected a stūpa (a *stūpa* is a pagoda; "liù" is pronounced like "liù," meaning to join forces; "mójié" refers to the makara, a sea monster;

"qí" is pronounced like "qí," and "liè" is pronounced like "liè"—the small fins along the sides of the fish's neck are all... and performed offerings in accordance with the ritual. ... (The *stūpa* is a pagoda. "Liù" is pronounced like "liù," meaning to exert effort together. "Mójié" is the makara. "Qí" is pronounced like "qí"; "liè" is pronounced like "liè. ... the small fins along the sides of the fish's neck are all...
It is called Lian (the "Zhen" in *Qin* being pronounced as *zhēn*).
Regarding the sacred image of Mount Gu:
from the Kāpuṭa Monastery in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India, traveling two or three *li* to the south, one reaches Mount Gu. Its...
The mountains are lofty and steep, and the forests are lush and verdant. Famous flowers and clear streams cover the cliffs and pour into the ravines.
Above, there are many monasteries and spirit temples, all executed with the utmost skill in carving and engraving. In the central monastery is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara;

although its physical dimensions are small, its majestic spirit inspires profound reverence. The Bodhisattva holds a lotus flower in his hand and wears a Buddha image upon his crown. There are always several people who practice fasting here.
One must focus the mind and seek to see the Bodhisattva for seven days, fourteen days, or even up to one month.

Those who possess such karmic resonance will behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, adorned with wondrous marks and radiant with majestic splendor, emerging from within the image to comfort and console them.
Formerly, the King of Siṃhala in the Southern Sea looked at his face in a mirror at dawn and did not see his own body. Thereupon—
He beheld a small mountain within the Tāla Grove in the kingdom of Magadha on Jambudvīpa, upon which stood this image of the Bodhisattva.
The King was deeply moved with joy and sought to have it replicated. Having arrived at this mountain, he found it was indeed a perfect likeness; consequently, he constructed a vihāra there.
They offered various forms of worship. Thereafter, successive kings, still admiring his legacy, established monasteries (*vihāra*) and shrines at the site;

offerings of incense, flowers, and music continued without ceasing. (The term *gālan* refers to a monastery. *Ji* is pronounced like "ji" [in "chicken"]; *jue* is the same as *jue*, pronounced like "jue. *Ji-jue* refers to carving, engraving, and sculpting. Master Qingbian...
In the southern Indian kingdom of Andhra, not far from the city, there is a great mountain cliff where the master of treatises Bhāviveka resided.
This was the place where he awaited the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood. The master possessed a noble and vast magnanimity and profound, ultimate virtue;
outwardly he wore the robes of a Sāṃkhya, yet inwardly he propagated the teachings of Nāgārjuna. He dwelt in quiet contemplation.

He said, "If not Maitreya attaining Buddhahood, who shall resolve my doubts? Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Svacittadhāraṇī*, abstaining from grain and drinking only water for a period of three years.

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifested a body of wondrous color and addressed the Master of Treatises, saying, "What is your aspiration? He replied, "I wish to remain in this body until I behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara...
The Bodhisattva Svatantra said, "Human life is precarious and fragile; the world is floating and illusory. One should cultivate supreme goodness and aspire to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
There, by paying homage and visiting [the Buddha], one may yet quickly behold him. The Master of Treatises said, "One's resolve must not be shaken, and the mind must not be divided.
The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, you should go to the southern mountain cliff of the city of Mahānanda in the country of Āndhra and take hold [of the teaching]."
"At the abode of the Vajra Deity, whoever recites and upholds the Vajrapāṇi Dhāraṇī with utmost sincerity shall have their vows fulfilled.
Thereupon, the Master went there and recited it. After three years, the deity said to him, "What is your wish? Why do you exert yourself so diligently?
The Master replied, "I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva pointed [to the way].

"I have sent you here to request [this favor]. That which shall fulfill my vow must lie with the deity. The deity then bestowed the method upon him and said, "Within this rocky cliff lies the palace of an asura.
If you perform the invocation according to the rite, the stone wall shall open; once it opens, enter within."

"You may wait to see it. The Master of Treatises said, "Dwelling in seclusion, I have nothing to behold; how could I know when a Buddha would appear? The spirit said, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you.
Having received this command, the Master applied himself with single-minded devotion to recitation and upholding [the scriptures]. After another three years had passed, he harbored no other thoughts.
He took mustard seeds and struck them against a stone wall, which opened wide and clear. At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of people beheld it.
He forgot to return home. The Master of Treatises (Śāstrin) stepped across his threshold and addressed the assembly, saying: "I have long prayed and waited to behold Maitreya.
Now that the holy spirit has granted its protection and my great vow is fulfilled, you should enter here together to witness the Buddha’s emergence.

Those who heard this were struck with terror and none dared to set foot upon the threshold, deeming it a den of venomous snakes and fearing for their lives. Though he spoke to them repeatedly, there were only six [who followed].
The man entered. The Master of Śāstras looked back and took leave of the assembly, then entered with composed grace. Once he had gone inside, the stone wall closed back together.
The assembly all lamented and sighed in regret, grieving over the error of their previous words. (Asura; formerly translated as *Āśura*. Maitreya; that is, Mili. Nāgārjuna;
formerly translated as Longshu. Tuṣita Heaven; formerly translated as Doushuaitian.)
King Jyotiṣka, King Jyotiṣka—this was the king of Kanyākubja in Central India. His eldest son was named Rājyavardhana;
his second son was named Harṣavardhana. Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne and governed with virtue, yet he was attacked by King Candrāditya of Suvarṇakuṇḍa.

The ministers, officials, and commoners offered encouragement and their joy increased. He was able to reconcile with his enemy. The prince said, "The gravity of the state succession has been difficult throughout antiquity and the present;

the establishment of the position of a sovereign must be deliberated with care. Now, on the banks of the Ganges, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara which possesses many miraculous responses.
I wish to go and request [the deity's] counsel. He then went before the Bodhisattva’s image and abstained from food.
He offered a prayer. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek? Why are you so earnest? The prince replied, "I have accumulated only calamities:
my compassionate father has passed away, I am now subject to this cruel punishment, and my benevolent elder brother has been slain.

Reflecting on my own lack of virtue, the people of the land have honored me and commanded me to succeed to the great throne to illuminate my father’s legacy. In my folly and ignorance at that time, I dared—"
"I hope for the Sage’s instruction. The Bodhisattva said: "In a previous life, you were an aranyaka bhikṣu in this very forest, practicing with diligent and tireless effort.
By the power of this merit, you have become this prince. Since King Golden-Ears has destroyed the Buddha-Dharma, once you succeed to the throne, you ought to restore it to its former glory.
Let compassion be your resolve and pity dwell within your heart; before long, [you shall achieve this]."
The King ruled over the territories of the Five Indias. Desiring to prolong his national destiny, he followed my instructions;
thus, divine blessings were bestowed upon him, and he had no powerful enemies in the neighboring states. He did not ascend the lion throne, nor did he assume the title of Great King.

Having received these teachings, he withdrew and immediately succeeded to the royal position, styling himself Prince and taking the name Śīlāditya (translated into Chinese as *Jièrì*, or "Sun of Precepts"). He devoted himself to the practice of frugality and moderation.
He cultivated merit and performed virtuous deeds, forgetting both sleep and food. He caused the five regions of India to abstain from eating meat;
if anyone took life, they were executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges River, he erected several thousand stūpas, each over a hundred feet high.
In the cities, towns, villages, alleys, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established monastic dwellings and stored food and drink.
He established medical facilities and provided for the hungry and the poor, distributing aid exhaustively without weariness. At sites of sacred traces, he constructed monasteries (*saṃghārāma*).

Every five years, he convened a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*paṃcavārṣika-mahāpariṣad*), emptying the treasuries to bestow gifts upon all living beings; however, he retained his weapons and did not offer them as alms.
Once a year, śramaṇas from various kingdoms would assemble, and for twenty-one days, they were provided with the four requisites.

He nurtured them, causing each to debate and deliberate with one another, to evaluate their relative merits, to praise the virtuous and censure the wicked, and to demote the obscure while promoting the enlightened.
If one’s observance of the precepts was steadfast and their moral cultivation profound, he would recommend them for the Lion’s Seat, where the King would personally receive the Dharma from them.

Even if one’s discipline was pure, if they lacked learning in the ancient traditions, he would merely offer them respectful salutations to demonstrate his esteem. As for those whose monastic regulations were disordered and whose conduct was defiled—

[The King] drove [the heretics] out of the national borders, unwilling even to hear or see them. The neighboring minor king and his ministerial aides cultivated merit without slackening and sought the good with tireless effort.
They immediately took him as their companion and called him a "virtuous friend. They divided the day into three periods: in one period they managed affairs and governed the state;
in two periods they cultivated merit and practiced goodness, striving diligently without weariness, as if the day were never enough. At that time, in the Tang...
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang arrived there at the invitation of King Śīlāditya to receive the precepts. (The above four items are from the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*.
Gaṅgā River; formerly called the Ganges.
Guṇavarma Tripiṭaka Master.
Guṇabhadra—translated here as Guṇabhadra (Virtuous Merit)—was a native of Central India. He was single-mindedly dedicated to his studies and possessed a profound mastery of the Tripiṭaka.

In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he arrived in Guangzhou. Wei Lang, the Regional Inspector, reported his arrival to the throne. Emperor Wu, the founder of the Song, dispatched a messenger to welcome him.
Upon reaching the capital, the Emperor conversed with him, greeting him with the joy of two travelers meeting under a roadside tree. Initially, he resided at the Jetavana Monastery.
Later, when Prince Xiao was stationed in Jingzhou, he invited Guṇabhadra to accompany him. Guṇabhadra settled at Xin Temple.
The Prince wished to request that he translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures, but Guṇabhadra reflected that his proficiency in the Song language was not yet sufficient;

feeling ashamed and sighing deeply, he immediately performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening, invoking Avalokiteśvara and praying for a hidden response. Consequently, he dreamed of a person dressed in white, holding a sword and carrying another man on their shoulders.
A head came before him and asked, "For what reason are you grieving? Bhadra related the matter in detail. The head replied, "There is no need for grief.
It then exchanged heads with him using a sword, replacing his own head with the new one. It told him to turn around and asked, "Is there no pain? He replied:
He felt no pain; suddenly he awoke, his mind and spirit filled with joy. When he rose in the morning, he discussed the meaning [of the scriptures] and fully mastered the Song dialect.
Thereupon, he proceeded to lecture. Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, Prince Xiao of Qiao plotted treason. Guṇabhadra wept and said, "I, a poor monk, cannot permit myself to accompany you.
However, because the Prince was one whom the public trusted, he coerced him into going down with him. Upon reaching the defeat at Liangshan, [the disaster was great].
The ship turned and pressed closer; it was now far from the shore, and he judged that there was no way to escape with his life.

With single-minded devotion, he invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara, grasped a bamboo staff in his hand, and threw himself into the river. The water reached only to his knees; as he prodded the water with his staff, the current became deep and swift.
He saw a young boy arrive behind him, who took hold of him by the hand. Looking back at the boy, he said, "You are but a small child; how can you save me?"

In a daze, I felt myself walk some ten or more paces and had already reached the shore. I immediately removed my patched robe, intending to reward the youth, but looking about, he was nowhere to be seen.
My hair stood on end; only then did I realize it was due to his supernatural power. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Dharma Garden*).
Honored title: Tripitaka Master.
The Tripiṭaka Master Nalandiyayaśas—whose name in the language of China is Zuncheng—was a native of Udyāna in Northern India.

At the age of seventeen, he resolved to leave the household life; soon thereafter, he encountered a renowned teacher, from whom he heard the complete and correct teachings. Having done so, he set out on his travels to distant lands.
While traveling to convert those in the north of the Snowy Mountains, he reached a precipitous summit where he saw two paths: one for humans and one for ghosts.

The human path was desolate and perilous, while the ghostly path was smooth and easy to traverse. Travelers, their minds confused, mostly sought the ghostly path; as they gradually entered its territory, they were immediately met with slaughter.
In the past, there was a sage king who erected a stone image of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa at the head of a road, with its finger pointing out the way for people.
He was accompanied by a fellow monk who mistakenly entered a path leading to ghosts. Yaśas, having realized this, recited the divine mantra of Avalokiteśvara.

He caught up with him after a hundred paces, but [the monk] had already been harmed by the ghosts; Yaśas himself, through the power of his mantra, escaped this calamity. Continuing forward, he encountered another...

The mountain bandits focused their minds on the aforementioned mantra and were immediately protected by its spiritual power. When the bandits came to attack them, they could not see [the monks] even when looking directly at them.
The bandits followed the road toward the east and fled far into the territory of Qi. In the seventh year of the Tianbao era, [the monks] arrived at the capital.
The Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta—“Dharmagupta” meaning “Dharma-secrecy” in the language of Han—was originally a native of the country of Lāḍha in South India.
With his mind set on traveling abroad, he traveled with six companions. From a merchant, he heard of the Great Country of China and its Three Jewels.

The kingdom was flourishing. My companions and I, with one mind and resolute intent, came here not merely to observe its customs and transformations, but with the aspiration to benefit sentient beings and propagate the sutras.

We then crossed the Snow Mountains, where we encountered hardships; seeking refuge, we turned toward the southwest. The road consisted entirely of sand and gravel, and both water and grass were utterly lacking.

The companions looked at one another; their lives had no place to turn. They then temporarily set aside the sutras and treatises they carried by the side of the road and crossed the mountains in search of water, hoping thereby to survive.
When their search proved fruitless, their exhaustion and distress increased all the more, so they devoted themselves solely to reciting the mantra of Avalokiteśvara.
A night rain suddenly fell. His body and mind were filled with joy. He soon retraced his steps, but looking around in all directions, he was utterly bewildered; the path was lost.
Hesitating whether to advance or retreat, he simply continued forward and eventually reached Jawzhou (Jiaozhou).

Having traveled on foot for many years, he arrived at this superior land in the tenth month of winter in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era. (The two preceding entries are from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang*. "Zhina" refers to the country of Tang.)

Amoghavajra, the Dharma Master Amoghavajra, was originally a Brahmin from Northern India. While traveling by ship toward the South Sea, he reached the borders of the kingdom of Ho-ling when he encountered a great black wind.
The merchants were struck with terror, and each performed the rites of his own country to avert the calamity, but to no avail. All...
They prostrated themselves in supplication, entreating him for protection. Guṇabhadra said, "I now possess a dharma; you need not worry.
He then took a five-pronged bodhicitta vajra in his right hand and held a case containing the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in his left.

Reciting the Avalokiteśvara Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī once, the wind immediately subsided and the sea became calm. Furthermore, they encountered a great whale emerging from the water, its spouting waves like mountains.
The calamity was even more severe than before. The merchants were willing to surrender their lives and performed the same rites as previously.
They had Hui-bian (also known as Bian) recite the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*, and all the difficulties were simultaneously extinguished.
The Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha was originally a native of Central India. At that time, there was a great drought in Central India, so they requested Śubhakarasiṃha to pray for rain.
Suddenly, they saw Avalokiteśvara within a solar disc, holding a *kuṇḍikā* (water flask) in his hand and pouring water onto the ground. At that moment...

The assembly was filled with joy and moved by emotion; they had never before experienced such a thing. (In India, formerly called Tianzhu [India]; *kundī*, which is a pure water flask. The above two entries are from the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*.
Liu Sahuo of the Jin-Qin period.
Liu Sahuo of Bingzhou made his living as a hunter. In the second year of the Taikang era, he died suddenly.
He saw two men leading him toward the northwest until they arrived at hell, where he beheld a golden-hued holy being. Those around him said this was the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
He rebuked him, saying: "Your transgressions merit entry into hell; now you are released and sent back.

You should go to five places—Luoyang, Linzi, Jianye, Muzhou, and Chengdu—and wherever there is a stupa of King Aśoka, prostrate yourself and repent. (Later, he left the household life and was named Huida; this is recorded in the *Tongji*). — Shi Huigian.
Dharma Master Huìqián’s secular surname was Huángfù, and he was a native of Beidi. He left home to become a monk in his youth and strictly observed the precepts;
his resolve and conduct were firm and resolute. He resided at Mount Lú for over ten years, and at the beginning of the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty, he went to Jiāxiáng Temple in Shānyīn.
There, he disciplined himself to guide others and exerted his body to lead the community. All the new scriptures [he encountered] were transcribed and expounded by him. He delved into...
After serving for five years, she suddenly fell ill. Having been bedridden for a short time, she knew in her heart that her life would surely end.

She then focused her thoughts on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and prayed with sincere devotion to Avalokiteśvara. At North Temple in Shanyin, there was a nun named Jingyan, who possessed long-standing virtue and pure preceptual conduct.

One night, she dreamed of Avalokiteśvara entering through the western city gate; his radiant and wondrous form surpassed the light of the sun and moon, and his banners, streamers, and flowered canopies were all [splendid].
It was adorned with the seven treasures. Upon seeing it, he prostrated himself and asked, "I wonder, Great Being, where are you going now?

He replied, "I am going to Jiexiang Temple to welcome Master Qian. Thereupon, he passed away. At that time, although his illness was severe and chronic, his countenance remained calm and composed, as if it were an ordinary day.
Everyone smelled a wondrous fragrance, which only ceased after a long while. Since Master Qian had already realized for himself that his end was certain...
At the end, auspicious signs were observed; both monastics and laypeople who heard of or witnessed them all felt joy and admiration.
Zhu Fachun, also known as Zhu Fachun, was the abbot of Xianyi Temple in Shanyin. He was a man of virtuous ascetic practice and was skilled at reciting the ancient *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
During the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty, while traveling to Langu on business to procure timber for the restoration of a temple, he returned at dusk.
Encountering a storm upon the lake, his boat was small; yet Zhiqian relied single-mindedly upon Avalokiteśvara, reciting the name without ceasing. Suddenly, he saw a large floating vessel.
By boarding it, they were saved. Upon reaching the shore, the boat was without a master; in an instant, it vanished from sight. Both monastics and laypeople marveled at this divine response.

Shi Faqiao—Faqiao was a native of Zhongshan—who from his youth had delighted in reciting scriptures, yet lacked a resonant voice. He often lamented that his recitations were not fully expressive. At that time, he...
He abstained from grain and practiced repentance for seven days and seven nights, prostrating before Avalokiteśvara to pray for an immediate response.
His fellow students earnestly admonished him, but he vowed not to change his course. On the seventh day, he felt a sudden opening within his throat; he immediately sought water to rinse it and said:
"I have a response. Thereupon he composed three *saṃghāṭa-sūtras*, the sound of which reached for a li. Far and near were struck with wonder and amazement; everyone came to observe and listen.
Thereafter, he recited hundreds of thousands of words of scripture, chanting day and night; his voice was so mournful and elegant that it moved the divine.
When he reached the age of ninety, his voice remained unchanged. (The above three items are from the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*).
Shi Daozhou:

His secular surname was Guan, and he was a native of Huile in Shuofang. He entered the monastic order at the Peacock King Cloister of Longxing Temple, where he received the pearl of the precepts and gradually perfected the moon of his mind.
He entered the White Grass Valley of Mount Helan and established a vow of constant recitation.
Moved by this, a dried-up spring surged forth once more, and a numinous serpent swam within it. He then ascended the Dharma platform to deliver lectures.

Furthermore, he drew blood to paint an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara. Whenever a severe drought occurred, he would fast and close his eyes, vowing that only upon the arrival of sufficient rain would he consider taking food again.
In the second year of the Zhonghe era, hearing of the turmoil in the Guanzhong region, he then...

At Nianding Monastery south of the city wall, he severed his left arm at the base of the stupa and burned it as an offering to the Great Compassionate One (Avalokiteśvara), vowing that even amidst the chaos of war, peace might soon be seen throughout the Central Plains and the northern frontiers. As soon as he finished speaking, a violent thunderstorm and torrential rain fell.

On another occasion, he cut off his left ear to pray for rain for the people, and later fasted for seven days to request snow; in both instances, his wishes were fulfilled. He was thus honored [for his piety].

At the age of seventy-eight, his remains did not decompose, as if he had entered a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Consequently, they were enshrined in lacquered and ramie-woven coffins. (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*) Regarding Shi Fayi:
On Mount Shining there was Zhu Fayi, a śramaṇa during the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty. He wielded his intellect with mastery over various scriptures and was particularly skilled in...
Fahua had always had more than a hundred disciples under his tutelage. In the second year of the Xian’an era, he suddenly suffered from a heart ailment.
Constantly keeping Avalokiteśvara in mind, he then dreamed of a man who cut open his abdomen and washed his intestines. Upon waking, his illness was immediately cured.
Fu Liang often remarked, "My late father associated with Master Yi, and whenever he spoke of the divine wonders of Avalokiteśvara, everyone, regardless of their status,
was filled with solemn reverence."
Shi Kaida (also known as Huida).
Shi Kaida climbed Long Mountain in the second year of the Long’an era to gather licorice root, where he was captured by Qiang tribesmen. At that time, there was a great famine.
The Qiang and Hu tribes devour one another; they then placed Da within a wooden cage and intended to eat him.

There were already more than ten people previously confined in the cage, whom the Qiang had been roasting on their cooking stands day and night, yet only Da still remained alive. From the moment Da was captured, he secretly recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.

He did not slacken his resolve in his heart. When the next day was to come and he was about to see Dan, at the very break of dawn, a great tiger suddenly appeared, pressing close to the Qiang people from afar.

It roared with fierce rage, and the Qiang, each struck with terror, fled in all directions. The tiger then stepped forward and gnawed through the wooden palisade, creating a small gap just wide enough for a person to pass.
The tiger then slowly departed, and Da immediately fled. Traveling by night and hiding by day, he finally succeeded in reaching his destination.
Mian-tuo (the character *mian* is pronounced like *que*; it means "separation" or "interval").
Guo Xuanzhi was a native of Taiyuan. In the fourth year of the Yixi era, he served as the Commandant of the Liangzhou Prefecture under Yang Siping.
Yang Yi was executed by law for the murder of Fan Yuanzhi and others; Xuān was likewise arrested and remained in prison. He focused his mind solely on taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Later, as evening approached and he was about to sleep, he suddenly beheld the Bodhisattva’s radiance illuminating the prison.
Xuān gazed upon him, prostrated himself, and offered prayers and vows. After a long while, the light vanished. Shortly thereafter, Xuān alone received [the divine favor].
He was granted a pardon and released. He then had images fashioned according to the forms he had seen and established a vihāra there.
Later, he died in office at Lingling and Hengyang.
Pan Daoxiu, Pan Daoxiu, was a native of Wudu. When he was over twenty years old, he served in the army on a northern expedition. Subsequently, the army suffered a slight defeat, and Daoxiu fled.

He was captured and plundered, serving as a slave in several places before being taken captive to a foreign land. Desiring to return home, he had no means to do so; he had little faith [in worldly matters].

Regarding the Buddha-dharma, she constantly and with a sincere heart called upon Avalokiteśvara. In her dreams, she would invariably see him. Later, as she fled southward, she became lost and could not find her way.

In the midst of a desolate mountain range, she suddenly beheld his true form, which resembled the present-day statues. She prostrated before him; having finished her prostrations, she suddenly awoke and did not know where she had been, and was thus able to find her way back.
She eventually returned to her native land. Thereafter, her spiritual practice became even more earnest. When she was nearly [seventy] years old...
He passed away at the age of sixty.

As for Luan Gou—Luan Gou—it is unknown where he was from. In his youth, he honored the Dharma; he once performed meritorious deeds as the Magistrate of Fuping and previously accompanied [the Emperor] on a military expedition.

The captors suffered a defeat. His boat was on the verge of being consumed by fire, and the rebels were closing in from all sides. Being right in the middle of the river, the wind and waves were terrifying to behold.

Although his life was at its end and he was utterly terrified, he continued to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. Suddenly, he saw a man standing alone and upright in the midst of the river, with his waist level with the water.
Guo knew in his heart that his prayers had moved the deity; yet as the fire and the rebels were already pressing upon him, he immediately threw himself into the water to seek refuge.
As his body floated up and down, it felt as though his feet were treading upon the ground. Shortly thereafter, the great army sent boats to receive them;
thus, those who had been defeated were able to escape and reach safety. — Shi Fazhi.
As for Shi Fazhi: while he was still a layman, he once traveled alone into a vast marsh when he suddenly encountered a fierce fire breaking out on all four sides.
His path of escape was cut off, so he single-mindedly prostrated and recited the name of Avalokiteśvara. In an instant, the fire passed by;
not a single blade of grass remained in that entire marsh, yet the place where Fazhi stood was large enough to shelter his body and remained unburnt. It was then that he first...

He reverently served the Great Dharma. Later, he became a general under Yao Xing and followed him on a campaign to subdue rebels. When the army retreated, he lost his horse and fell into the enemy encirclement.
He then hid himself among the thorny thickets by a ditch, managing to shield his head. There, he again called upon Avalokiteśvara with the utmost sincerity and diligence.
From across the ditch, a man called out from afar to the rear guard, instructing them to kill him. However, as the troops searched everywhere, they could not find him at all;
thus he escaped and was saved. Subsequently, he left the household life and became a monk.
Zi’ao, also known as Nángōng Zi’ao, was originally a native of Píng. While on garrison duty at Xīnpíng City, he was defeated by the Fúfú barbarians under Lǐ Chánglè;
the several thousand people within the city were all slaughtered. Although Zi’ao knew his death was certain, he nevertheless proceeded to—
He called upon Avalokiteśvara in his mind. When it was next his turn to be executed, Zia’o stood before the crossroads of many blades, some raised high and others held askew.

Suddenly, the executioners grew weary and slackened; their limbs no longer obeyed them. At that moment, the Duke of Changle personally presided over the execution and asked him in astonishment what he had done.
Zia’o replied casually, "I could make a horse saddle. Thereupon, the Duke ordered his release. Zia’o likewise did not... [The text ends here].
Knowing the reason for these words, he was subsequently able to escape. He fashioned a small image, placed it within a fragrant casket, and carried it upon his head whenever he traveled.
— Recorded by Sun Daode.
Sun Daode was a native of Yizhou. He served as a *jijiu* (Libationer) and was over fifty years old, yet he had no offspring.
Living near a monastery, a *śramaṇa* said to Daode during the Jingping era: "If you truly desire a son, you should single-mindedly pay homage and recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*;
then there is hope for this. Daode consequently ceased his service to the Way and devoted himself with total sincerity, taking refuge [in the Buddha].
Within a few days, Guanshiyin appeared in a dream as a response; the wife immediately became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a son.
(The person referred to as "Jiǔ" [Sacrificial Libationer] was the Daoist of the present day.
— Liu Du.
Liu Du was a native of Liaocheng in Pingyuan. There were over one thousand households in his hometown, all of whom followed the Great Dharma, fashioned images, and made offerings to monks and nuns.
During the reign of the Rouran ruler Murong Wei, fugitives from this county once took refuge there.

Murong Wei became enraged and intended to exterminate the entire city. The people were all terrified, feeling certain that they would surely perish entirely. Liu Du then purified his sincerity and led [the people]...

The multitude took refuge in Avalokiteśvara. After a short while, they saw no object descend from the sky; however, when they looked up in surprise, it was the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* encircling the pillar of the house where he resided.
He had people read it, yet he did not feel great joy until he reduced the infliction of punishments and executions.
Thereupon, this city was immediately delivered from harm.
Regarding Dou Zhuan:
Dou Zhuan was a native of Henei. During the Yonghe era, Gao Chang was the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Bingzhou, and [Dou Zhuan served as] the Regional Inspector of Jizhou.
Lü Hu and [Wang] Chuan each commanded their own private troops, and they were at odds with one another. Chuan was employed by [Wang] Chang as an official.
Lü Hu dispatched cavalry to raid and attack him, and Chuan was captured by his soldiers. Six or seven of his companions were bound together and cast into a single prison;

their shackles and manacles were extremely severe, and they were to be executed on a fixed date. At that time, the śramaṇa Zhidao Shan was in Lü Hu’s camp; he had previously been acquainted with Chuan.
Fotianxuan heard that he had been captured and went out to the prison to wait upon and observe him. Speaking through the door, Fotianxuan asked Shan, "Today you are in dire straits;
your life hangs by a thread. By what means can you be saved? Shan replied, "If you can with a sincere heart take refuge in and pray to Avalokiteśvara, there will surely be a response.
Fotianxuan had previously heard somewhat of Guanshiyin, and upon receiving Shan’s words, he subsequently focused his devotion exclusively upon her.

His mind was focused on this thought. For three days and nights, he took refuge with utmost sincerity. As he looked at his shackles, he perceived that they were loosening; they were different from what they had been before.
He gave them a slight push, and suddenly they fell away from his body. He then returned to his mind with renewed resolve, saying:

"Now, having received your compassionate protection, my fetters have already been made to loosen themselves. Yet my companions are still many, and I have no heart to depart alone. [He invoked] the divine Avalokiteśvara.
"By my power, I shall provide universal relief; let us all be spared. Having spoken, he again pulled and dragged the remaining people, and they were all released one after another.
When anyone attempted to cut or gouge him, he would open the door and run out. Amidst the watchtowers and patrols, no one noticed him. He then leaped over the boundary wall and fled directly away.
As the night was turning toward dawn, he traveled four or five *li* until daybreak, at which point he stopped and hid together with his companions.

He hid himself among a thicket of hazel trees. In a short while, he realized the prisoner had been lost. He galloped his horse in all directions to search and capture him, burning the grass and trampling through the forest until there was nowhere left unsearched;
yet, with the exception of the single mu of ground where he was hidden, no one ever reached that spot. Thus, he managed to escape and return safely.

The people of his hometown revered and trusted him beyond measure, and all of them honored the Dharma. Later, while traveling across the river at Daoshan, he related these matters in detail to the layman Xie.
[This was recorded by] Zhu Changshu.
Zhu Changshu was originally from the Western Regions. His family had possessed wealth and goods for generations and were among the great rich.
During the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty, they moved their residence to Luoyang. He served the Dharma with the utmost devotion and was particularly fond of reciting the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
Later, a fire broke out in the neighborhood; Changshu’s house was made entirely of thatch and was situated downwind. As the flames drew near, he recited [the sūtra] with single-minded sincerity.
After a short while, the fire burned the house next door, but the wind suddenly shifted and the flames stopped at the edge of that house.
At that time, everyone considered it a miracle. However, there were four or five frivolous and reckless youths in the village who mocked it together, saying:

"The wind merely turned of its own accord; what divine power could this possibly be? We shall wait for a dry evening and set fire to his house. Only one who can prevent it from burning may be considered worthy.

Later, when there was a severe drought, a group of youths secretly bound torches together and threw them onto the roof of the house. Three times they threw them, and three times they were extinguished.
They were greatly terrified and each fled back to their own homes. At dawn the next morning, they went together to Changshu and related what had happened.
Regarding the events of yesterday, [the villagers] bowed their heads to the ground in apology. Changshu replied, "I am entirely devoid of any spiritual power.

It was simply through the protection of the majestic majesty of Avalokiteśvara that this occurred. You gentlemen need only cleanse your hearts and place your faith in him. From then on, the neighbors and fellow villagers all held him in deep respect and wonder.

To the south of his county, there was a stream with swift currents and steep banks that wound back and forth like a coil; it was also filled with many large boulders, such that even those traveling by day felt a sense of peril and dread. His father once traveled through a mountain stream some ten li from home when evening approached. Suddenly, wind and rain broke out, and the darkness became as pitch-black as lacquer;
he could no longer distinguish east from west and was certain to be capsized and drowned. He did nothing but turn his heart toward Avalokiteśvara, reciting and contemplating the name.
In a brief moment, a firelight appeared on the bank, like someone holding a torch, illuminating the stream clearly so that he could see it distinctly from afar.
He was able to return home. The fire constantly led the way, remaining about ten paces ahead of the boat. He later recounted this to Xi Jabin.
Xu Rong, a native of Langya, once traveled to Dongyang and was returning via Ding Mountain when his boatman, being unaccustomed to the waters, accidentally fell [overboard].
Tossed in swirling eddies, they danced upon the waves and were on the verge of being submerged. With no hope for their lives remaining, they called out to Avalokiteśvara with utmost sincerity.
In an instant, as if dozens of people had exerted their strength together to pull the boat, it leapt out from the whirlpool and returned to smooth waters.
As the sun was already setting, the sky became pitch black and the wind and rain grew increasingly violent; they knew not where they were headed, and the waves—
The waves grew increasingly fierce. Rong continued reciting the sutras without ceasing. After a short while, he saw a brilliant blaze upon the mountain peak;
he turned the rudder toward it and reached the harbor directly. The entire ship was safe and sound. Once they arrived, the light was no longer visible.

His fellow travelers marveled at this, and in the morning they asked the people of the harbor, "What kind of fire was that on the mountain last night? Everyone was struck with astonishment and said, "Last..."
"With wind and rain such as this, how could there be any principle for fire? None of us saw it; we know it must have been divine light.
Zhang Chong, Zhang Chong—originally from Duling in Jingzhao—had served the Dharma since his youth. During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, after Fu Jian had been defeated, Chang...
The settlement had more than a thousand households. They fled south to seek refuge in the Jin state, where they were detained by local garrisons.
Mistaking them for marauding bandits, the garrison killed the able-bodied men and captured their women and children. Sengchong and four others were bound hand and foot;
a pit was dug and they were buried up to their feet, each twenty paces apart. The next day, the guards intended to amuse themselves by shooting at them from horseback.

Lèchóng was contemplating the ultimate exhaustion of all worldly hopes. He focused his pure mind and single-minded devotion on Avalokiteśvara. In the middle of the night, his shackles suddenly broke off from his body;
he seized this opportunity to flee and thus managed to escape. Because Lèchóng’s feet were in pain, he passed by a temple along the way.
He then again invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara and paid homage with a sincere heart. Placing a stone before the image, he made this vow:
"I now wish to cross the river eastward to petition the Emperor of Jin regarding the chaos, to right these vengeful spirits, and to rescue their wives and children.
If my heart's desire is fulfilled, may this stone split in two. After Fasheng had finished his prostrations, the stone immediately broke apart. Fasheng then proceeded to...
In the capital, the names of those who had suffered injustices were listed in full. The Emperor then granted them all clemency. This was personally witnessed by the monk Zhisheng.
(The fourteen items above are from the *Mingxiang ji*. Shi Tanwuqie.
The Tripiṭaka Master Dharmodgata, hearing that Faxian and others had personally traveled to the Buddha-land, was moved with such profound resolve that he made a vow to sacrifice his own life.
In the first year of the Yonghe era, he gathered twenty-five like-minded companions, including Tanlang and Sengmeng, and set out from Chang’an.

He crossed the shifting sands to the west; above, no birds flew, and below, all traces of running beasts were cut off. Looking out in all directions, the world was vast and desolate, and he knew not where he was going.
He could only rely on the sun’s position to determine east and west, and observe human bones to mark his path. Upon reaching the Pamir Mountains, snow accumulated there both winter and summer;
malevolent dragons spat forth poison, and winds rained down sand and gravel. Having previously crossed the Snow Mountains, he found a great river flowing beneath them.
The current flows as swiftly as an arrow. On the flanks of the mountains to the east and west, ropes are fastened to form bridges;

ten people pass across at a time. Once they have reached the opposite shore, they raise smoke as a signal. Those behind, seeing the smoke, know that the preceding party has already crossed and may then advance further.

If no smoke is seen for a long time, it is known that a violent wind has blown the ropes away and the people have fallen into the river. They then cross the Snow Mountains, where there are precipitous cliffs and sheer walls.
He stood there; there was no place to set his feet. On the wall were old wooden pegs, each pair facing one another.

Holding four of these pegs, he first pulled out the lower one and then hauled himself up to the upper one. By pulling himself along from one to the next, he finally reached level ground after three days.
He counted his companions and found that twelve had perished. Continuing toward Central India, the road was vast and desolate, and they carried only rock honey as their provisions.
Among the thirteen people, eight more died. Although Wujie repeatedly encountered perilous and thorny situations, he maintained his mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara without ceasing for even a moment.
Upon reaching Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of elephants; he then took refuge in Avalokiteśvara, whereupon a lion suddenly appeared.
The elephant then bolted away and reached the Ganges River, where it encountered a herd of rhinoceroses; it again took refuge as before.
Soon after, a large vulture flew over, and the rhinoceroses also scattered in alarm. Later, in South India, he boarded a merchant ship and arrived at Guangzhou, returning with the scriptures.
(From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Record of Venerable Conduct*. [Note: "Xi" (兕) is pronounced with the second tone; it refers to a one-horned wild ox. )

Nimi Minggan was originally surnamed Zhu and was a native of Gaoping. Her family had served the Great Dharma for generations. She was captured by barbarian raiders who intended to take her as their wife;

they subjected her to various forms of torture, yet she vowed never to suffer such humiliation. They punished her by forcing her to herd sheep, and after ten years had passed, she longed to return home.
His resolve became even more earnest, yet he had no means to return home. He constantly kept the Triple Gem in mind and also aspired to leave the household life.

Suddenly, he encountered a bhikṣu, from whom he requested the five precepts; the monk also bestowed upon him the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. Consequently, he was able to practice its recitation, doing so day and night without ceasing.
Wishing to return home to erect a five-story stūpa, he could not bear his anxious thoughts and fled toward the east. At first, he did not know the way, [and traveled] by day...
Traveling by night, he entered a mountain directly and saw a striped tiger only a few paces away. At first, he was terrified;
however, after stepping back a short distance, his mind settled and his aspiration grew even stronger. He then followed the tiger on foot for many days, up to ten, until he reached Qingzhou.
As they were about to enter a village, the tiger suddenly vanished.
The nun then sent Zongling;
Zongling’s original surname was Man, and he was a native of Jinxiang in Gaoping. From his youth, he possessed pure faith, for which he was praised by his fellow villagers. His family encountered...

During the chaos of the rebellion, he was driven off as a captive by the barbarians. With utmost sincerity and devotion, he invoked the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, recited the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), and offered his plea;

consequently, he was released. Following the road back home, he traveled beyond Jizhou, where he was again pursued by bandits. He climbed a withered tree and focused his mind with single-minded devotion upon Avalokiteśvara.
The pursuers looked up ahead but never once glanced upward; they searched for him but could not find him, and in an instant—

Sengzong departed again from below. Late in the evening, he reached Mengjin, but there were no boats available for crossing. Terrified and filled with anxiety, he redoubled his sincere recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he saw a white deer appearing from nowhere; it descended into the river and began to wade across. Sengzong followed the deer and was thus able to cross.

He was never once wetted by water; he walked as if on dry land. Consequently, he reached home safely and immediately entered the monastic path. His practice and conduct were refined and sincere; his study of the profound meanings of the sutras reached a divine level.
When Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty heard of him, he sent a letter to inquire after him. He passed away at the age of seventy-five.
(The above two accounts are from the *Biqiuni zhuan*). Hugu was a native of Shanyang.
He was imprisoned and sentenced to death; for three days and three nights, he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara without ceasing in his mind.

Immediately, he saw Avalokiteśvara emitting light that shone upon him; his shackles fell off and the gate opened. Following the light, he departed and traveled twenty li before the radiance finally faded.
Zhang Chang was the Senior Secretary (Changshi) to Prince Qiao. When both the Prince and Zhang were imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review (Tingwei), he recited the sutras one thousand times;
his shackles broke piece by piece, and they were released before long. [The account] regarding Xucheng is as stated above.
Pei Anqi, Pei Anqi!
Having defected from the barbarians and returned to the south, he reached the riverbank but was unable to cross.
Seeing the pursuing cavalry behind him, his death was imminent. Thereupon, he invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara and beheld a white wolf; Anqi then embraced it. One—
Upon being thrown, he immediately crossed to the southern bank and lost the wolf’s trail. The pursuing cavalry on the northern bank gazed after him, sighing with boundless lamentation.
(The three items above are from the *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara*, by Xu Yi.)
Xu Yi was a native of Gaolu. In his youth, he had devoted himself to the Dharma and served as a Minister of State under Fu Jian.

Toward the end of Jian’s reign, when the clamor of war broke out, bandits captured Yi and were about to execute him. They buried his feet and tied his hair to a tree. During the night, he focused his mind single-mindedly on Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, he fell asleep and dreamed that someone said to him, "The situation is now urgent; how can you afford to sleep?"
Yi was startled awake. Seeing that the guards were all exhausted and asleep, he attempted to move himself;
once his hands and hair were freed, his feet were also released. He then fled, hiding in a small thicket after walking some one hundred paces.
He heard the pursuers galloping toward him, their torches forming a shimmering array as they circled the thicket, yet none could find him. At daybreak, the bandits dispersed.
He sought refuge at a monastery in Ye and was thus able to escape.
Bilan was a native of Dongping. Having served the Dharma since his youth, he followed Murong Chui on a northern expedition; he was captured by the barbarians but managed to escape on horseback alone.

While fleeing, the pursuers were about to overtake him. Senglan invoked Avalokiteśvara with utmost sincerity. Having escaped, he entered deep into the mountains, where he became disoriented and lost his way.
Again, he focused his mind on taking refuge in the Buddha. At midnight, he saw a practitioner clad in dharma robes and holding a *khakkhara* staff, who showed him the path.
He was thus able to find his way back home, arriving safely and in peace. (The two preceding accounts are from the *Mingxiang ji*).
The Dharma Master Sengbao of the Song dynasty was a native of Jingzhao. He resided at Qihuan Monastery and lectured on various sutras, continuing his propagation of the Dharma. [End of] Chen.
Xie Lingyun of the commandery heard of his reputation and went to visit him. Upon seeing Bao’s divine bearing, he was filled with even deeper admiration and respect.
Someone asked him, "What do you think of Master Xie? Bao replied, "Lingyun has an abundance of wealth, yet his insight is insufficient;

he will likely not escape the consequences for his own person. Once, while traveling on the road, Bao saw six thieves being arrested. He preached the Dharma to them, exhorting them to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Yin. At a moment of extreme peril, the bandits prayed with such earnest sincerity that, before long, the escorting officials became heavily intoxicated from drinking wine.
The bandits then unfastened their shackles and escaped.

The Dharma Master Daowang of the Shi clan was surnamed Pan and was a native of Changle. In his youth, he followed his uncle to the capital; at the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
He studied the essential scriptures and the Vinaya, and was particularly adept in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Once, while traveling through Liangzhou, he was captured by Qiang bandits.
They surrounded him, and he was on the verge of losing his robes and bowl. Wang and several of his disciples vowed together to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, they felt as if clouds and mist were covering their bodies; the bandits searched for them but could not find them. Thus, they escaped with their lives.
Shi Senghong:
Shi Senghong was a native of Yuzhou. He resided at Waguan Monastery in the capital. From his youth, he cultivated his person with strict integrity and purity.

Later, he led those with whom he shared a karmic affinity to create a sixteen-foot golden image. Once the casting was completed, before the mold had even been opened, it was the time of the Jin dynasty...

The prohibitions against copper were extremely strict; those who violated them were invariably executed. During the time of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, [Tanyao] Hong was imprisoned in the Prime Minister’s residence on account of a crime.
He did nothing but recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and single-mindedly take refuge in the Buddha image.

One night, he dreamed that the cast image came to him, stroked his head with its hand, and asked, "Are you afraid? Hong replied, "I think only of my certain death. The image said, "Have no fear. Hong then saw the image.

The area of his chest was about one foot square, and it appeared as if it had been scorched and boiled by copper. It was destined that he should undergo execution, with a provincial councilor supervising the killing.

However, the ox bolted and the carriage was overturned; consequently, the date for the execution was postponed. Subsequently, an imperial edict arrived from Pengcheng stating, "As for the monk Senghong, he may be pardoned.
He was thus spared and returned home. When the mold was opened, it was seen that there were indeed marks of scorching and boiling upon the chest of the image.
Shi Daojiong. His secular surname was Ma. He was a native of Fufeng. When he first entered the monastic order, he became a disciple of Daoyi.

While Daoyi was ill, he once dispatched Daojiong and three others to Mount Huo in Henan to collect stalactites. After traveling several li into the cave, they had to cross a stream by stepping across wooden beams. Three...

The man drowned, and the torch was extinguished as well; it was clear that there was no way to save him. Jiong had always recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and relied solely on this practice, while also maintaining mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, he saw a light like a firefly; though he pursued it, he could not catch up, and so he managed to escape from the cave.
Thereupon, he advanced in his cultivation of dhyāna, and his disciplined conduct became ever more refined. Later, he traveled south with his fellow students to Mount Shang.
In the capital, while observing the customs and transformations of the world, [Wang] Jiong was crossing the river at night by ice. Midway across, the ice broke, and three people drowned.
Jiong again turned his heart in sincere devotion to Guanyin; he then felt as if there were an object beneath his feet and saw a red light before him.
He immediately followed the light and reached the shore.

Shao Xin, a native of Wuxing, was a devout follower of the Dharma. When he contracted a severe case of *shanghan* (febrile illness), no one dared to attend to him. He then wept bitterly while reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Suddenly, he saw a monk arrive who said he was a disciple of Beidu. The monk spoke to him, saying, "Do not worry; your master will soon..."
He came to visit him. [The master] replied, "Master Du has already died; how could you possibly come? The practitioner said, "What difficulty is there in coming?

He then took a handful of powder from his head-dress, about the size of a small box, and gave it to him to take. The illness was immediately cured. (These five items are taken from the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*. Zhang Xing.
Zhang Xing was a native of Xinxiang. He had some faith in the Buddha-dharma and used to receive the eight precepts from the śramaṇas Sengrong and Tanyi on occasion.
Once, Zhang Xing was implicated by bandits; while the husband managed to flee, the wife remained imprisoned. She was subjected to flogging and interrogation for many days.
At that time, a fire broke out in the county seat, and the prisoner was being held by the roadside. Sengrong and Tanyi were traveling together and passed by her side. The wife cried out in alarm.
"Upādhyāya, why do you grant me rescue? Tánróng replied, "My strength is weak; how can I rescue you? You should simply recite the name of Avalokiteśvara with diligence, and perhaps you may escape.
His wife then prayed and recited day and night. After about ten days, she dreamed of a śramaṇa at night who stepped on her with his foot and said, "Ho!
Ho! You may rise! The wife immediately started up in alarm, but her shackles and fetters remained as they were.
Suddenly, she understood everything at once and ran toward the door. At that moment, the door was still closed; the guards were exceptionally vigilant, and there was no way to escape.
Fearing someone might wake up, she returned to her shackles and soon fell back asleep. Again she dreamed that the śramaṇa said to her, "The door is already open.
Her wife woke up and rushed out; the guards were all in a deep, drunken sleep. Her wife then walked away with steady steps. At that time—

The night was extremely dark. After traveling several *li*, they suddenly encountered a man. His wife was terrified and fell to the ground. After they had conversed for a while, it turned out to be her husband.
Supporting one another, they were overcome with both grief and joy. That night they sought refuge with the monk Yi, and thus they managed to escape. This was at the beginning of the Yuanjia era.
(Sengrong; the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records him as Daorong.
Wang Yan was young when he was in Jiaozhi. There was a Dharma Master Xian there, a monk of virtue and morality, who bestowed upon him the five [precepts].
Regarding the precepts: [Yan] received a single statue of Avalokiteśvara made of gold. Its craftsmanship differed from those of the present day, yet it was not of extreme antiquity.

Yan reverently brought it back to the capital. At that time, he was still in his childhood; together with his two younger brothers, he constantly applied himself with utmost diligence and devotion, never wearying.
Later, while renovating their dilapidated dwelling, they found no room to house the image, so they enshrined it at Nanjian Temple in the capital. At that time—
The common people vied with one another to cast coins. There were even those who would steal and destroy golden images to provide the material for casting.

At that time, the image had already been in the temple for several months. While Yan was napping during the day, he dreamed that the image stood up in the corner of its seat; he found this most extraordinary. By then, the sun had already set.
He immediately galloped back to welcome them home. That evening, more than ten statues from the Southern Gorge were all stolen by bandits.
A long time thereafter, during the twilight, the statues emitted light that illuminated the ground for about three feet; a brilliant golden radiance rose up, so dazzling it blinded the eyes.
Yan’s brothers and their servants, numbering over ten, witnessed this together. It was the autumn of the seventh year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty.
...also. [I] prostrate for ten thousand years of longevity;

[I] prostrate for ten thousand years of longevity. A native of Pingchang, in the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he served as a subordinate military officer (*xingcan*) in the Guard (*wei-fu*) at Guangling.

When the military service was completed and he returned to his province, he crossed the river at the beginning of the fourth watch. At the moment he first began to cross, the long waves flowed peacefully;

however, as he reached mid-river, a wind arose like an arrow. It was also extremely dark, and no one knew where they were headed. Wanshou had previously been exceptionally diligent in serving the Dharma.
With single-minded devotion, they took refuge in Avalokiteśvara, their mindfulness never ceasing for a moment.
Suddenly, several people on board the ship together beheld a light on the northern shore, appearing like a village fire. They said to one another with joy, "This must surely be the fire of Ouyang."
He turned his ship toward it and arrived before dawn. When he questioned the people there, they all said that no one had lit fires the night before.
Only then did he realize it was through supernatural power. Upon arriving, he established a vegetarian feast assembly.
Gu Mai, Gu Mai, was a native of Wu Commandery. He observed the Dharma with great diligence. In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he was returning from the capital to Guangling.
Upon departing from Shitou City, he encountered a northwesterly wind that blew violently across the lake; the force of the wind did not subside, yet the boatmen pressed on.

As he proceeded, upon reaching the middle reaches of the river, the waves were already formidable. Hui-mai traveled alone in a single boat, filled with anxiety and despair as he had no means to escape the danger.
He recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* about ten times; consequently, the force of the wind gradually subsided and the waves also became somewhat smaller.

Shortly thereafter, while in midstream, he repeatedly smelled a wondrous fragrance that was rich and pervasive without ceasing. Hui-mai felt a singular sense of joy and thus continued his recitation with steadfastness, never stopping. In this way, he was safely ferried across.
Shi Huihe: Shi Huihe was a monk at Zhongzao Temple in the capital. During the Yijia crisis of the Liu Song dynasty, Huihe was still a layman and was enlisted under the command of Liu Hu.
Hu once dispatched several dozen officers and soldiers on a reconnaissance mission down to the east, and Huihe was also among them.

He traveled on until he reached Quezhu (Crow Island), where he encountered the troops of the Imperial Court advancing from the west. The scouts were scattered and dispersed, each fleeing into the marshes.

Senghe then folded his robes, took up a basket, and shouldered a load, appearing like a common field laborer. At that time, the roaming soldiers captured these scattered scouts; upon seeing Senghe’s appearance, they suspected him and questioned him.
Senghe’s responses were evasive and confused, so he was subsequently flogged and plundered. The military commander ordered him to be executed. Senghe—
They scattered and fled. Huihe constantly recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. When the time came for him to be executed, his prayers became even more earnest.

Subsequently, whenever the soldiers raised their blades, they repeatedly stumbled; three times they lifted them, and three times they broke. All were struck with awe and released him. Thereupon, Huihe left the household life and eventually achieved mastery in his spiritual practice.
Han Hui: Han Hui was a man of unknown origins. He lived by the Zhijiang River. His uncle had been imprisoned, and the legal jeopardy extended to Hui as well;

both were confined in the county jail. Iron wood was driven through their bodies, and their shackles and fetters were extremely severe. Hui was terrified and desperate, with no means of escape, awaiting his death.
This was all. Huī had previously served the Buddha and had for some time devoted himself to the recitation of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.

Thereupon, he recited the sūtra day and night until several hundred times had been reached during the daytime, when the lock suddenly sounded of its own accord, like the crackling and popping of stones or tiles being scorched by fire.
After a while, he looked at it and found that the lock had opened by itself. Fearing that the prison official would suspect he had cut it open, he hurriedly called out to inform him.

Although the officer was astonished, he nevertheless re-nailed the iron plate. Senghui continued reciting the sutras as usual. After another day, the lock again made a sound and opened, appearing exactly as it had before.
The officer then reported the matter in full to his superior. The official took the lock and examined it closely; he was convinced by Senghui’s spiritual penetration.
Moved by this, [the official] immediately released him. Huī is still alive today; his dedication to his religious practice is truly extraordinary.
Pēng Tzŭ-chiao: Pēng Tzŭ-chiao was a native of Yìyáng County. He served as the Administrator of the Secretariat for the Prince of Běn. The Crown Prince was Shěn Wén-lóng.
In the first year of the Jianyuan era, because of Qiao’s crime, [the Emperor] was in a state of great rage; his shackles were extremely tight, and he was determined to kill him.
Zi Qiao was filled with anxiety and fear, having no other recourse but to recite the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra with utmost sincerity more than a hundred times.
Exhausted, he fell asleep during the day. At that time, there were about ten other people imprisoned together with him who were also sleeping. There was an official from Xiangxi County named Du...
Daosce was also imprisoned there. While he was still half-asleep and not yet fully awake, he suddenly saw two white cranes alighting upon Zi Qiao’s screen.
After a short while, one crane descended beside Zi Qiao; at that moment, it appeared to Daosce as the form of a beautiful human being, and then vanished.
Dao Ce looked up and saw that Zi Qiao’s double shackles were detached and hanging outside his feet, yet the locks remained firmly in place.
Startled, Dao Ce looked closely until it was finished; Zi Qiao also awoke, and they looked at the shackles together in wonder. Dao Ce asked Zi Qiao, "Did you have a dream?"

Qiao said, "I did not dream. Daoce recounted what he had seen as previously described. Although Ziqiao knew the truth, he still feared that the prison authorities might suspect him of intending to escape;
thus, he removed their shackles and fetters and put new ones on them. After four or five days, they were released.
Yan’s cousin, Lian, was personally acquainted with both Ziqiao and Daoce, and upon hearing what the two men said, he found it to be exactly as they had related.
Xing Huaiming, Xing Huaiming, was a native of Hejian. He served as a military aide (*canjun*) to the Great General of the Song dynasty.
