Before his voice had even ceased, he saw a celestial general standing behind his bed, approximately one zhang in height, wearing yellow leather trousers and a tunic, holding a vajra-pestle and brandishing it at them.
The ghosts were immediately terrified and dispersed; their armor and accoutrements were shattered into fine powder.

Shi Huijian: As for Huijian, it is unknown where he was from. He entered the monastic path at the beginning of the Liang dynasty. His observance of the precepts and his religious practice were vast and lofty; he was exceptionally extraordinary, resourceful, and courageous.
To the east of the main hall of Jingzhou, there had previously been three separate chambers that were frequently haunted by ghosts and spirits. Huijian resided there.
He himself occupied one room, while the other was used for housing scriptures and images. Suddenly, he saw a person dressed in black clothes and lacking eyes emerge from within the wall;
this figure then leaned against the door frame. At that moment, Sim’s vision cleared and his mind became lucid, yet he was unable to speak. He focused his thoughts on Avalokiteśvara.
After a long while, the ghost said, "I have come to test you because I recognized your diligent cultivation. Since your countenance remains unmoved, how could I possibly coerce you further?
With a sudden flicker, it retreated back into the wall. Huijian slowly rose, washed his face, and completed his ritual recitations; he then returned to sleep as usual.
He spoke to someone in a dream, saying, "I have resided here since the end of the Han dynasty for several hundred years. By nature I am rigid and upright, and I find much that I cannot endure."

"You are truly a man of pure conduct and goodness; I have merely tolerated you until now. From this point on, it shall cease. Thereafter, Jian lived for many years, remaining as peaceful and secure as before.
Yet, whenever he traveled elsewhere, no one else was able to remain in that place. Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, Liu Ji’s mother fell ill.
He recited the name of Avalokiteśvara several tens of thousands of times, whereupon he dreamed of a monk who said, "The lady's lifespan has come to an end, but I shall extend it by six [years]."
Ten days later, it was exactly as in the dream. (From the *Tongji*).
Shi Sengshi of the Zhou and Sui dynasties.
Chan Master Sengshi’s secular surname was Cheng, and he was a native of Wuling in Xianyang. His eyes possessed double pupils, their radiance shining outward;
his armpits held "phoenix eggs," and all seven parts of his body were perfectly even. His extraordinary features surpassed those of his peers, earning him renown in the capitals of Jing and Luo.

Furthermore, his realization of the Way was innate, and his transformative influence extended throughout the Guanzhong region. Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou dynasty remarked, "The Master’s talent is profound and his virtue is vast; he ought to..."
To protect both the clergy and the laity and to exalt the ritual canons, he personally presented his supplication for a Tripitaka Master for the sake of the state.

[The Master], truly embodying benevolence and yielding not, silently accepted the request. This ensured that the great beams of the Dharma remained and provided a model upon which others could rely. Since the Zhou dynasty established its realm, it has truly looked up to this profound influence.
Their rites differed from those of previous dynasties, as they received the *śaraṇagamana* precepts. Suddenly one day, he informed the monks, saying: "Prepare incense with haste."

Fire. To perform rites for repair and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara in order to save a temple hall in a certain monastery in Jiangnan from collapsing, several hundred monastics and laypeople were gathered within the Yangdu Lecture Hall, engaged in formal debate and the assembly of the Dharma.

Hearing a strange fragrance from the northwest and the sound of celestial music in the air, the entire congregation rose in astonishment and listened together; at that moment, the hall suddenly collapsed.

The temple was destroyed, yet the great assembly suffered no harm. When this was reported to the Prince of Liang, he moved [the matter] to Zhou for inquiry; it indeed turned out to be as Sengshu had said.
Shi Hongman—Hongman’s surname was Liang and he was a native of Anding—was fifteen years old when he encountered a contemporary illness that left both his feet withered and paralyzed.
He constantly recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* for three years. Suddenly, a monk appeared, holding a water pitcher, and stood before him without speaking.

[Mǎn] asked, "From where have you come, Master? He replied, "I have come because you, the donor, called me constantly. Mǎn prostrated himself repeatedly and asked, "For what offense did this disciple receive this retribution of being bound and crippled?
Why have you now bestowed this upon me? The monk said, "In your previous life, you bound and confined living beings. [The remainder...]"
"Your calamity has led to this. You need only close your eyes; I shall treat you. Faman followed these words and closed his eyes.

He felt only that, upon each of his knees, something like a six or seven-inch nail had been extracted. When it was finished, he opened his eyes, intending to express his gratitude, but he lost sight of the monk.
He rose and walked as before. Faman then realized it was Guanyin. From then on, with sincere devotion, he vowed never to marry.
Later, he suddenly entered into meditative contemplation on his own accord and sat unmoving for three days and seven days.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he changed his secular life to follow the Way and resided at Jiudu Temple. He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of eighty-three.
Dharma Master Huigong:

Dharma Master Huigong was a native of Chengdu in Yizhou. His secular surname was Zhou. During the period when the Buddha-dharma was suppressed at the end of the Zhou dynasty, he formed a bond of study with Huiyuan of the same monastery.
While Huiyuan traveled directly to Chang’an to attend lectures, Huigong remained behind for a long time.
Jing and Yang traveled to the capital to seek the Way, where they listened to various sutras and treatises until they had mastered them all.
Upon returning to Yizhou, they lectured and taught; their realization was so outstanding that they surpassed their peers, earning the deep respect of both the clergy and the laity.
Later, Gong returned from Jiangzuo and the two met with great joy. They recounted their parting over more than thirty years, staying together for several nights as they conversed and shared stories.

Huiyuan’s words flowed forth like a spring; Huicong was ultimately unable to say anything in response. Huiyuan asked Huicong, “We have been separated for a long time, and now that we have met, I rejoice in this joyful reunion.
What is there to discuss? Yet I perceive that you, Venerable Sir, have nothing to say. Is it perhaps that you have attained the state of ‘having nothing to attain’?
Huicong replied, “By nature I am dull and inferior; I understand nothing at all. Huiyuan said, “It is excellent to have nothing to understand.”
"Can you not recite a single scripture? Gong replied, "I can only recite one scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
Yuan changed his expression to one of severity and said, "The Avalokiteśvara Sūtra is something even small children can recite. Why trouble someone of your great stature?
Furthermore, when you were a youth, you left the household life and made a vow with me to realize the fruits of the Way; how could you now turn back after thirty years?"
"In my remaining years, I have done nothing but recite a single scroll of scripture. This is the work of one who is dull-witted and indolent; I pray that you sever ties with me.
I hope the Dharma Master will depart soon, so as not to increase the distress of our long journey. Gong replied, "Though this scroll is small, it was spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Those who honor and respect it shall obtain immeasurable merit; those who treat it with contempt shall incur immeasurable sin. I entreat you to cease your anger for a moment."

"Xin, you should recite this for the Dharma Master once; then we shall part forever. Yuan laughed loudly and said, "The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* is the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
I have already lectured upon it more than a hundred times. Why do you now wish to disturb my ears?
Gong replied, "A secular text says, 'It is man who can propagate the Way, not the Way that propagates man. However, please listen with a sincere heart."
The Buddha said, "How can one discard the Dharma because of a person? Thereupon, he established an altar before the courtyard and placed a high seat within it.
After circumambulating the altar several times and prostrating himself, he ascended the seat. Yuan, having no choice, sat upon a low stool beneath the eaves to listen.
As Gong began to chant the title of the sutra, a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air, filling the entire chamber. When he entered into the text, celestial music was heard from above.
Music played, raining down four kinds of flowers; the music was resonant, shaking the void, while the flowers fell in fragrant profusion, covering the ground.

When the sutra recitation concluded, he descended from his seat and personally performed the ritual for dispersing the assembly; only then did the music and flowers cease. Huiyuan prostrated himself at [the Master’s] feet in worship, his tears flowing freely, and thanked him, saying:
"Huiyuan is but a foul and putrid corpse; how could I dare to walk beneath the light of heaven? I beg you to remain for a moment and grant me your instruction."

Tanyong said, "This is not within my capability; it is solely through the power of the Buddhas. That very day, he shook out his robes, performed a long bow, and departed downstream. (The preceding five items are from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang*.

The commentary states: "A single phrase, when clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. Master Huiyuan’s exegesis surpassed that of his peers, yet why was he not as devoted to recitation as Master Tanyong? This may be because Master Huiyuan’s conduct and realization were not yet in accord.)

"Or perhaps, although one may explain the text according to its literal words, one has not yet truly mastered it. This is what is meant by the saying: 'To interpret the meaning based on the scriptures is to be an enemy of the Buddhas of the three periods. Since it is said that a single phrase can transcend ten billion [worlds], how could Master Gong’s holding of even a single scroll of the sutra be considered insufficient?
Indeed, his practice and realization remain beyond the reach of thought.
— *Guanyin Cilin Ji*, Middle Volume.
*The Collection from the Forest of Avalokiteśvara’s Compassion*,
Volume Lower. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Mount Dinghu in Guangdong (during the Tang Dynasty [and appended with the Five Dynasties]).

Shi Tanzang: Dharma Master Tanzang’s secular surname was Yang; he was a native of Huayin in Hongnong. His family was a prominent lineage of long-standing reputation, and from youth he had cultivated a mind of purity and detachment.
At the age of fifteen, a diviner predicted that his life would be short. His parents, grieving for him, immediately arranged a marriage for him. Since this was their original intention...
Feeling that he was being pursued and coerced by non-sentient forces, he fled into the mountains and marshes, thinking only of who might save him.

As he traveled through the wilds, there were few places where he had previously wandered, and he knew not where to seek refuge. He did nothing but recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. After a long time, he encountered a man with a dark complexion driving two oxen.
He asked the man where he was going and whether he might stay the night. The man then told him, "There is a temple to the west; it is not far away."
Upon arrival, he heard the sound of a bell and suddenly beheld a monastery. He requested ordination and thus fulfilled his original aspiration. The monks immediately sent him out the gate;

after walking about a hundred paces, he looked back and could no longer see it. It was only after a long time that dawn broke. This was truly a sacred realm, which he was able to reach through the power of the Bodhisattva’s inspiration.

Shi Fachang, the Dharma Master Fachang, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Baishui in Nanyang. He had traversed the gates of profound meaning and excelled in both practice and understanding; thus, he was highly esteemed by all.
He took refuge in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and revered the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as his primary model. He devoted himself to his daily recitations and the cultivation of the Way. Six...

At that time, he exhorted himself to diligence, leaving not even a slight deficiency in his practice. There was a great divine king, dressed entirely in white, who led his retinue to follow him as he circumambulated.
This was occasionally witnessed by both monastics and laypeople, who secretly held him in high esteem.

Furthermore, once during the night, when he entered the Buddha hall, the painted celestial musicians on the walls all rose at once to dance. Later, in the middle of the night, again in the Buddha hall, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara appeared from—
He entered the gate from outside and stayed suspended in mid-air. His physical form was magnificent and extraordinary, and the necklaces he wore shone with a rare brilliance.

After a long while, he vanished. Five years later, as dawn was about to break, he again perceived the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra approaching from the east at a height of five or six *zhang* above the ground.
Such were the signs of response resulting from his constant and dedicated cultivation.

Shi Puming, the Dhyāna Master Puming, was originally named Fajing. His secular surname was Zhu, and he was a native of Kuaiji. From his youth, his aspirations and conduct were extraordinary compared to ordinary children;

he constantly recited the name of the Buddha and did not engage in worldly play or idle talk, but was solely intent on honoring the Dharma. During the tenth year of the Taian era of Emperor Taijian of the Chen dynasty...
For four years, he came to Tiantai and took refuge with Zhizhe, attending upon him day and night without slackening.

He devoted himself exclusively to seeking the methods of Chan while concurrently practicing the Vaipulya (fangděng), Pratyutpanna (bānzhōu), and Guanyin repentance rites, as well as reciting the Lotus Sūtra.

Following Zhizhe, he went to Donglin Temple on Mount Lu, where he performed the Guanyin Repentance Method within the Hall of the Auspicious Image (Ruìxiàng Gé) that had appeared during the time of Tao Kan. In the tenth month of winter...

For one month, he did not wear any cotton clothing, practicing the Way with rigorous austerity. He encountered a monk who said, "The name 'Fajing' (Dharma Capital) you bear is not a fitting appellation;
it should be changed to 'Puming' (Universal Radiance). This name signifies clarity and brightness, illuminating the three periods of time. After completing his repentance, he informed Zhiyi.
The Wise One said: "What is shown here in this darkness is that you should immediately abandon the old and follow the new.
Shi Jingzhi, the Dhyāna Master, was surnamed Zhao and was a native of Gaoling in Yongzhou. His parents were devoted to the good, yet they had no offspring at all. [They] prayed...

He sought universal attainment and loathed the defilements of desire, severing all pungent and foul attachments forever. After his birth, at the age of seven or eight, he delighted in the contemplation of Amitābha and studied it according to the texts.
By nature he enjoyed the life of a renunciant. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he stayed at Huaguang Monastery for over ten years;
he constantly sat in a thatched hut rather than dwelling in the monks' quarters. Those who gathered from the four quarters numbered more than two hundred. Six.

At that time, his three karmas did not fail to reflect the light [of the Dharma]. At one point, his nose was afflicted by a blockage of flesh. Although he tried a hundred methods, none were effective.

A monk instructed him to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* ten thousand times. Thereupon, the fleshy growth fell away. (The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* elucidates the wisdom-practice of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
— Recorded by Shi Zhiquan.

Zhiquan’s secular surname was Zhu. From his youth, he made it his heart's resolve to protect and uphold the Dharma. Whenever he was among the assembly, there was no word he spoke that was not harmonious and conciliatory.

He was refined, sincere, and courageous; in all his affairs, he received spiritual protection from the unseen realm. Initially, when his mother fell gravely ill, he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Upon the leaves of trees within their home, transformed Buddhas appeared one after another, visible to the entire family. Thereupon, his mother’s illness was cured.

Shi Fatong: Fatong’s surname was Guan; he was a native of Hu in Jingzhao. He entered the monastic order at a young age and was extremely frail and weak, collapsing like grass blown by the wind as if dressed in fine silks.
Because of this, his companions treated him with considerable disdain. Fatong would frequently shed tears; one day, in the presence of an image of Avalokiteśvara, he [made a vow].
Kangkai said, "I have heard that the Bodhisattva’s holy discernment grants all that is wished for. I beg you to bestow your guidance and instruction so that I may be spared from such contempt.
Thereupon, he recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* day and night without ceasing. More than a year later, he returned to his native place to visit his mother.
After finishing his morning meal, he dozed beneath a tree in the courtyard. A short while later, saliva and froth flowed from his mouth in an amount of about three sheng.

His mother, thinking he had been struck by some external object, hurriedly called him to wake up and asked, "What is it that has made you like this? Tong replied, "Just now I saw someone leave behind three donkeys loaded with sinews.
I ate from one donkey, but as my mother called me, I woke up and lost the other two. From then on, his awakening became self-sustained and his strength grew heroic;
his skin and flesh became firm and tough, such that he could lift large timbers and stones without regarding them as heavy. There was a monk at the temple who...
Kān was the most preeminent in physical strength. Tōng secretly stole a *kāṣāya* robe and placed it beneath a pillar. Kān did not see it at first and thought it was the work of spirits or ghosts.
Tōng laughed and, lifting a beam, pulled it out. Kān was greatly startled and submitted in awe. There was also a large stone mortar.
It weighed over five hundred jin. It was used to transport water from the Southern Mountains to provide for the monks' needs; it remains there now as a water reservoir.
Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty held it in high esteem.
[Recorded by] Shi Zhixian.
Master Zhixian resided at Huming Monastery in Liaozhou. Having left home to become a monk in his youth, his observance of the precepts was pure and stern, and his character was upright and resolute.

He devoted himself exclusively to seated meditation; no one knew where his mind’s reach extended. Later, while traveling with more than ten monastics and laypeople, they encountered a Turkic raiding party and were all seized and plundered.
Zhixian then concealed himself and vanished from sight. When he was later found and interrogated, he simply said: "I..."
Because he called upon Avalokiteśvara, he did not encounter bandits. (The above seven items are from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang Dynasty*).
Dharma Master Yuankang:
The family name and clan of Dharma Master Yuankang are unknown. During the Zhenguan era, he traveled to study in the capital. Previously, he resided in the mountains and wilds, constantly...

He devoted himself to the recitation of the name of Avalokiteśvara, seeking the increase of his wisdom and understanding. Consequently, he was moved by a response: a deer appeared with a single head and eight-pronged antlers; its form was utterly extraordinary.
Seng-kang saw it, stroked it until it became tame and submissive, and subsequently raised it as a pet. He would ride it for long distances, yet it never showed any sign of weariness.

Emperor Wen heard of Seng-kang’s unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and issued an edict for him to enter An-guo Monastery to lecture on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). Thereupon, he [the Emperor] constructed...

Commentary: Master Tripitaka Xuanzang compiled two fascicles of the *Xuanshu* (The Mysterious Pivot), which explains the principles of the Madhyamaka school and provides a comprehensive elucidation of the essential tenets of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*.
(From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).
The Master’s original name was Hui. His secular surname was Chen, a descendant of Chen Zhonggong of Taichou during the Han dynasty. His father, Huíyīng, was pure and possessed refined integrity.
When the Master was first born, his mother dreamed that he, dressed in white robes, departed toward the west.
The mother said, "You are my son; where do you wish to go now? He replied, "I am going for the sake of seeking the Dharma. This was thus an omen of his future travels abroad. At the age of eleven...
From his elder brother, Dharma Master Jie, he daily received instruction in refined principles and was concurrently exposed to ingenious discourses.

He was preeminent and upright, refusing to conform to the trends of his time. At the age of thirteen, he ascended the seat to lecture; his words and reasoning were exhaustive, and his reputation spread ever further.

When he reached the age of twenty-nine, he reflected privately, saying: "In study, one prizes long-term persistence; in meaning, one values thorough penetration. To delve into and revere only a single school..."

Sengqie Tanji thought to himself: "If I do not disregard my life and sacrifice my very existence to vow to travel to the Western Heaven, how could I possibly fully behold the words of the Buddha and thereby communicate with his divine understanding?
He then proceeded directly to Guzang and gradually reached Dunhuang. Crossing the Yumen Pass, his route lay through Tiansai.
Wrapping my provisions and mourning in solitude, I gazed ahead into the distance; it stretched out boundlessly. I saw only level sands extending for more than eight hundred li.

Above, no birds flew; below, no beasts ran. Furthermore, there was neither water nor grass. With single-minded devotion, I recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā as I proceeded toward the northwest.
Looking around in all directions, everything was desolate and vast; both men and horses were utterly lost. At night, malevolent spirits raised fires that blazed like the sun.
The stars were numerous. By day, a fierce wind swept up the sand, scattering it like seasonal rain. For four nights and five days, not a single drop fell to moisten his throat;
his mouth and belly grew parched and withered, and he was on the verge of death. Unable to take further food, he lay down upon the sand and silently recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Though exhausted, he did not abandon his practice. He addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "I, Xuanzang, have come on this journey not seeking wealth or profit, nor do I hope for fame."

"Yù, you have come solely for the sake of the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment and the True Dharma. I look up to the Bodhisattva’s compassionate regard for all living beings, whose primary concern is to rescue them from suffering.
This is indeed suffering; how could you not know this? When he was thus addressed, his thoughts continued without ceasing."
When the fifth night had reached its midpoint, a cool breeze suddenly touched his body; it was as refreshing as bathing in cold water.
Consequently, his vision was restored and the horse was able to rise. After traveling several *li*, he suddenly saw several acres of green grass; he dismounted and ate his fill.
He also saw a pond with water as sweet and clear as a mirror, whereupon he drank from it. His life was fully restored, and both man and horse were revived.
Xī said, "I reckon this must not be the old water and grass; it is surely the result of the power of my sincere resolve and the compassionate bestowal of a Bodhisattva.

From there, he was able to cross the shifting sands and reach the kingdom of Gaochang, where the king received him with great honor. Although the king earnestly requested him to stay, Xuanzang would not remain.
He was subsequently escorted to the Western Regions. The Master traveled through the territories of the Five Indias for eighteen years, visiting one hundred and thirty-five countries.

All the perils and hardships he encountered along the way were met with safety. While this was due to the power of the Master’s long-cherished vows, it was truly the result of the Bodhisattva’s compassionate protection. (From his original biography.)
Shi Zhi-xuan, Dharma Master Zhi-xuan, styled Hou-jue, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Hongya in Meizhou.

He expounded upon the sutras and śāstras, and those who looked up to him among both monastics and laity were so numerous that the shoes outside his door had already become many by day’s end. Furthermore, he studied the classics and scriptures of non-Buddhist traditions, numbering in the hundreds.
In his discourses on the family [of the Buddha], there was nothing he did not encompass. He often regretted that his native accent was not correct;

thus, while reciting the *Mahāpratisarā-dhāraṇī* at Mount Xianger, he dreamed of a divine monk who cut out his tongue and replaced it with another. The next day, his speech suddenly changed to the Qin dialect.

During the Taiping Hengguang era of Emperor Wenzong, while an imperial dish was being prepared in the palace kitchen, the Emperor’s attendants suddenly heard the sound of "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" calling out from within a cluster of eggs.
Consequently, an edict was issued prohibiting the use of chicken eggs. Furthermore, the Emperor was excessively fond of oysters and clams; prior to this, the officials along the coastal regions...

They were presented in succession. The attendants were also weary from their labors. One day, among the imperial delicacies being served, there was one that filled the entire platter; it was a melon that could not be split open.

The Emperor, observing its extraordinary nature, immediately burned incense and offered a prayer. Suddenly, it took the form of a Bodhisattva, with all the features of a Brahma-realm being perfectly complete and its appearance most lovely.
He then placed it in a casket of *suvarṇa* sandalwood and covered it with jade-embroidered silk, bestowing it upon Xingshan Monastery.
The Emperor ordered that he be shown due courtesy. He questioned his ministers, asking, "What auspicious omen is this? Prime Minister Li Gongdeyu replied, "Your servant does not know;

I only know that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue has manifested in a clear response. Regarding the principles of the Buddhas, I have heard that there is the Chan Master Hengzheng at Mount Zhongnan, who possesses great illumination regarding the Buddha-dharma and is of vast learning and powerful memory.
Thereupon, an edict was issued for him to enter the palace, and the Emperor questioned him. Hengzheng said, "I am but a poor..."

I have heard that all things respond to stimuli without fail; this is precisely to awaken and nourish Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, it is said in the sutras: "To those who are to be saved by this body, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "I have already seen the Bodhisattva’s body, but I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma. Zheng replied, "Does Your Majesty regard this body as permanent or impermanent? [The Emperor] replied, "It is certainly impermanent. Zheng said, "If it is impermanent, how can it be called real? The Emperor said, "It is indeed unreal. Zheng said, "If it is unreal, why do you not believe that the preaching of the Dharma is likewise unreal? The Emperor said, "I see that the preaching of the Dharma is indeed unreal, but I do not yet believe that my own hearing is unreal. Zheng said, "If Your Majesty does not believe that your hearing is unreal, then you must believe that the preaching of the Dharma is real. If you believe that the preaching of the Dharma is real, then you must also believe that your hearing is real. "Is this true? The Emperor said, "It is a rare and marvelous thing; I believe it deeply. Zheng replied, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma.

The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy and contentment, such as he had never experienced before. He issued an edict to all the monasteries throughout the realm, ordering each to establish a statue of Avalokiteśvara in gratitude for this extraordinary blessing.

Sengqie (Saṃgha) was a bodhisattva-monk from the country of He (Khotan) north of the Pamir Mountains. Accompanied by his disciple Huinan, he arrived together at Linhuai and requested land from the inhabitants of Xinyi Ward.
Having marked the boundaries, he declared that he would establish a monastery at this very spot.

Lan then dug into the earth and recovered an ancient stele; it was for the Xiangji Temple of the Qi Dynasty. He also obtained a golden image whose robe leaves were inscribed with the characters "Buddha King Universal Radiance" (Puzhao Wang Fo).
The local residents marveled at this wonder, saying, "His divine eye saw this beforehand; how could we not abandon our [former] ways?
Once, while staying at the home of the Hedaba clan, his body suddenly grew three chi longer than the bed and couch, leaving everyone in a state of astonishment.

It was strange. Next, he manifested the form of Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara. The entire family rejoiced and celebrated, their faith and reverence redoubled, and they subsequently donated their residence.
In the second year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Xiaohedao of the Zhongzong reign, the temple was granted the name Puguangwang.

In the fourth year, the Gengxu year, he manifested illness; sitting upright, he passed away, his divine countenance appearing as if still alive, with only his eyes closed. He was eighty years of age by secular reckoning.
13. His dharma-ordination age was unknown. He had spent thirty years in his native land and fifty-three years transforming the land of Tang.

He frequently manifested miraculous traces. The Emperor was filled with sorrow and grief; he then issued an edict for the ministers to escort the funeral procession, and the commoners and officials crowded the gates.
The Emperor asked Master Wanhui, "Who was that monk Saṃgha? He replied, "He was an emanation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."
Does not the Sūtra say: "To those who should be saved by a bhikṣu, he manifests in the form of a śramaṇa"?
During the Xiāngtōng era, there was one Páng Xūn, originally a garrison soldier of Xúzhōu, who had deserted from the Guì region and committed plunder along the way.
He attacked Sīzhōu and besieged its city. Atop the pagoda, [the deity] manifested his form; the external invaders all fell asleep, while those within the city were able to emerge.

He struck it; [the spirit] fled in terror and fell into the pit. The Prefect of Sizhou reported the matter to the throne, and the Master was subsequently conferred the title of Great Master Zhengsheng (Certified Sage).

From then on, he frequently appeared atop the pagoda in the form of a young monk. The entire prefecture turned out to gaze upon him; however, his appearances served as omens of both good and ill fortune.

At that time, those who sought wind obtained wind; those who sought children obtained children. Now, it is heard that among those who personally pay their respects, there are many who do not see the physical form of the deity at all.
If one sees a smiling countenance, it is auspicious; otherwise, it is ominous. Such is the difficulty of fathoming this matter.
It continued until the reign of Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty, when he turned his affairs toward the south of the Yangtze River and first attacked and captured Si.
The Venerable Ga appeared in a dream to a local citizen, saying, "It is not appropriate to underestimate the enemy. When this reached the Prefect, he did not believe it.
However, from then on, every household had the same dream. Upon being informed of this, [the enemy] finally surrendered, and the entire population of the prefecture relied upon Ga’s protection.
Whenever anyone in the world builds a sacred hermitage, they invariably erect a true image of Ga, labeling it "The Great Sage Monk Śāṅgha."
Furthermore, he made requests for blessings that were mostly fulfilled according to people's hearts.
Chan Master An was a native of Bingzhou. He took the Pure Land as his true place of refuge and practiced the Vaipulya Repentance while wearing [the prescribed robes].

He was diligent without fail. Though he suffered slightly from illness, his practice of meditative contemplation did not diminish. He beheld the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, appearing in the sky;
they remained there for a long time without vanishing. Dao’an summoned painters from within his jurisdiction, but none were able to depict them.

Suddenly, two men appeared, saying they had come from the Western Capital and intended to travel to Mount Wutai. They volunteered their services to paint the forms and features of the Bodhisattvas. He had them painted.
When the task was completed, he presented him with two pairs of shoes and suddenly vanished without a trace.

Knowing that his karmic conditions for the Western Paradise had ripened, Hu’an told his disciples, "I am now going to be reborn there; who can accompany me? A young boy prostrated himself and said, "I wish to follow my teacher."
He then ordered [the boy] to go bid farewell to his parents. The parents thought it was a joke and had him bathe and put on clean robes;

he entered the dharma-hall and, after reciting the Buddha’s name for a short while, passed away. Da’an rebuked them, saying, "How could you have let him depart prematurely? Da’an then took up a brush and composed a hymn of praise for the two Bodhisattvas:
"Avalokiteśvara assists from afar to receive him; Mahāsthāmaprāpta aids from afar to welcome him. The precious vase is manifest upon his crown; The transformation Buddhas appear."

The light before my crown shines as we travel together through the lands of the ten directions. Holding flowers and awaiting the nine births, I pray that with your hands of compassion, you will uplift and encourage me as we journey westward together.
Having finished this eulogy, he took leave of his disciples, entered the ritual arena, and commanded his followers to assist him in the practice of Buddha-recitation.
He passed away sitting upright; he was eighty years of age.
Shi Falang:
Falang was a native of Gusu. He recited the *Avalokiteśvara-vidyā-mantra*, and its divine efficacy manifested repeatedly. In the second year of the Longshuo era, [he...]
Princess Chengyang fell gravely ill. Someone informed [the Emperor] that Tanlang was capable of reciting secret mantras and could frequently cure illnesses through such practice.

The Emperor summoned Lang to the palace; he established an altar and performed recitations, and after two nights, the Princess recovered. She then petitioned the Emperor to change the name of the temple to Guanyin Temple so that he might reside there.
Shi Sengxuan:
Shi Sengxuan was a native of Bingzhou. At the age of ninety-six, he encountered Master Daocuo’s *Anle ji* (Collection on Peaceful Joy) and lectures on the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.

He then first turned his mind toward the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*). Fearing that his life would soon come to an end, he performed one thousand prostrations to the Buddha day and night and recited the name of Amitābha.
For five years, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha eighty thousand times with single-minded devotion and without indolence. As his end approached, he told his disciples:
"Amitābha Buddha has come to bestow upon me his fragrant robe; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta stand in formation before me, and transformation Buddhas fill the void of space.
From here to the west lies nothing but the Pure Land. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Shi Huaiyu:
Master Huaiyu’s secular surname was Gao, and he was a native of Danqiu. He strictly observed the Vinaya precepts with a character as upright and sharp as a mountain peak.

He maintained the practice of eating a single meal a day and remaining seated in meditation throughout the long hours, such that fleas and lice multiplied freely upon him. Wearing only a single garment of coarse cloth, he practiced the method of repentance, reciting his daily liturgy with devotion.
He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times and chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand scrolls.
On the ninth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, he suddenly beheld sacred images from the West, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

One person was carrying a white silver platform and entered through the window. Yù said, "I ought to have received a golden platform; why has this silver platform come out instead? Yù then redoubled his devotion.

At that time, the Buddha’s light filled the room. On the thirteenth day, during the hour of the Ox (2–4 a.m.), a white tuft of light appeared once more, and the assembly of holy beings filled the room.
Yu said, "If you smell a wondrous fragrance, know that my life is coming to an end. After she spoke this verse, the fragrance permeated the room and the assembly of disciples filled it completely.
They beheld Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, their bodies the color of purple gold, together with Vajrapāṇi.
The platform came to welcome her, and Yù ended her life with a smile; her physical body remains present to this day.
As for Shénzhì Shénzhì, he was a native of Yìwū in Lī Prefecture. His secular surname was Lì. From his youth, he possessed pure integrity and earnestly delighted in renouncing the household life.
He took Veyixiao (Weixiao) of Yunjian Temple as his teacher. He ate but one meal per day and maintained the *Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-mantra*.

He constantly consecrated water with this mantra to cure the hundred ailments; those who drank it were mostly healed. The common people followed him in succession, providing him with an immeasurable amount of offerings daily, and they called him the "Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika" (Dabei Heshang).
During the Dazhong era, he entered the capital of Jingzhao. At that time, the daughter of the Chancellor Pei Xiu was possessed by a ghost.

A deity possessed him. After he maintained his mantra for seven days, he was restored to health. He subsequently petitioned for the temple’s official plaque, naming it "Dazhong Shengshou" (Great Zhong Prosperity and Longevity).
(The above eight items are from the *Song Gaoseng zhuan* [Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty].
Compiled by Dong Xiong.)
During the Zhenguan era, there was Dong Xiong of Hedong, who served as an Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review (Dali Si).

Having been a person of faith and reverence from his youth, he had maintained a vegetarian diet for ten years. In the fourteenth year [of Zhenguan], on account of the matter involving Li Xiandong, the Sovereign became greatly incensed.

He dispatched the Imperial Commissioner Wei Cong to conduct an interrogation with extreme urgency, resulting in the detention of several dozen people, including Li Jingxuan, the Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review, and Wang [Shizhi], the Head of the Office of Records.

Xin was seated in the same row as him. Xiong was confined in the same cell with other prisoners, yet he focused his mind on the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), reciting it thirty times every day.

At night, while sitting in meditation and chanting the sutra, his shackles suddenly loosened of their own accord and fell to the ground. Startled, Xiong informed Xin and Xuan; Xin and Xuan came together to look at them.

The locks were firmly secured on the ground, yet the hook and the lock were separated by several feet. He immediately informed the guards; that night, Surveillance Commissioner Zhang Shouyi was on duty.
He ordered an official to fasten the locks and examine them with a torch. Seeing that the locks remained unfastened despite being separated, he found it most strange.
He locked and sealed them again with paper and a written note before departing. Xiong, as usual, continued reciting the sutras. Five...
During the middle watch, the lock again fell off with a sound. Sengxiong again informed Xinxuan and the others. When dawn arrived, they told Jingxuan to examine it;
the seal and title remained as before, yet the lock had separated of its own accord.

Jingxuan had long been a non-believer in the Buddha-dharma, and his wife, who recited the scriptures, would often say to him, "Why do you allow yourself to be seduced by barbarian deities and read these books? Upon witnessing this miracle performed by Sengxiong, [he was moved].

He then deeply realized the fault of his lack of faith and only then understood that the Buddha is a Great Sage. At that time, Xīn also recited the names of the eight bodhisattvas thirty thousand times.

When he unlocked the door during the day, it fell off; looking at it, it was as if it were a male [animal]. He marveled at this extraordinary event, and before long, both were released from their ordeal. (From *Mingbao Shiyi*)
Xu Shancai, Xu Shancai, was a native of Liquan County. He regularly observed the fasts and precepts and recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra more than a thousand times.
He frequently performed meritorious deeds at Yanxing Temple in the capital. This continued until the eleventh month of the second year of the Wude era.

On his way home from a business matter, he encountered Hu bandits on the road and was captured and taken away. Upon reaching the southern border of Youzhou, the Hu bandits—who were cruel and vicious—had already seized several thousand Han people.
Each was bound hand and foot and led toward Hongya Cliff, where they were to be executed one by one; their heads would fall over the precipice.
Seeing that those before him had all been killed and knowing for certain that he could not escape, Shancai did nothing but recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
It continued without ceasing for even a moment. Next, he arrived at the place where Śrīgupta was; when the blade first descended and as it struck, his mind remained unconscious.

At the very moment of the killing, the sun was just in the hour of Shen (5–7 p.m.), and by the time the first watch had passed, he realized his body was sitting on a tree branch deep within a ravine, more than three hundred paces from the bank. He thought to himself, "Why am I here? After a long while, he finally understood.

Today he was about to be killed; for what reason did he not die? His body remained whole upon the tree. He then rubbed his head with his hand and felt a slight pain at the nape of his neck, yet there was no injury.
He immediately realized that by recollecting Avalokiteśvara, he had preserved his life and limbs. At that time, the fifteenth-day moon was bright;
as he had no clothes and could find no food, several days passed until he became extremely hungry and cold. In the morning, gradually...
Descending from the tree, he followed the stream eastward for two li. Within the stream, he found a sheepskin cloak and a pair of leather boots;

putting them on, he was relieved of the cold. After traveling another li, he obtained a bowl of peaches and jujubes—vivid green and crimson-white, appearing as if freshly plucked—amounting to about one *sheng*;
eating them, he was relieved of hunger. This could not have happened were it not for the supernatural power of Avalokiteśvara.

How could it be that in the middle of winter, one obtained fresh peaches and jujubes? Having been spared from hunger and cold, one’s physical strength was restored. Gradually ascending the southern slope, I reached the south bank;
looking back toward the north, I saw the enemy camp for several li, where men and beasts were clamoring and had not yet retired to sleep.
Looking toward my home, I hurried along for about fifty li; knowing the bandits were gradually receding, my body and mind became peaceful and at ease. I remained there alone.
He rested beneath a tree, sitting cross-legged in recitation and contemplation, until he fell asleep without realizing it. At the fourth watch, he suddenly woke;
opening his eyes, he saw a massive blue wolf crouching directly before him, pressing its snout against his nose. Upon seeing this, Cāi closed his eyes again and thought:
"If you are truly my enemy, I pray that you devour my body to repay my past transgressions. Let us each cast aside our bonds of enmity and together give rise to benevolence."

"O Compassionate One! If you are Avalokiteśvara, I pray that you save this disciple and grant them peace and security. Having spoken these words, he opened his eyes and looked, but saw no trace of her.
One should know that the power of the roots of goodness of the Buddhas' kindness and compassion responds to conditions according to circumstances, bringing infinite benefit.
That those who recite [the name] today find no efficacy is truly due to a light-hearted attitude, as well as the influence of past and present karmic evils.
This is why it is difficult to evoke a response. When Śubhakarasiṃha reached his destination, he presented some leftover peaches and jujubes to the monastics and laypeople;
they knew that [the prophecy] was real and not false. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*, by Śramaṇa Cizang.)

Chan Master Jizang’s family name was Jin; his father’s name was Wulin. Having attained the first rank of officialdom, he was the preeminent authority in state deliberations, yet he had no offspring at all.
His anxiety grew ever more profound. Having long revered the principles of Buddhism, he sought its protective grace.

She commissioned one thousand copies of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, praying for the birth of a single child. She further vowed that if the child were to grow up, he would resolve to attain the Bodhi-mind and deliver all living beings.
A spiritual omen appeared as a manifest response: she dreamed that a star fell into her lap, and she subsequently became pregnant. On the eighth day of the fourth month, [she gave birth].
On this auspicious day, both monastics and laypeople shared in the celebration; it was a rare and wondrous occasion. As his years had already advanced, he grew weary of worldly splendors.
Profoundly realizing that all things are impermanent and ultimately return to emptiness and stillness, he subsequently left the household life during the Zhenguan era.

Moved by his sincerity, two bodhisattvas descended from heaven and personally conferred the precepts upon him. He extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma, bringing vast benefit to humans and devas, just as his father had prayed.
"May this vow not be in vain. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang Dynasty*) Shi Zijué was a native of Wangdu in Boling.
From his youth, he grew weary of worldly life and devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya, Sutras, and Shastras, laboring with diligent perseverance for nine years.
For many years, he had delved into the subtle mysteries of the Dharma. While traveling through the borders of Pingshan County, he came upon the Chonglin Mountain Monastery.

Its forests were dense and its valleys deep; tigers and wolves frequented the area, their tracks overlapping one another. He subsisted solely on gathered fruits and vegetables, eating but a single meal at dawn. He reflected that since first entering the Dharma, he had been practicing in this manner.
He made forty-eight vows, equal in number to those of the Buddhas during their causal stages. His first vow was that he would always follow the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika.
Subsequently, he vowed to cast an image of Mahākāruṇika and establish a temple for it. As soon as he spoke, his words were answered by a response, and offerings poured in from all directions.
He had the image cast in pure gold; it stood forty-nine feet high, with a majestic and solemn countenance. Upon reaching the following year...
The harvest ripened, and the temple was completed accordingly. Thereupon, he recited before the altar until the third watch of the night. He beheld two rays of divine light, the color of pure gold;
within that brilliant radiance, he saw Amitābha Buddha, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attending him on his left and right.

The Buddha extended his golden arm and called out in a self-awakening voice. Gradually descending from the clouds, he touched the crown of [his] head and said: "Maintain your vow without wavering; you must not be negligent or indolent.
To benefit all beings should be your priority. You may go; I shall follow. Act according to your own will. Having finished speaking, the clouds withdrew.
There was not even a trace of his whereabouts. Having fulfilled his vows, Huizhao returned to the mountain forests to select a place for his final rites.

On the night of the full moon in the second month of the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, a divine being appeared with only half his body visible, resembling Vaiśravaṇa, and said to him, "Master, you shall pass away this year.
Huizhao raised his hand in thanks to the divine being and said, "The destiny of coming and going is fixed."
"I have received your command. On the fourteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he suddenly returned to the state of quiescent extinction.
As for the monk Sengren: his secular surname was Shi; he was a native of Chenliu in Pei Commandery. Sengren pricked his own blood to transcribe various sutras. Because of this—
He read the *Mahākaruṇā-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* and investigated the forty-two arms until he reached the "Fearless Hand. Doubting its authenticity, he established a ritual altar and prayed for ten days.
Suddenly, the true mudrā appeared from the sky; both hands were clearly visible. He then commissioned an artist to paint these arms.
Some people criticized and slandered him, but he endured it, once again applying himself with refined sincerity and making a devout appeal. The artist washed his brush in copper...
Within his bowl, he suddenly perceived a single *ratnagarbha* flower; its stem, calyx, and petals were all vividly clear. Those who beheld it were struck with wonder and admiration.
He drew blood from his own body to transcribe scriptures, totaling two hundred and eighty-three fascicles. He painted a Vaiśravaṇa pavilion thirty-five feet high and a gate sixteen feet wide.
He produced three scrolls as models for the painting of the merits of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and he himself composed the *Dabei* (Great Compassion) [Sūtra].
His treatises comprise six fascicles, all of which are preserved in various bookcases. He passed away on the tenth day of the seventh month in the twelfth year of the Xiantong era.
His posthumous title was Guanghui (Extensive Wisdom), and his stupa was named Nianding (Mindfulness and Concentration).
Shi Huiri, the Dharma Master Huiri, was surnamed Xin and was a native of Donglai. He received full ordination during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong.

Later, he encountered Tripitaka Master Yijing and vowed to travel to the Western Regions. Initially, he embarked upon a ship to cross the sea, and after three years had passed, he reached the South China Sea.
Having traversed various kingdoms—including Kunlun, Fo-shih, and Siṃhala Island—he reached India.
There he paid homage to the sacred sites, sought out Sanskrit manuscripts, and visited virtuous teachers for thirteen years, inquiring after and receiving their dharma instructions.
Desiring to benefit others, he struck his mendicant’s staff and set out alone on his journey home. Through the Snowy Mountains and the lands of the Hu, he traveled for another four years. Once...

Having endured manifold sufferings, he felt profound weariness with Jambudvīpa. He inquired throughout India among the masters of the Tripiṭaka: "In which country or direction is there joy without suffering?
What Dharma or what practice can lead one to quickly see the Buddha? All those consulted praised the Pure Land in unison, saying: "Regarding swiftness, this is the path for a single lifetime;
at the end of this present body, one will certainly attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss."

Jie personally obtained the opportunity to serve Amitābha Buddha. Having heard [the teachings], he received them upon the crown of his head. He gradually traveled to the kingdom of Gandhāra in North India.
To the northeast of the royal city, there was a great mountain; upon this mountain was a statue of Avalokiteśvara. He prayed with sincere devotion.
He obtained many manifestations of the Buddha’s body. Day after day, he prostrated for seven days, vowing to fast until death as his ultimate limit.
When the seventh night had not yet ended, Guanyin appeared in the air with a purple-gold body over ten feet tall, seated upon a precious lotus flower.
Extending his right hand, he stroked the crown of Ri’s head and said, "If you wish to transmit the Dharma to benefit yourself and others, [seek rebirth in] the Pure Land of the West."
He exhorted them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, recite the sutras, and dedicate their merit toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the realm of Amitābha Buddha.

He said, "Once you have reached that land, you will see the Buddha and me, thereby attaining great benefit; you should know for yourselves that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished. As I was exhausted from fasting for days, hearing this strengthened my resolve. Upon reaching the mountain ridge, I returned home.

In total, he traveled through more than seventy countries over a period of eighteen years. It was not until the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era that he finally reached Chang’an, where he presented the Emperor with authentic Buddhist icons, Sanskrit scriptures (*brahmalipi*), and other items.
These awakened the Emperor’s mind, and the Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Tripitaka Master Cimin.

Throughout his life, he constantly and diligently cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land, composing the *Wǎngshēng Jìngtǔ Jí* (Collection on Rebirth in the Pure Land), which has circulated in the world. His path was consistent with that of Shandao.
Shao Kang. This is an instance of different times converging in a single transformation. (The above three entries are from the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).

A Mian soldier was a native of Changsha; his surname was Wu. He was a soldier who campaigned against the Mian tribes and made his living by fishing and hunting. Once he caught a white tortoise, which was beautiful and...
He ate it, whereupon his entire body broke out in sores. They became festering and painful, such that he could not endure the agony for even a moment.
His eyebrows, beard, and the fingers of his hands and feet all fell off, yet he did not die immediately. He then went to beg in the market of An-nan. A monk, moved by pity, said to him:
"You should turn your mind toward the recitation of the Great Compassion Mantra; I shall orally transmit it to you. If you can practice with diligence, you will surely receive a favorable reward."
He followed her words and accepted them, reciting them with single-minded devotion. Thereafter, his sores gradually subsided and his fingers grew back until they were fully restored.
He then shaved his head and became a monk.
Ouyang Can was a physician in Xuzhou. He habitually recited the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī at home.

One day, he entered the city and was returning late in the evening when he encountered heavy rain and torrential downpour, accompanied by the crashing of thunder and lightning. Midway along the road, there were mountains and forests flanking both sides of the path.
The dense forests and deep valleys were teeming with fierce beasts. Càn was filled with constant terror.
Just as the rain grew even more violent, suddenly a massive creature appeared before him, only ten-odd paces away and over a zhang in length, its color pure white;
he could not distinguish its hands or feet, but it simply led the way forward. Càn’s fear and trembling reached their peak; at that moment, he wished to recite divine mantras aloud, yet his mouth—

The mouth was already sealed shut. Xu Yan then focused his mind on reciting [the mantra] without ceasing. Suddenly, the demon vanished. As he drew closer to his home, the rain also gradually subsided.
Xu Yan.
During the Linqi era, Xu Yan of Yongxing Ward in the capital made his living by catching fish. Later, he fell gravely ill;

he was as if dead, his body red as fire and in pain as if being scorched by flames. He said that he saw only chariot fires coming to burn his body, for the authorities had demanded that he provide too many fish and had sent him to undergo retribution for his sins.
Several days had already passed, and he was repeatedly born and died again. His relatives exhorted him...
He performed meritorious deeds by subsequently commissioning two statues of Avalokiteśvara and ensuring that his entire household abstained from wine and meat; consequently, he was cured.
(The above three items are from the *Zhuan yin lu* [Record of Transformed Causes].
By Shi Daoyi.)
Chan Master Baoyun Daoyi was a man of unknown origins. In the fourth year of the Tiānfú era of the Shí Jìn dynasty (939 CE), he established a hermitage on the northwest side of Mount Tiānzhú.
Clad in grass and subsisting on wood, his lofty conduct transcended the mundane. One night, he saw a light illuminating the heavens atop the front peak;
tracing its source, he looked and discovered a wondrous tree that no one could identify. The Master then took it.
He commissioned the artisan Kong Renqian to carve an image of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. One night, he dreamed of a person in white robes who said, "The statue is already completed.
Tomorrow, a monk will arrive from Luoyang carrying ancient Buddha śarīra relics; you should seek them.
Subsequently, the monk indeed arrived. Following the dream, he sought them and obtained three śarīra, which he enshrined within the [statue].
As for the crown of the Master’s head, thereafter the śarīra constantly appeared within his crown and *uṣṇīṣa*, with brilliant white light radiating forth.
From this time on, his spiritual wonders became widely renowned. —Recorded by Shi Zhijue.
Chan Master Zhijue Yanshou was a native of the Wang family of Yuhang. In his youth, he served as the military commander of Huating;

because he used official funds to release captive animals, he was sentenced to death. At the time of his execution, his countenance remained unchanged. King Wenmu marveled at this and granted him permission to leave the household life.

He resided at Longce Monastery, where he performed manual labor to provide for the community and maintained a single meal a day, sitting upright without lying down. He received the Dharma from Tiantai.

National Teacher Shao initially resided at Xuedou, and subsequently returned to West Lake. In the second year of the Jianlong era, King Zhongyi invited him to serve as the second patriarch of Yongming.

He remained there for fifteen years, during which his assembly regularly numbered two thousand. He was bestowed the title Zhijue (Wisdom Enlightenment) and performed the rite of offering food to spirits at night.
He released living beings at dawn. Six times a day, he scattered flowers and practiced the Way, reciting one hundred and eight items daily without ever failing for even a moment.
With his remaining strength, he chanted the *Lotus Sūtra*, totaling thirteen thousand fascicles. He was also known by the sobriquet Baoyizi (The One Embracing the One).

Previously, while in meditative contemplation, he had been graced by the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who poured nectar into his mouth, whereby he attained great eloquence. He composed the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred [fascicles].
His works comprise twenty fascicles, which harmonize the differing views of the Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien schools. His poems and verses number several million words and have been propagated abroad;
the King of Goryeo sent a letter expressing his devotion as a disciple and presented him with a *kāṣāya* robe woven with gold thread, a rosary of amethyst, and a golden water pitcher as offerings.
He passed away in the eighth year of the Kaibao era [975] and was cremated.
Śarīra relics fell like rain; the stūpa was established at Mount Jingci. (The preceding two entries are from the *Wulin gaoseng shilüe*).
Huìbō was from Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang Province. There is a mountain in the ocean that he took as a model for Potalaka in South India, and there the Great Being...

He constantly manifests himself therein. During the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, a monk from the Western Regions arrived at Putuo Cave and offered prayers while burning all ten of his fingers.
He personally beheld the wondrous form of the Bodhisattva, who preached the essentials of the Dharma to him;
thus, his fame and traces first became renowned. Subsequently, a Japanese monk named Huie obtained a painted image of the Bodhisattva at Mount Wutai and intended to return with it.
When the boat reached the cave in his home country, [the image] would not go inside. Consequently, it was enshrined at the residence of a local man named Zhang by the side of the mountain.
Zhang repeatedly witnessed divine wonders and eventually abandoned his dwelling to establish the Guanyin Temple (Guanyinyuan).

When the regional governor heard of this, he dispatched a court official to welcome the image to the city to bestow blessings upon the people. Shortly thereafter, a monk named Jizhong came seeking [the site].
He carved it into a wooden door-bolt. After one month, the image was completed, yet the monk did not appear; what is currently installed here is that very image.

In the third year of the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty, Wang Shunfeng was dispatched as an envoy to the Three Han kingdoms. When his ship reached the cave, a black wind suddenly arose.
A giant tortoise carried the boat toward the mountain. Shun performed an offering and prayer, whereupon the Bodhisattva manifested his form. The boat returned safely.

When this was reported to the imperial court, gold and silk were bestowed, and the temple was moved to the southern slope of Haicen Mountain; its plaque was inscribed with the name "Baotuo. Whenever prayers were offered for rain or fine weather, they were invariably answered.

(This is recorded in the *Jige lüe* and the *Tongzai*. [The monk] Huikuan of the Tang dynasty was an emanation of the tenth incarnation of Guanyin; details may be found in his biography. This account is from the *Shimén Wénzì Chán*; it is not elaborated upon here.)
Recorded. Cen Wenben’s manuscript.
He constantly recited the "Universal Gate Chapter" (Pumenpin). While traveling by boat on the Wu River, his vessel capsized; he followed the waves to the shore. Later, at home...
He held a vegetarian feast. One monk said, "The world is currently in turmoil; fortunately, you have not been caught up in the calamity. You will ultimately attain wealth and honor.
Indeed, he reached the court of Emperor Taizong and served as Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling). (From the *Tongji*, Song dynasty.)

Master Jiyi of Shiyi was styled Changzhao; his surname was Hu, and he was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. He lectured on various sutras and treatises and composed commentaries and annotations for them.
While residing at Yuwang Temple in Siming, he dreamed that he ascended Mount Guoqing, where above him stood a precious pavilion.
The majestic dharma-throne was inscribed with the title "Mañjuśrī’s Platform. It was enclosed by a railing and barrier, making it impossible to enter.
Suddenly, he beheld Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva slowly emerging from the hall; after a brief moment of meeting, he felt his own body and that of Avalokiteśvara merge indistinguishably.
Thereupon, he awoke in a start. From that time forward, his joy in expounding the Dharma became inexhaustible. Some say this was his entry into the wisdom of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*).

Riding upon the compassion that benefits all beings, they accord with the awakening of the Buddhas above, for they have realized the Unsurpassed; they accord with sentient beings below, for ordinary and sage share the same essence.
Who else could it be, apart from Avalokiteśvara, who has attained this mind?
Shi Zongyuan:
As for Zongyuan, his surname was Gongs and he was a native of Gaodi. He was solitary, pure, and upright; ordinary people could not see him even on casual occasions.
Every day he separately recited the *Avalokiteśvara-parivarta* chapter [of the Lotus Sutra]. Previously, there had been a physiognomist who said that Zongyuan’s life span would be short.

He urged [the disciples] to receive and uphold the "Universal Gate Chapter. In the tenth month of the fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he predicted the time of his passing and instructed the carpenters to fashion a seat in the shape of a deer's head, repeatedly urging them to hasten the work, saying, "It must be ready for the midday meal tomorrow."
At this time, he indeed passed away while seated in meditation at the age of eighty-three. He compiled the *Luoxi ji* (Collection from the West of Luoyang) and composed fifty elegies (*wanci*).
One of them states: "In all the world, there shall likely be no one who reaches a hundred years; at the end of a hundred years, one becomes dust within a tomb.
I am now eighty-three; I myself compose this dirge to bid farewell to this body. He was buried in a single set of paper garments. Later, when the grave was opened, his spirit...

The physical appearance remained vividly present. His disciple, maintaining a serene composure, received these instructions and interred him within a mountain cave. (These two entries are from the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* [Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty] by Shi Jizhong.)
The Dharma Master Jizhong, whose courtesy name was Facheng, was of the Qiu clan of Yongjia. His parents sought an heir at a Buddhist shrine;

they both dreamed of a monk who bestowed upon them a fine child, saying, "A venerable one from Luoxi has entrusted this child to you for your care. From the moment his mother conceived, she loathed meat and blood.
From childhood, whenever he saw a Buddha image, he would invariably pay his respects. At the age of eight, he entered Kaiyuan Temple and received the grace of ordination.
He immediately went to Nanhu to study under Guangzhi. Due to the hardships of his studies, he fell ill; thereupon, he practiced the Samādhi of Invoking Avalokiteśvara.

The Great Being (Mahāsattva) emitted light and poured water over his head, whereupon his illness was instantly cured. Subsequently, he attained profound insight into both the teachings and contemplation, becoming free from all obstructions. Guangzhi...
He held him in deep esteem and frequently commissioned him to lecture on his behalf. When Chan Master Xuedou Xian saw him, he sighed and said, "The Way of Siming now has a successor.
Wang Gu.
In the summer of the second year of the Yuánfú era, there was no rain for four months. Wáng Gǔ, the local governor of Yuánzhōu, went to pray at the Śāri-stone stūpa on Mount Mùpíng.
A light shone from within a rock cave, and he beheld the Great Being dressed in white robes, his body adorned with golden necklaces.
He obtained śāri relics, five-colored and as large as jujube fruits, each containing the form of a pavilion and tower. He then went to the stūpa site on Mount Yǎngshān and saw the [relics of] Sī...
The Great Being of the Prefecture, Vimalakīrti, and the Arhats were seated on his left and right. Thereafter, a great rain fell in abundance.
The Prefecture reported this to the Court, and by imperial decree, the Muping Pagoda was named Huìqìng (Assembly Celebration) and the Yangshan Pagoda was named Ruìqìng (Auspicious Celebration).

Shi Yanlun: Dharma Master Yanlun was a member of the Zhou clan of Qiantang. His courtesy name was Qingbian. In his youth, he underwent the ritual for receiving the precepts after passing the scriptural examinations.

He studied the teachings and contemplations under Master Huixian at the Faming Monastery. Once, he suffered from a contagious disease that could not be cured by any medicine; consequently, he applied himself with great diligence to the practice of contemplation.

Regarding his title "Yin Zun" (Honored by Sound): He once dreamed of a woman who, using a chisel, opened his chest and replaced his heart. He then rubbed it with his hand, whereupon his ailment was immediately cured.

Everything he had previously read, he could now recall without fail; he composed writings at the speed of a running pen, all of which were characterized by elegance and refinement. Everyone regarded this as a manifestation of *pratibhāna* (eloquence).

Shi Huicai, the Dharma Master Huicai of Leifeng Monastery in Hangzhou, conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the monk Lingzhi Yuanzhao and a thousand members of the monastic and lay communities in the third month of the first year of the Yuanfeng era.
At the moment of the *karmavācanā* ceremony, he beheld the image of Avalokiteśvara emitting light from within the lecture hall.
The Great Ming. Recorded by Chan Master Shouyi Fazhen of Jingci Temple as "Jianguang. Calligraphed by Mi Fu.
Dharma Master Biancai erected this stone at Longjing.
Zhi Bai, the Vice Minister, while traveling from the capital to Linchuan in the second year of the Yuanfeng era, contracted an illness due to the heat.

He suddenly dreamed of a person dressed in white who sprinkled water upon him; from crown to heels he felt a refreshing chill. Upon waking, he was instantly restored to vigor. Thereupon, he compiled the *Gujin* (Collection of the Ancients).

Now, regarding his spiritual efficacy, he compiled the *Guanyin Ganying Ji* (Collected Records of Avalokiteśvara’s Responsive Manifestations) in four fascicles, which circulates in the world (carved on wooden blocks at Upper Zhong; the above five items are from the *Tongji*).

The Great Being’s divination slips consist of one hundred from India and one hundred and thirty from Yueyuantong, used to determine good and ill fortune; their responses are like echoes. Their manifestations are as follows:
This was recorded as being told by a transformation body of a Great Being (Mahāsattva). (From the *Shì mén zhèng tǒng*).
Scholar Zhang Kang:
Zhang Kang accumulated much merit and made a vow before the Buddha to recite the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
Tu was over sixty years old when he fell ill. With single-minded devotion, he recited the Buddha’s name and said to his family members, "The Western Pure Land is right here in front of the hall.
Amitābha Buddha sits upon a lotus flower, and I, your grandfather, am on the Golden Ground prostrating before the Buddha.

Having finished speaking, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away. Weng’er was his great-grandson; he died at the age of three. (The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "If one recites and upholds the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī...")

Regarding this chapter and its phrases: at the time of death, the Buddhas of the ten directions will all come to extend their hands to receive one. Whatever Buddha-land one wishes to be born in, one shall attain rebirth there in accordance with that vow. As for those who recite and uphold [this teaching], if they bathe in a river, a stream, or the great ocean, the sentient beings therein [shall likewise attain benefit].

If one receives the water used for this person’s ablutions and it moistens their body, all evil karma and heavy transgressions will be entirely extinguished, and they will immediately attain rebirth in a pure land in another direction, born by transformation from a lotus flower. How much more so for those who maintain the recitation!
If one makes a vow to recite it one hundred thousand times seeking rebirth in a pure land, there is no doubt that their aspiration will be fulfilled.
(The Daughter of the Wang Family)

The daughter of the Wang family was a native of Jixian. She recited daily the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, and sought deliverance through the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name).
Together with her stepmother, she cultivated the pure practices of the Pure Land. Later, she fell ill and invited a monk to explain the meditative methods of the Pure Land.

Suddenly, she asked for her robes and lay down in the auspicious posture (*śayyāsana*). Grasping the banner held in the hand of Avalokiteśvara, she remained silent and motionless. Her mother scattered ash upon...
To verify the manner of rebirth, he saw several lotus flowers emerge from within the ashes. (The two preceding entries are from the *Wǎngshēng jí*).

Master Zhūnshì of the Tiantai school was a native of Línghǎi in Tàizhōu. His learning and conduct were lofty and ancient, his fame eclipsing that of all in the Two Zhe regions. He was single-mindedly devoted to peace...
Yang once practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi for a period of ninety days. He studied so diligently that he vomited blood.

Upon entering the dharma hall, the skin on both his feet cracked; he vowed to die there. Suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw Avalokiteśvara extending a finger into his mouth and drawing out several worms.
Then, from the tip of the finger, nectar flowed forth and poured into his mouth. Upon awakening, his body and mind were refreshed and cool, and his illness was immediately cured.

He composed the *Jingtu jueyi xingyuan* (Resolving Doubts Concerning the Practices and Vows for the Pure Land) and the *Jingtu chanfa* (Repentance Ritual for the Pure Land), both of which were practiced throughout the world.

During the Tiānshèng era, on the eve of his passing, he lit incense and prostrated before the Buddha, vowing that the Buddhas would bear witness to his rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). That evening, he sat upright and passed away.
People saw a great star fall upon Mount Lingjiu (Gṛdhrakūṭa). He was then known as the Chan Master Ciyun. Furthermore, he constructed the Gōngmíng Chàntáng (Hall of the Repentance of Radiant Light).
At that time, whenever a single rafter was set up or a single tile was laid, he would invariably recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times.

Although it has repeatedly suffered from the ravages of war and fire, the structure remains standing tall and alone; this is due to the power of his vows. (From the *Wangsheng ji* and the *Wulin gaoseng zhuan*, by Shi Guding)
Chan Master Guding Ming was the fifteenth-generation descendant of Linji. As he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "Avalokiteśvara has arrived, holding a lotus flower.
He sat upright and passed away. When cremated, his tongue, teeth, and prayer beads remained unburnt.
There were countless five-colored śarīra relics. The national historian Mr. Wei composed a stele for him. His *Recorded Sayings of the Four Assemblies* (*Sìhuì yùlù*) circulates in the world.
(Cited from the *Jílüè de Míngsēng* [Compendium of Famous Monks of the Great Ming] and the *Xuéshì jí* [Collected Works of Scholar Sòng Jǐnglián].
— Śramaṇa Qiésōng.
Chan Master Mingjiao Qisong was the son of the Li family of Tanjin in Tengzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven.

After receiving full ordination, he habitually wore an image of the Holy Avalokiteśvara and recited its name ten thousand times daily. Among the sutras, treatises, and miscellaneous books, there was nothing he did not memorize extensively.
Having received the Dharma from Venerable Dongshan Cong, he styled himself Qianzi. His single room was serene and tranquil; he kept his door closed.

He composed writings, including the *Fujiao lun* (Treatise on Assisting the Teaching) in over one hundred thousand words, clarifying that the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism are fundamentally unified.

He also authored the *Dingzu tu* (Chart of the Determined Patriarchs) and the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage). Carrying these works with him, he entered the capital and presented them through the Prefectural Governor, the Imperial Academician Wang Su.
King Inmyong sighed in admiration and issued an edict for the work to be compiled by the Court of Dharma (Ch’waryo).

He honored him with the title Myǒnggyo (Enlightened Teaching) and granted his writings entry into the Buddhist canon. Both Duke Han Chung-hon and Duke O Yang-wǒn praised him; consequently, his fame resounded throughout the land.
When he entered parinirvāṇa and was cremated, three of his six sense organs remained uncorrupted: namely, the eyes, the tongue, and the organ of youth (the penis).
Together with his cranial bone and his prayer beads, these five items were preserved. The śarīra relics that emerged were red and white, pure and lustrous, shaped like large soybeans.
He was interred in a stūpa to the left of Yong’an Temple. His disciples compiled his writings, titled the *Xinjin ji* (Collected Works of Xinjin). (From the *Wulin gaoseng shilüe*)

Zhang Xiaochun had a grandson of five years who was unable to walk. Someone told him: "Recently, among the farmers in the Huaidian region, there was one who suffered from a chronic ailment of his legs and feet for a very long time.
He simply maintained the recitation of the name of Avalokiteśvara every day without ceasing, and consequently, he was moved by Avalokiteśvara’s manifestation."
He appeared and, leaving behind a four-line verse, said: "Great wisdom arises from the mind; within the mind, there is nothing to seek.
All meanings are fully accomplished; there is neither past nor present. After the farmer recited this verse for a full hundred days, his chronic illness was suddenly cured.
Thereupon, Xiaochun subsequently taught his grandson and the wet nurse to observe the precepts and recite it for two or three months; their gait and movement then became as they were before.

Those whose children suffer from ailments of the legs or feet will find that all are cured by reciting this. (From the *Yulu* [Recorded Sayings]; those who sought wisdom and intelligence all attained their desired results.
Zhai Ji, Zhai Ji, resided in Sian Town in Huzhou. At the age of fifty, he had no son; he painted an image of Avalokiteśvara and prayed to it most earnestly.
