When he arrived, his wife was pregnant. She dreamed of a woman dressed in white who presented her with a child on a platter; the child was exceedingly handsome and elegant.
The wife was overjoyed and wished to take him in her arms, but an ox lay across the middle, so that she could not reach him.
When the child was born, he died before the month was out. She prayed once more as she had before. Someone who heard of this told her, "The child craved beef; could it be for this reason? Jie.
He stood up in solemnity and made a vow that his entire family would no longer eat beef. Once again, he dreamed that the woman from before brought the child to him;

he took the child into his arms, and his wife subsequently gave birth to a son who grew to adulthood. (From the *Guǎngsì lù*. In secular tradition, it is commonly said that Guanyin is female in form; therefore, the Bodhisattva often manifests in a female appearance to facilitate easy awakening.
Recorded by Xǔ Zhikě.
Xu Ke was a native of Piling. Having once passed the local examination, he returned home after failing in the provincial palace examination.

One night, he dreamed of a person dressed in white who said to him, "You have no hidden virtue (yin-de), which is why you have not attained the rank. Xu Ke replied, "My family is poor and has no resources; how could I give anything to others?
The person in white said, "Why do you not study medicine? I will assist you with wisdom. Upon waking, Xu Ke followed these words, and indeed—

He attained the subtle mastery of Lu and Bian. Whenever there was a sick person, regardless of their noble or humble status, he would examine their condition and prescribe medicine without taking any payment.
Those whom he saved were beyond counting. Later, his nomination was again approved by the local assessment; he set out for the Ministry of Personnel and moored his boat at Pingwang.
Again, he dreamed of the aforementioned man in white robes, who presented him with a verse, saying: "The merit of your dispensing medicine is great.
Between Chen and Lou, in the hall, you called 'lu' and summoned 'six,' yet it was made 'five. Though you pondered it, you did not realize it; I have recorded this on a tablet.

In the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxing era, he was ranked sixth in the imperial examination, but because the Emperor did not include his name in the official record, he was subsequently raised to fifth place. Above him was Chen Zuyan, and below him was Lou.
Cai Fangsheng was formerly known as Boping; his courtesy name was Xinzhi.

A native of Jiaxing, he was a man of broad learning and high talent who failed to pass the civil service examinations despite repeated attempts. He devoted himself to the two teachings (Buddhism and Daoism).

One day, while traveling by the Mòhú Lake, he happened to visit a village temple. Seeing a statue of Avalokiteśvara standing exposed and drenched in rain, he immediately opened his bag and took out ten *jin* of silver.
Calling the presiding monk, he handed it to him, instructing him to repair the buildings.

The monk informed him that the project was large and the funds insufficient to complete the work. He subsequently provided four bolts of hemp cloth and seven garments, including one made of fine *kṣauma* silk.
The folds were newly fashioned. His servant requested that he stop them, saying, "As long as the sacred image remains unharmed, what does it matter to me even if I am left naked?
The monk wept and said, "It would not be difficult for you to give up silver, clothing, or cloth; however, these refreshments—how could they be easily obtained?
Later, when the work was finished, the official stayed overnight at the temple. In a dream, the guardian deity of the monastery told him, "Your descendants shall enjoy prosperity."

He enjoyed hereditary emoluments. His son, Zhou Bian, and his grandson, Zhou Chengfang, both passed the imperial examinations and became prominent officials. (The above two entries are from the *Yinzhi lu*).

Zhou Shengheng, a local official of Poyang, after being exempted from corvée labor, served the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) with great reverence. At the beginning of the Qingyuan era, he... [text fragment ends]
He vowed to transcribe two hundred fascicles of the sutras by hand to bestow upon others for recitation.

Having fasted and purified himself while copying, he had reached twenty fascicles when, as he held his brush with a steady hand, dozens of crows began to shriek and clamor upon the roof, refusing to depart despite being chased away. He rose and offered prayers before the image.
He went out to investigate and saw a crow struck by an arrow, bleeding profusely. A flock of crows tried to pull it out but could not; thus, the wounded bird cried out piteously.

Zhou Su recited the names of Ratnaśrī Tathāgata and Avalokiteśvara, the Savior from Suffering, and pointed with his writing brush at the wound. The arrow pulled itself out, and the crow flew into the sky.
While Zhou was offering praises, the arrow fell from within the skylight onto the side of the Buddha shrine. Such was the miraculous nature of this event.
At the end of the Chunxi era, Yang Liang, a foot soldier from Jianchang, fell ill. He saw two officials holding warrants who pursued him to the government office.
A king asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform while alive? He replied, "I served as a runner and laborer; whenever I encountered an assignment, I did not dare [to neglect it]."

He had exceeded the time limit. The King said, "I am not asking about this matter; what other meritorious deeds do you have? Liang then realized it was the Office of the Netherworld and said, "I have merely recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
The King asked again, "What other good deeds do you have? He replied, "A humble person like me—what good deed could I possibly claim?
I simply maintain my station and do no harm to others. The King ordered the registers to be inspected, and they were found to be as he had said. Thereupon, [his sentence] was changed.
The woodworker Lin,
from Nantai Temple in Fuzhou, requested to take back the old statue after a new Guanyin image had been fashioned and the former one destroyed. The woodworker Lin sought its restoration.
He served [the deity]. Later, while navigating a boat into the sea, the vessel was wrecked and he was drowning. In desperation, he called out to Guanyin, saying, "Will you not save me?

Suddenly, his body began to float. He found a plank and climbed upon it; amidst surging waves as high as the heavens, he traveled some several hundred li before being carried by the current into a small inlet.
There he recovered a chest of lost goods, which provided him with considerable means for his return home. This was not due to Guanyin Bodhisattva...
What need is there for the assistance of others? (The three preceding lines are from the *Zhuan yin lu*).
Praise to the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (Composed by the Dharma Master of Siming based on the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*).
Homage to the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa of the past. Present before us is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, who has perfected wondrous merit.
Possessing great compassion, within a single body and mind, he manifests a thousand hands and eyes to illuminate and perceive the dharma-realm,

protecting and sustaining all sentient beings, causing them to give rise to the vast bodhicitta, teaching them to uphold the perfect divine mantra, so that they may forever leave the evil realms behind and attain rebirth before the Buddhas.
The grave transgressions of the Avīci Hell, the evil diseases that entangle the body—none can save them, yet [this power] causes them all to be eliminated.

The samādhis and eloquence, whatever vows one seeks in this present life, shall all be fulfilled; of this there is no doubt. It can cause one to swiftly attain the Three Vehicles and early ascend to the stage of Buddhahood.
The power of its majestic spirit is beyond the reach of praise. Therefore, with a single mind, I take refuge and pay homage. (Siming said: "Contemplating...")

The "One Body with a Thousand Hands and Eyes" means that the hands possess the power to lift and pull, while the eyes possess the function of illuminating; this is precisely the thousandfold supernatural powers and wisdom.

That one body is endowed with a thousand hands and eyes, and the thousand hands and eyes do not depart from the one body, represents the fact that a single thought-moment is itself the thousandfold supernatural powers and wisdom, and that the thousandfold supernatural powers and wisdom do not depart from a single thought-moment. "Evil paths" refers to the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras. "Namo" (namas) means, in the language of China, "taking refuge in life" (*guiming*), also called "taking refuge" (*guiyi*).

"Samādhi" means, in the language of China, "right concentration" (*zhengding*). "The Three Vehicles" refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas. "Avīci" (Uninterrupted Hell) refers to the *Abhidharma* hell.

The Liturgy for Contemplating Avalokiteśvara (Composed by Chan Master Dahui Zonggao. Having repeatedly received the grace and protection of the Great Being, he wrote this text to further his aspirations.

Purify the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind). With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself with the five limbs touching the ground (the two hands, the two knees, and the head resting upon the earth).

Take refuge in Namo, the Compassionate Father of the Ten Directions, the Greatly Responsive and Miraculous Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. I have heard that the Bodhisattva [arises] from hearing and reflection...

Cultivation: Entering samādhi, one attains two kinds of conformity (above, conforming to the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing their identical power of compassion; below, conforming to the pure source of sentient beings in the six realms, sharing their identical yearning for pity).

One also attains the four inconceivables and the fourteen fearlessnesses (as both are elucidated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*). There are nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma: (1) manifesting the body of a Buddha to preach the Dharma;

(2) as a pratyekabuddha; (3) as a śrāvaka; (4) as a Brahmā king; (5) as Śakra-devendra; (6) as the god Īśvara; (7) as the god Maheśvara; (8) as a celestial general; (9) as Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Heavenly Kings; (10) as a minor king; (11) as a long-lived [deity]...

1. Laymen; 2. Laywomen; 3. Ascetics; 4. Kings; 5. Ministers; 6. Brahmins; 7. Vaiśyas; 8. Śūdras; 9. The fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and so forth; 10. Women; 11. Men; 12. Lay devotees; 13. Government officials; 14. Brahmins; 15. The fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and so forth; 16. Women; 17. Boys and girls; 18. Devas, nāgas, and so forth; 19. Vajrapāṇi deities.

The details are as in the "Universal Gate" (Pumen-pin) chapter; if categorized separately, there are thirty-five manifestations. Regarding the seven calamities and two requests: the seven calamities are (1) being burned by fire, (2) being swept away by water, (3) rākṣasas, (4) blades and staves, (5) malevolent spirits, (6) shackles and fetters, and (7) vengeful bandits.

The two requests are (1) requesting a son and (2) requesting a daughter. The details are as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Regarding the thirty-two manifestations: the details are as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. According to the *Avataṃsaka Commentary*, based on the "Universal Gate" chapter:

The thirty-five manifestations are enumerated as follows: first, the body of a Buddha; second, a Pratyekabuddha; third, a Śrāvaka; fourth, a Brahmā King; fifth, Śakra Devendra; sixth, Maheśvara; seventh, Mahāmaheśvara; eighth, a celestial general;

ninth, Vaiśravaṇa; tenth, a minor king; eleventh, an elder; twelfth, a householder; thirteenth, a government official; fourteenth, a Brāhmaṇa; fifteenth, a bhikṣu; sixteenth, a bhikṣuṇī; seventeenth, an upāsaka; eighteenth, an upāsikā; nineteenth, the wife of an elder; twentieth... [and so forth].
10. Householder women; 21. Women of the administrative class; 22. Brahmin women; 23. Boys; 24. Girls; 25. Devas; 26. Nāgas; 27. Yakṣas; 28.
Gandharvas; 29. Asuras; 30. Garuḍas; 31. Kiṃnaras; 32. Mahoragas; 33. Humans; 34. Non-humans; 35. [The thirty-fifth].

Fifth is the Vajradhara deity. If one were to combine the bodies of a householder, a lay devotee, a government official, and a Brahmin woman into a single form, there would be thirty-two manifestations. However, in principle, the four classes of women are actually distinct from one another; this is clarified in the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound."

In that chapter, there are further mention of the bodies of Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*) and Bodhisattvas; furthermore, these include those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and animals, as well as all places of adversity. How could it be that he does not possess those bodies? Thus, even thirty-five [bodies] would not be exhaustive.
If one were to divide the four types of women into two each—since they become individuals through their distinct spouses—then this number would already reach thirty-nine.

Possessing immeasurable merit and manifesting great sovereign power, he makes great vows to flow equally throughout the nine realms (the ten *dharmadhātus*, excluding the Buddha-realm) and the six destinies and four modes of birth (the six being devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; the four being womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born).

Moistening [the roots of goodness] and transforming them into four [types of merit], throughout the realms of birth and death, I have for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *Ganges-sand* kalpas cultivated skillful means of virtuous conduct to rescue and deliver all sentient beings without ceasing. I now entreat you with compassion;

please grant your grace and protection. I humbly reflect that I, [Name], have by fortunate destiny in past lives encountered the Buddha Vehicle (*Buddhayāna*); though my body has left the household life, my mind has not...

Afflicted by the path of passion (if one is a householder, this should be changed to "the dust-like conditions of bodily suffering," as the mind is largely distracted), mired in ignorance and false views, with the sense faculties clouded and obstructed, one may study internal and external scriptures;
yet, despite such practice, one understands neither the phrasing nor the sublime principles. Furthermore, there is fear that one's power of merit is shallow and meager.

My lifespan is not long; I have entered the Gate of Emptiness in vain (for laypeople, this should be changed to "I have merely obtained a human body"). My life has been lived in emptiness and my death will be in vain.

Now, with a cleansed heart and shedding tears of blood, I prostrate my forehead in sincere devotion. Day and night, I maintain the visualization of the Holy Countenance, uphold the Holy Name, and pay homage to the Holy Image.
I pray only that the Bodhisattva’s divine ear may hear my voice, that your compassionate heart may rescue me from suffering, and that you may grant your pitying protection by emitting—
Great Divine Light shines upon my body and mind. You pour forth great nectar, drenching the crown of my head.

It washes away the grudges and transgressions accumulated over successive lifetimes and cleanses the defilements of a thousand births. My body and mind become pure, and demonic obstacles are eliminated.
Day and night, whether sitting or reclining, I behold the Bodhisattva emitting great divine light, opening my wisdom-nature, and enabling me, [Name], to immediately...
At that time, their supernatural powers will shine forth clearly; they will be wise and intelligent.

All scriptures will be naturally committed to memory, and all principles and meanings will be naturally understood. They will attain great eloquence, great wisdom, a long life, and great peace and happiness.

In practicing Chan and studying the Way, they will be free from all demonic obstacles; they will realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and practice the path of the Bodhisattva in birth after birth, life after life.

The Way: universally repaying the four debts of gratitude, providing equal sustenance to all within the three realms of existence, so that all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm may together perfect the seed of omniscience. (This text is divided into four major sections.)

From the first phrase up to "the Great and Vastly Responsive Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" is the expression of homage. From "Thus have I heard" up to "without ceasing" is the offering of praise. From "I now" up to "awakening to the patience of non-arising" is the request for empowerment.

From "life after life" up to "together perfecting the All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)" is the vow and dedication. The character *zhǒng* (seed) is pronounced in the level tone. Only the Buddha possesses all-knowledge; this means that the Tathāgata is able, by means of a single wisdom, to know the path and teachings of all Buddhas and to know the causal seeds of all sentient beings. Regarding the four debts of gratitude:

the debt to one's father, the debt to one's mother, the debt to the king and the elements of earth and water, and the debt to Heaven and Earth for their covering and supporting. Regarding the three realms of existence (*tribhava*): the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. Sentient beings undergo birth and death; therefore, they are called "existence."
Emperor Renzong.
His posthumous name was Shun. He was the son of Emperor Zhenzong. In the first year of the Tiānshèng era, the Emperor habitually wore a jade crown upon which was placed an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Because the jade was heavy, his attendants requested that it be replaced. The Emperor said, "The Three Dukes and the hundred officials bow below [this image]."

"These individuals are all the most eminent and wise men of the realm; how could Your Majesty dare to presume upon such honor? It is simply that, according to the distinction between sovereign and subject, it must be so.
When Your Majesty donned this crown, it was intended to cause you to return the courtesy to the Great Being (the Bodhisattva). (From the *Zheng Jingchong Jiashiji*) — Emperor Yingzong.
Emperor Yingzong, whose posthumous name was Zongshi, was the elder brother of Emperor Renzong.

In the second year of the Zhìpíng era, Shen Wéntōng, the Governor of Hángzhōu, submitted a memorial stating that since the time of the Shíjìn dynasty until the present Zhìpíng era, Guānshìyīn Púsà of Tiānzhū Temple had brought blessings upon the empire.
The marsh gave rise to the people, and its sacred traces have been remarkably prominent from ancient times to the present.

Prime Minister Zeng Gongliang recounted these events, whereupon the imperial plaque was bestowed, naming it Linggan Guanshiyin Yuan (The Temple of the Responsive Avalokiteśvara). (Cited from the Tongji and Jintang.
—Zeng Gongliang.

Zeng Gongliang, courtesy name Mingzhong, was a native of Quanzhou. Once, while returning home from mourning his mother’s death, he encountered a monk named Yuanda on a boat who traveled with him as far as Qiantang.

There, the monk entered Tianzhu Monastery to pay homage to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). Upon entering the gate, he saw a woman dressed in plain white robes, who said to him, "Scholar Zeng will enter the Zhongshu Menxia at the age of fifty-seven;
you, Senior Monk, shall also receive a title of honor this year. After this, she vanished. This was Zeng Liang.
At the age of fifty-seven, he was appointed as Grand Preceptor (Chengxiang). Da was subsequently granted the title of Great Master (Dashi) by imperial decree.

(From the *Tongji*). Emperor Xiaozong: His posthumous name was Shen. He was selected by Emperor Gaozong to be the Crown Prince. Upon his accession to the throne, in the seventh month of the first year of Longxing—
In the month of [blank], the Emperor presided over the Seondeokjeon Hall and composed a hymn of praise for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "How magnificent is the Great Being!

Originally self-perfected and all-pervading, he manifests speech and discourse to serve as the patriarch of the world. His illumination is without peer; with universal observation and compassion, he responds immediately to every stimulus—his wondrousness is inconceivable.
Furthermore, the Emperor once visited India to pay his respects to the Bodhisattva, where he beheld an image of Avalokiteśvara engaged in circumambulation.
He summoned Chan Master Xiatang and asked him, "When a Bodhisattva holds a rosary in his hand, what is he reciting?
Tang replied, "Seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself. The Emperor was greatly pleased. (From the *Ziji*).
Emperor Lizong.

Emperor Lizong, whose personal name was Yun, was the nephew of Emperor Ningzong. In the first year of the Chunyou era, the Emperor dreamed that the Great Being (Mahāsattva) was seated amidst bamboo and rocks.
Upon awakening, he had an image painted and carved upon stone, inscribing his own eulogy: "His supernatural powers are most wondrous, appearing and disappearing beyond measure;
His merit is boundless, yet His response is so swift. May there be peace in the seasons and abundance in the years, to bless all the people under Heaven."

With the cessation of military conflict and the laying aside of punishments, this royal kingdom was brought to peace. He inscribed the four great characters "Great and Vastly Responsive Power" (Guǎngdà Línggǎn) above the sacred title of Avalokiteśvara,
and further inscribed one scroll of the Heart Sūtra, which he granted for carving upon stone at Upper Tianzhu Monastery (funded by the Directorate and the monastery’s stele).

Zhen Dexiu, courtesy name Xi-yuan, was originally surnamed Shen. He changed his surname to Zhen to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Xiaozong. During the Duanping era, he participated in the highest administration;

he was posthumously titled Wenzhong and styled Xishan (Western Mountain) Master. He once wrote a colophon for the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter), in which he said: "Formerly, the Tang dynasty's Li..."
Duke Wen asked Zen Master Yanshan Yan, "What is it like when black winds blow a ship and cast it adrift into the land of ghosts?
The Master replied, "You little fellow Li Ao, why do you ask such a thing? Duke Wen was startled, and his anger manifested on his face.
The Master smiled and said, "To give rise to this heart of anger and resentment is itself to be blown by black winds and cast into the land of ghosts. Alas! Yanshan may truly be called...

This is a skillful exhortation for others. One should know that when profit and desire blaze fiercely, they are a pit of fire; when greed and attachment cause one to sink, they are a sea of suffering.
When the mind is purely focused, the fierce flames become a pool; with a single thought of awakening, the boat reaches the other shore.

Even when bound by calamities and afflictions, one remains at peace wherever one is; I have no fear, like shackles falling off of their own accord. When evil people invade and oppress me, I await them...
"Though others may act with violence and oppression, I harbor no anger or resentment; it is like a wild beast fleeing on its own.

Those who read this sutra should contemplate in this way, and will then know that the Great Being of Potalaka acts with sincere concern for others, and his words are not idle speech. (Cited from the *Wenxian Tongkao*, Yuan dynasty).

Shi Mengrun, whose courtesy name was Yugang, was a native of Jiahe. His surname was Gu. While his mother was pregnant with him and at the time of his birth, she experienced extraordinary dreams on both occasions. At the age of fourteen, he left the household life;
however, due to his arduous studies, he contracted a strange illness. He then practiced the Seven-Seven-Day Repentance of Invoking Avalokiteśvara, through which he attained [his recovery].
His spiritual responses were such that his illness was cured and his mind became doubly clear and sharp; he became a vessel of great capacity.

He presided over the Dharma assemblies of various Indian masters, surrounded by thousands of disciples. He frequently practiced the Samādhis of the Lotus Sūtra and the Great Compassion, and his auspicious manifestations were beyond counting.
Thus, his hidden virtues and secret realizations cannot easily be fathomed by those of shallow insight.
Shi Zhenjing, whose courtesy name was Ru’an, was the son of the Yao family of Huating. His mother dreamed that a white moon fell into her lap and she became pregnant.
A strange monk told her, "This child is the reincarnation of Dharma Master Haoyue. He left home at the age of nine and relied upon Master Wuji.

The Dharma Master Du exhausted himself in the study of the nature of reality. During the Tai Ding era of the Yuan dynasty, the Chancellor Tuo Huan appointed him to reside at the Lower Tianzhu Monastery.

Previously, while suffering from illness at Jingyin Monastery, he dreamed of the Great Being (Bodhisattva) dressed in white, who held a flask of water and poured it into his mouth, saying, "You shall recover on your own.

The Yuan sovereign admired his Way and bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Mind Broad Discernment" (*Foxin Hongbian*), as well as purple robes with golden patterns. He entered *nirvāṇa* at the Jia... [Monastery].
His tongue-root remained unimpaired because he had long upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Shi Hongji (弘濟), whose courtesy name was Tongzhou (同舟) and pen-name Tian'an (天岸), was a native of Yuyao. His surname was Yao. He left home to become a monk in his youth and once practiced the Dharma.
The *Huayan*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and other repentance rituals produced miraculous responses. In the first year of the Taiding era of the Yuan dynasty, he resided at Wanshou and Yuanjue monasteries.
The following year, the coastal region of Yanguan was devastated; the tides surged violently, and it was feared the area would become a dwelling for fish and turtles.

The Chancellor Tuo-huan was deeply concerned about this and requested that Jie offer prayers to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) at Upper Zhushan. He further established a Water and Land (Shuilu) vegetarian feast on the seashore.

Ji entered the *maitrī-citta-samādhi* (samādhi of the compassionate mind). Taking sand, he recited the Great Compassion Mantra (*mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*) and led the assembly in scattering it everywhere over the site.

Wherever his footsteps reached, the riverbanks were all restored to their former solidity. The multitude revered him as if he were a deity. (The three preceding accounts are from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*, by Shi Nianchang.)
Master Nianchang, styled Haiwu, was a native of Huating. His surname was Huang and his mother was Lady Yang.

She had prayed to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and in a dream, an old monk with a bushy beard entrusted her with lodging; she subsequently conceived. At the time of her delivery, auspicious light illuminated the room and a wondrous fragrance pervaded those nearby.
He left home at Yuanming Monastery in Pingjiang and extensively studied various scriptures. He received the Dharma transmission from Master Huiji Xi and was honored as an Imperial Preceptor.

Chong was included among the scriptures inscribed in golden characters. He authored the *Fozu tongzai* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) in twenty-two fascicles, which circulated throughout the world;
at that time, he was acclaimed as the "Ban and Ma" [of the Buddhist clergy].
Shi Yuanchang, whose courtesy name was Wuming and style name Qianyan Chanshi, was a native of Xiaoshan. His clan was Dong and his mother was surnamed He.

When he fell ill as a child, his mother prayed to Guanyin; she was granted permission to renounce the world, and only then did he recover. He mastered the nine schools of thought and the various masters of antiquity, and studied the Vinaya.
From Master Lingzhi, he received the transmission of the mind-seal from Master Zhongfeng. While living in seclusion at Tiantong, two snakes would come daily to coil around his Dharma seat.
The Master preached the Three Refuges and Five Precepts to them; the snakes raised and lowered their heads in a manner resembling prostration and dance before departing.
From that time on, his reputation grew exceedingly great. The imperial court specially bestowed upon him named incense, purple robes, and the title "Puying Miao."
The title of his posthumous name was honored and revered by both those within the Central States and those from foreign lands. (The above two entries are from the *Jiegu lüe*).
"Eulogy on the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion," composed by the Emperor Taizong Wen of the Ming Dynasty.
Avalokiteśvara realized the wondrous and perfect penetration; Entering the stream, he forgot the object from which it arose within his own hearing.
From hearing he entered into awakening, whereby that which is perceived became empty; His pure, precious awakening achieved the samādhi of perfect fusion.
The power of his compassion is equal to that of the Buddhas; He has accomplished the merit of sovereign and wondrous power.
Adorned with necklaces and a hundred shimmering jewels, On Mount Potalaka, you manifest a face like the full moon;

Your eyes are mani-gems with pupils like lotuses, And from the branches of the willow in your vase, which holds the water of the ocean waves, A spring breeze arises with every leaf. Transcending the world, your wondrousness is inexhaustible.
The thirty-two manifestations respond according to the needs of beings; the four kinds of fearlessness are sublime virtues.
His name is extolled like the striking of a bell; its resonance reaches through walls without obstruction, penetrating all with clarity.
He rescues those drowning in the sea of suffering and opens the eyes of the deluded and ignorant.
The power of great compassion is truly reverent and respectful; Like the sands of the Ganges, it bestows models and protection.
Adapting to circumstances through skillful means, each has its function; Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, blessings are most magnificent.
The two aspects of movement and stillness leave no trace; Subtle, luminous, and tranquil, it reveals the school of the intrinsic nature.
The light of wisdom universally illuminates the seven-jeweled crimson; Only those who can penetrate this void of the ten directions [may perceive it].
Praise for the Image of the Fish Basket Guanyin (Composed by Wenxian Gong Song Lian).

I have consulted the *Guanyin Ganying Zhuan* (Biographies of Guanyin’s Responsive Manifestations): In the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, on the banks of the Jinsha River in Shaanxi, there was...
There was a beautiful woman who carried a basket and sold fish; people vied with one another to take her as their wife. The woman said, "I can teach the scriptures.

Whoever can recite the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) in a single night shall have me. At dawn, twenty men were able to do so. The woman declined, saying, "How could a single body be fit for many husbands?
Please change it to the *Jingang jing* (Diamond Sutra). When the same conditions were set again, those who succeeded were once more reduced by half.
The woman spoke again, requesting that they exchange the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for her, setting a deadline of three days, adding that only the son of the Ma family was capable of this.
She then ordered the formal rites for marriage to be completed. Upon entering the door, the woman died immediately; having died, she instantly decayed and vanished. They hurriedly buried her.
Later, a monk and the son of the Ma family opened the tomb to observe it; only golden-linked skeletal remains remained. The monk said: "This..."
"Avalokiteśvara has manifested himself to transform you. Having spoken these words, he flew through the air and departed. From that time on, those who recited the sutras became numerous in Shensi.
Liu [Surname] of Wushang commissioned the man Wu Fu to paint a single scroll using gold and lapis lazuli pigments.

On the first and fifteenth days of each month, he would unfurl it and pay his respects. He requested me to write a preface for this matter. Having completed the preface, I append to it this eulogy: "O, I..."
"O Great Being, out of compassion for sentient beings who are addicted to the five desires and do not seek liberation, you manifested as a woman, beautiful and exquisite.
By means of their own longing, you led them into the gateway of goodness. Yet in a single kṣaṇa, she suddenly decayed;

what was once like a red lotus, its fragrance and beauty overwhelming the senses, has now become foul and putrid, infested with maggots and oozing away. All the forms in this world are fundamentally [of such a nature]."

Emptiness and the provisional: sentient beings, in their ignorance and delusion, mistake the provisional for the real. Like moths rushing toward a lamp, they fly after it without ceasing; until their lives are lost, how can there be any rest?
This true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is perfectly identical to the vast void; it is neither ugly nor beautiful—how could anyone destroy it?
The spiritual power of the Great Being is like the moon in the sky: it does not distinguish between the pure and the defiled, but illuminates all universally. When ordinary beings take refuge...

As for "yi" (rely/depend): it means to obtain great benefit; may one's vows thus lead to the same destination within the ocean of *sarvajñā* (*sarvajñā*, in the language of the Huas [Chinese], meaning "all-knowledge").
Liu Guxian. Guxian was a native of Huangzhou. He was enrolled in the ranks of the Left Tiger Guards (*huben zuowei jun*). He once followed the Grand Secretary Zheng He on an expedition...
The ship set sail for various countries overseas. While crossing the great ocean, Xian suddenly lost his footing and fell into the water.

At that time, the wind and sails were driving the vessel at great speed, making it impossible to rescue him. He ordered the crew to climb the mast to look out; from afar they saw a person submerged in the waves, rising and falling.
Being several tens of *li* away, they believed there was no longer any hope for his survival. A short while later, Xian reached the ship.
The boatmen were greatly delighted and quickly pulled it in with a net. There was a large fish over ten feet long that had been gliding peacefully nearby; everyone marveled at this.
Hui-xian said, "That I did not drown when I fell into the water was due to the power of this fish. It carried me here just now.
When I was about to sink, several fish repeatedly lifted me up with their fins and gills; for this reason, the water did not enter."
The assembly questioned Xian: "What virtuous deeds did you perform throughout your life to obtain this? Xian replied: "I simply recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
(From the *Zhuanyin lu*, recorded by Shi Xianshi.)
The Chan Master known as Gus'an was surnamed Lu in secular life. His mother was of the Jin clan; he was born amidst five-colored clouds that appeared in her dream of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.

Having received the tonsure in his early twenties, he relied upon the two masters Tian’an and Fohai, through whom he mastered the textual meanings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sections of the Tiantai teachings.
His eloquence flowed like a cascade. Furthermore, by personally attending to such venerable elders as Huyan and Xiansou, his realization of the Way flourished even more.
He resided at Longshou and Yanfu Monasteries, guiding those yet to come. In his later years, he focused exclusively on the Western Paradise;
moved by a miraculous sign, he passed away. Shi Baojin.
Chan Master Baogin, styled Bifeng, was a native of Yongshou. His clan name was Shi; his father was known as a *changzhe* (elder), and his mother was of the Zhang family.

She was diligent in performing good deeds without weariness. A monk carrying an almsbowl presented an image of Avalokiteśvara to Zhang and instructed her, saying, "Serve this with reverence, and you shall give birth to a son of wisdom.
Not long thereafter, the Master was born, and a white light illuminated the room. At the age of six, he followed the Dharma Master Yunji.

He became a disciple, shaving his head and receiving full ordination. He exhausted himself in the study of the nature and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Later, he succeeded to the separate transmission in Western Sichuan under Master Zhenguang (Zhengong).

He established Lingjiu Hermitage to house the assembly, and those who offered support were very numerous. Emperor Yuan Shundi bestowed upon him robes and the title "Yuanying" (Complete Enlightenment).
In the third year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned for an audience and pleased the Emperor's mind; he was granted generous favors and bestowed with twelve poems.

As for rhyme: there are phrases such as "having fully realized the profound pivot, one has already attained perfect enlightenment," and "wherever he goes, all are transformed; it is no less than the arising of Buddhas.
[The monk] Shi Yuan Deng.
Yuande (style name Dayou) was a native of Gusu. His mother, surnamed Tao, conceived him after praying to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.

From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and precocious; he took Master Jingjue of Nanjing as his teacher. He extensively mastered the texts of India and the classics of Lu, leaving nothing uncomprehended.

He served as the abbot of Suixi Temple and authored the *Inner and Outer Chapters of the Son of the Contemplation of Illusion*, which unified the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism. [He was honored by] the Imperial Scholar...
Song Lian recommended him to the Great Emperor Hongwu. He was received with great honor, and by imperial decree, he was appointed to a position in the Hanlin Academy.
Regarding Zen Master Muromachi: his name was Jikō; he was a native of Seishū Province in Japan. His mother had prayed to the Great Being Fumon (Avalokiteśvara), and in a dream...
She conceived after swallowing golden light. At birth, auspicious light filled the room. At the age of nine, she left the household life and paid homage to Vinaya Master Jikwan.
At twenty, she received full ordination. Later, she studied under National Preceptor Ilsan. Ilsan said, "In my school, there is no dharma to give to others;

you must exert yourself in practice. She practiced until her eyes could not meet for sleep. Under the guidance of National Preceptor Gopong, she attained enlightenment. Her verse contains the line: "By chance, a blow..."
He shattered the skeletal bones of empty space; Gao Feng certified his realization. He served as the abbot of renowned monasteries such as Nan Chan, Shan Ying, Rui Guang, Doushuai, and Putuo.
He was granted the honorary title "Zhengjue" (Correct Enlightenment). His Way shook the three courts, and his fame soared across the four seas;
the nation regarded this as its glory. (The above four points are from the *Jigelüe*).

Niche Chengjingchengjing, whose secular name was Shixiu, was a native of Gougang in Guangzhou. Her family name was Zhang. From her youth, she observed the fasts and precepts, maintaining herself with purity and integrity.

She took the master Zhenfan of her home district as her teacher; upon shaving her head and donning the robes, she devoted herself exclusively to the recitation of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the Mahāyāna scriptures.
In all the sutras, he was especially diligent in serving his teachers. Having received full ordination in middle age, he constantly sought instruction from me regarding the Vinaya.

He fixed his mind on the Pure Land, never ceasing to recite the name of Amitābha with both heart and mouth. Compassionate and serene, he delighted in giving; his dignified demeanor served as a model for others.

Teaching with gentle persistence and skillful guidance, he was revered by both the gentry and the commoners. I considered him to be one who had returned to this world through the power of his vows. He once exhorted the assembly to create a *kṣatriya* [banner].
The sacred image of the Great Compassionate One with a Thousand Hands and Eyes was enshrined at Daci-an in Fengcheng. In the following year, he fell slightly ill;
knowing his time had come, he repeatedly instructed his disciples and took leave of his various donors. On the following day, he said to his disciples:
"The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes has come here to receive me. You all must pay him due respect."
He went to welcome him. [The master] then closed his eyes and passed away. His worldly lifespan was fifty-nine years.
By the Pure Monk Zhisong.
Zhìsōng, whose courtesy name was Língyuè, was a native of Táoyáng. He resided at Lìān Mountain in Gāoyào County, Duānzhōu. In the year of Dīnghài, troops attacked Lìān Mountain.
They seized Zhìsōng and forced him to carry their supplies; they even snatched the prayer beads from his hand. Zhìsōng resisted them, whereupon the soldiers drew their blades and slew him.
As Zhìsōng invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the blade struck his body but became snagged in the hem of his robe. The edge of the sword—
He did not fall upon Mount Song, and thus escaped with his life. One knows that the majestic spiritual power of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) surpasses even the resonance of an echo.

At that time, a follower of the Mount Song school who was practicing in earnest hid within a thicket of mountain brambles, single-mindedly reciting the Great Compassionate Divine Mantra (*mahākaruṇā-mantra*).

While the soldiers searched throughout the mountains for the local villagers, they used their weapons to pierce the thorny forest; as the wounds were about to reach the edge [of the thicket], the soldiers suddenly stumbled and fell down the mountain.
Below. The Sutra says, "It returns to attach itself to the original person. This is surely not false. Zhang Mingda, Mingda: a native of Shunde.
His father was Yinliang, a student from Nanhai. His mother was Lady Deng. Because she had given birth repeatedly... [text ends]... without success.

She conceived as a result of praying to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. It was on the very morning that the Great Being attained enlightenment; on this day, according to custom, many people abstain from meat and vegetables to celebrate the Great Being’s attainment.
Her mother and attendants were preparing pure offerings when, after they had been presented, the east had not yet broken into dawn.
Intending to rest for a short while, she did not realize she had given birth. At that moment the child cried; everyone, both great and small, rushed to look and saw—
A light radiated throughout the room, and everyone marveled at it. Deng then said to her sister-in-law, "This child’s birth was unlike that of ordinary infants;
could this not be an auspicious sign? Before he had reached five years of age, his mother passed away. His grandmother, Lady Yu, raised him as if he were her own late son.
When he reached the age of fourteen, his grandmother was on the verge of death and privately left him several ingots of white gold. During the wuzi year, many people were suffering from malnutrition;
Da distributed the inherited gold to them, and the number of passersby who were saved and restored to life can be counted.
Later, a greedy neighbor slandered him to his father, who instead rebuked Da for secretly misappropriating family wealth and squandering it. Da did not defend himself at all. Afterwards, there was...
Dá encountered a beggar who, having been exhausted by his lack of wealth, had come from afar to seek alms. After several days, the beggar died of hunger and exhaustion.
Upon hearing this, Dá thought privately to himself, "I am still unable to relieve this person's urgent distress; is it not because my power of merit is thin that I have failed him?
Thereupon, he made a vow to relinquish his body and take rebirth in a royal household, so as to practice universal salvation and satisfy the desires of the multitude. He then immediately ascended...
At this site, Guanyinyan, he paid his respects to the Bodhisattva for witness and empowerment, then cast himself down from a precipice several hundred *ren* high.
Unconsciously, he fell onto a rock at the base of the mountain and sat there, without sustaining even the slightest injury.

Knowing himself to be protected by the compassion of a Great Being, he did not shatter even when falling from a great height. He then followed those who sought him back and persuaded them to return home;

from that time on, he observed the fasts and gave rise to the aspiration to leave the mundane world. His father alone had no faith in the Buddha, making it difficult to enlighten him through ordinary means.

At the age of seventeen, his past roots of virtue ripened in due time, and he presented his long-held resolve to his father. His father rebuked him in anger, but he withdrew and reflected incessantly, focusing solely on his purpose.
Nian Dashi further sought permission from his grandfather. Seeing that his resolve was unshakeable, the grandfather exhorted his son and finally acquiesced.
Nevertheless, obstacles still remained. Ten days later, in the middle of the night, he dreamed of a man in white robes who said to him, "Son of the Buddha, go forth;
do not let this auspicious opportunity pass you by. Da Ruo immediately rose and went out the door; at that time, all the streets, lanes, gates, and portals were—

The cave opened wide. It happened to be a day of heavy rain and deep darkness; the path ahead could not be discerned. There were only a few fireflies, flickering low to the ground as they moved along.
Following them, he advanced for over ten *li* before the light finally faded. He then went to seek ordination under Master Dinghu, who gave him the name Kaijing.
Not long after, he suddenly fell gravely ill. One day, his countenance and spirit both changed, and his breath departed, never to return. Upon seeing this—
Everyone said it was absolutely impossible for him to recover. He focused his mind on a single point of right mindfulness; after a long while, he suddenly revived and gradually returned to health.

How could this have been anything other than the secret empowerment of the Great Being? Consequently, with solemn sincerity, he commissioned the painting of a sacred image of the Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara to serve as an object of veneration.

When painting the image, one should construct a mandala and maintain the recitation of mantras. Each day, one must change clothes and bathe. The painter shall likewise cover his mouth with a cloth to prevent the emission of breath.
Pigments must not contain ox-hide glue or ink-based substances. As for the paper and brush, each must be consecrated through the application of mantra-rites.
On the evening the image is completed, it emits a great radiance that shines beyond the mandala, illuminating the surrounding woods and walls with a brilliant golden glow.

All who saw him were moved to wonder and admiration. From the time he emerged from the womb until his departure from the secular world, [the author] repeatedly received the great protection of this Great Being (Mahāsattva), whose compassionate grace is beyond description.

For this reason, he earnestly requested his Master to compile these accounts for inclusion in this collection, so that all sentient beings on this earth who possess consciousness may know that the wondrous virtues of this Great Being are inconceivable;
thus, they shall not fail to keep him in their thoughts, for he is truly a vessel and a rudder upon the ocean of suffering.
Pan Guozhang, whose courtesy name was Guozhang, was a native of Shunde County in Guangzhou. He placed his faith in the Triple Gem and engaged in trade at Guangli in Duanzhou.

During the upheavals of the Bingxu year, when beacon fires flared up in all directions, he boarded a boat to return to his hometown. Upon reaching Sanshui, he encountered a storm and his vessel capsized; thereupon, he focused his mind with single-minded devotion.
He called upon the name of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Since he was not skilled at swimming, he sank straight down to the bottom of the sea, where it was vast and boundless.

Relying solely on his earnest and fervent mindfulness, he stepped forward with confidence as if walking on solid ground. In a short while, he reached the shore; the travel expenses he had brought remained in the palm of his hand.
Looking back, he realized for the first time that he had previously been submerged in the sea. How extraordinary! Truly, the divine power of the Great Being is beyond comprehension.
How inconceivable! This was also because the man’s mind was free from dualistic thoughts and he had completely forgotten both self and object;
thus, he did not perceive the water touching his lips or his breath. Was this not a partial attainment of the "entering the flow and forgetting the source" (*rulaowang suo*)?
After this chapter, [Zhang] went forth as a monk at Mount Shao on the day he personally visited the mountain; his style name was Xuánqiú (as Zhang himself told me).

Huang Keming, Keming—son of a wealthy family from Dongguan—was traveling by boat to Wuyang at the beginning of the Great Qing dynasty when he was plundered at sea. He was taken to the pirates' stronghold and shackled to the door panels.
While the bandits went on another raid, they left a woman to guard him. At that time, Keming’s family had invited a monk to recite scriptures for his sake.
She recited the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) Sutra. That night, the thief’s wife saw an extraordinary colored auspicious light at the edge of the brightness.

When questioned at dawn, Ming remained silent, knowing for certain that this must have been divine protection. She waited until the woman had gone to a neighbor's house, then she took up the fan and fled.

Leaving her nest, she climbed a ridge and encountered a woodcutter; she asked him to break the fan so she could escape from her shackles. After traveling several tens of li, she finally reached Pingfang.
(An account related by Mingdui himself:
Liu Leishu—Liu Leishu was the son of Magistrate Zhong Lei of Shunyi County in Guangzhou. In the autumn of the Dinghai year of the Shunzhi era, he departed...

Xiangshan was captured by pirates at sea. When the pirates failed to extort the ransom they demanded, they pushed him into the ocean. While still a youth, Luei had been raised under his father’s instruction and maintained devout faith in the Triple Gem;
he thought to himself that only the Bodhisattva could be relied upon. He then recited the name of Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart.
At that moment, his hands were bound and he was about to sink to the bottom of the sea; though his suffering was nearly fatal, he redoubled his earnestness. Suddenly, he became aware—
His big toe reached the sand; after drifting for some time, he gradually arrived at a shallow place.

Truly, as it is said, "When one is swept away by a great flood, if one calls upon the name [of the Buddha], one immediately finds a shallow place"—this faith is not false. At that time, the bandits saw him and pulled him onto their boat.
They kept him for several days, intending to wait for news from home so they might ransom his life with his wealth. While those bandits plundered along the river, Luei (Lai) did not [suffer harm].
They suffered calamity. After five or six days had passed, a violent storm arose; the pirates' ships found no place to anchor and were thus forced to change their minds and release them.
They said, "I believe this is the result of your entire family observing the fasts and precepts. Furthermore, when I was young, I too was once captured.
From the morning until noon, I was able to escape and be set free; all of this was due to the power of the Bodhisattva. And so it was with the world...
Changes occurred; those who encountered calamities were beyond counting, yet the Lüei family alone remained free from misfortune.
Was this not the result of his profound faith in the past? (This was Lüei’s own account.
[Endorsed by] Shao Yizhen.

Yi Zhen was a provincial student (zhusheng) of Guangzhou Prefecture who had placed his heart in the Buddhist faith. In the year Wuzi, there were new soldiers in the city of Shaozhou who forcibly took clothing from a merchant in the marketplace.

The merchant spoke out against them, whereupon the soldiers reported the matter to Lord Li, the Provincial Governor, claiming that the common people intended to rebel and were using short-sleeved garments as a signal.
However, it was the custom in Lingnan for inner shirts to generally be short; consequently, the city was sealed off and a search was launched.
The executioner merely saw that their collars were short and cut them down. Master Li had no opportunity to plead for them; thus, dozens were executed one after another.
At that time, Zhen was among the ranks, yet she focused her mind solely on earnestly reciting the name of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). When it was her turn, the execution stopped.
Consequently, all those who had been unjustly targeted were likewise spared. Zhen therefore requested me to include this account in my compilation.
Nini Dengling was a native of Panyu in Guangzhou. Her secular surname was Deng and her mother’s was Hong. She entered the monastic life at the beginning of the Daqing era.

Morning and evening she performed ritual recitations, setting her aspirations upon the Pure Land; she incessantly chanted the great name of the Bodhisattva, never ceasing from her lips. In the year of Gengyin—
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, during the mid-night recitation of the ritual, the four walls were silent and desolate, and I was alone.
Suddenly, it felt as if there were something in the palm of my hand; unconsciously, I brought it toward my mouth and swallowed it. Yet, when I opened my fist, three pills remained in my hand.

Its color was a vivid crimson, and its shape resembled cinnabar. From that point on, she abstained from food entirely, yet felt no hunger or thirst; her ritual prostrations and recitations remained as diligent as before.
Nowadays, she occasionally partakes of seasonal fruits, yet does not touch her lips to the seven grains; her physical frame remains as it was, and her spirit is even more robust.
He currently resides at Yanjing An in Guangzhou.
Huang Kuosheng (Kuosheng) was a student from the new district of Guangzhou; his family was immensely wealthy, yet he was fifty years old without having raised an heir. In the year Wuzi...
In his [fifteenth] year, he received the five precepts and abstained from pungent roots and raw garlic. He served the Great Being with exceptional reverence;

morning and evening, he would invariably bathe and perform a hundred prostrations while reciting the name of the Great Being. Even amidst the bustle of worldly affairs, he never ceased this regular practice. Before three years had passed, [he attained realization].

The wife and concubine each gave birth to a son on the same day. When they grew up, they were quite intelligent and wise; this is what the sutra means when it says, "One immediately gives birth to a son endowed with merit, virtue, and wisdom.
He was named Helong.
Liang was a student at the school in Panyu, Guangzhou. Having exceeded the age of fifty and remaining childless, his heart had already given up all hope.

In the year of Yiwei, he invited me to spend the summer retreat at my garden, whereupon I bestowed upon him the text for the Six Fasting Days and an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Great Compassionate One.
He immediately constructed a separate room to offer worship and paid reverent homage morning and evening. Every morning, he would invariably finish his prostrations before partaking of tea or broth;
such was the depth of his sincerity. After several months had passed, he dreamed that the Great Being personally bestowed a red child upon him.

The following day, he joyfully informed me, saying, "I have received an auspicious omen. In the subsequent year, he indeed gave birth to a son. In the third year, he produced three sons in succession.
Mai Chuan-sheng, a native of Mai Village in Shun County, was a devout observer of the six fasts. On the second day of the eighth month in the year of Jiachen (1684) during the Kangxi era,
while traveling to a neighboring village, he was seized by bandits on the road and brought to their stronghold, where his neck was bound with four iron chains.

He was confined in a dark chamber and ransomed for a hundred taels of silver. Cheng immediately recited the great name of the Bodhisattva day and night, with single-minded devotion and without distraction.
After four days had passed, the bandits brought him food; finding no chopsticks, he went outside to find a bamboo branch, broke it off, and gave it to them.
They then locked the door again and departed. However, the bandits opened the door several times each day to inspect him. On this particular day—
He immediately lost his key and could do nothing but peer out from the doorway. Sheng then split a bamboo stalk and tested it against the lock;
he managed to open it three times in succession, though the single lock at the top remained stubbornly immovable.

Realizing that he had already been granted salvation by the Great Being, his earnest prayers became even more fervent. On the eighth day, he tried again to pierce it with the bamboo, and the lock suddenly gave way with a sharp snap.

He fell down, intending to flee, yet fearing that the bandits would discover him, he hesitated and could not decide. Previously, Xiang had possessed a piece of fresh ginger about the size of a finger;
when he was captured, the bandits had already divided it, leaving only half. He then used the remaining ginger as a vessel for his wine and knelt before the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara), saying:
"Disciple, I have already received your compassionate protection, and my bonds have been suddenly released. Now I wish to escape, yet I fear those who guard me."
If captured, there would be no further possibility of survival. If you permit me to go immediately, I beg you to grant me the five superior means of verification to dispel my anxieties and doubts.
If it truly be as I have prayed, I shall immediately climb onto the roof to look for them. Seeing that they were across the stream at his father-in-law’s house, he hurried toward them.
The external bandits became aware and called out; Seong then leaped across the stream and fled. Upon reaching the bank, he was intercepted once more by the bandit faction.

Sheng pulled them apart with both elbows, charging like a boar into a flock of sheep; none could restrain him. He forced his way into his father-in-law’s house, where the bandits besieged the gate demanding him back.
His father-in-law pleaded, "Sheng’s family is poor; I beg you for ten days’ grace so that I may prepare some silver according to my means.
After several days had passed, suddenly government troops arrived to suppress the rebellion. The bandits fled in disarray, and Sheng returned home directly by the path.
Not a single coin was spent. As it is said, "By invoking his name, one immediately attains liberation. Is this not truly beyond reproach?
Furthermore, Sheng had a paternal uncle named Lianfeng who had long observed the precepts of fasting and abstinence. In the first month of that year, he traveled to Yangcheng.

On the riverbank, he encountered bandits plundering those attempting to cross; more than fifty men and women were seized and dragged back to their lair. Having passed the summit of a mountain, the bandits—
Using a wooden board as a prop for his seat, he rested for a short while. From behind him, Feng pulled out the board, and both man and board tumbled together into a pit.

He immediately fled to an empty house on the outskirts of a village and covered himself with broken bamboo mats and silkworm trays. The bandits surrounded the village and issued a proclamation to the local people, saying:
"There is a long-bearded man with a hemp-like face who has fled into your village; you must surrender him quickly. Otherwise, we shall raze it."
Feng heard that the village households had been leveled, and he was struck with great terror. He fervently called the name of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) once;

as he did so, he plucked several strands of his beard, and then plucked them all out at once, yet he felt no pain whatsoever. Suddenly, a man came from elsewhere and said, "The Bearded One has already passed over the mountain.
Thereupon, the bandits dispersed. Feng then went out to report this to the owner of the empty house, who immediately—

He presented him with clothing and a hat, treating him as a kinsman, and purchased a boat to escort him back home. Seong and his uncle felt deeply indebted to the Great Being for his immense kindness, which they could not repay;
they thus earnestly entreated me to include this account in the collection.

Peng Yicheng was a man from Foshan in Nanhai who had placed his faith in the Dharma and observed the six days of fasting. In the twelfth month of the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, he was returning home from Wuyang with five other people on the same boat.
Midway through their journey, they encountered a violent storm that capsized the vessel; all the others... [were lost]. Peng alone... [survived].

The raft floated away, reaching the shore; only the man remained trapped within the boat, unable to escape. He focused his mind with single-minded devotion, earnestly reciting the name of the Great Being.
In a brief moment, water filled half the boat; as he drank it while continuing his recitation, he suddenly felt someone pull him by the hand out onto the water.
He then hauled at the sail of the boat, which drifted along until it reached the shore. Those on the shore questioned him together, saying: "A short while ago..."
He saw a person in white clothing who had hurried to the boat through the awning; now seeing only him, he wondered, "Could it not be that the other was drowned by the water?

Zongmeng said, "There were no others at all; there was only I alone. After repeated questioning and investigation, he finally realized that the person in white clothing was the Great Being (Mahāsattva) appearing to rescue him.
Zongmeng recorded this himself and requested its inclusion in the collection.
Deng Chengzhao, whose style name was Shifeng, was a native of Panyu, Guangzhou. He had been a devoted follower for many years and had received the precepts of taking refuge.

In the fifth month of the Wushen year of the Kangxi era, his eldest daughter-in-law, Lady Huang, suddenly developed two goiters in her throat. For half a month, she was unable to take food or drink. Her body...

Her spirit was exhausted and her mind disordered; she suffered from swelling and pain that were difficult to endure. She had requested a physician to lance the wound, and once the pus and blood had been drained, the swelling and pain returned within moments, exceeding what they had been before.

Her suffering lasted for over ten days, and medicinal treatments proved ineffective. By chance, as I was returning to the mountains, my boat passed by her door. I sent word to inquire after her condition and asked why she was so ill.
She replied, "My eldest daughter-in-law is currently afflicted with a throat abscess. The agony is extreme. A skilled physician examined her pulse and said—"
"The poison has entered his heart and kidneys; medicine will surely find it difficult to cure him, and his life may only be prolonged for a day or two.
Although I knew that my destiny was fixed, I could not avoid being filled with grief and anxiety. "I wonder, Master, if you possess a dharma capable of saving one from fixed karma?
I replied, "The Great Being Avalokiteśvara possesses inconceivable majestic power and can bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings. He frequently grants [instruction] within dreams."
Regarding this scripture of the Dharma: those who recite it shall immediately receive liberation whenever they encounter illness or hardship. The Emperor asked, "May I hear this scripture?
I immediately ordered my attendant to copy ten passages from the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra on Saving Sentient Beings* and gave them to him. He took them back with him.

He had someone instruct his daughter-in-law; after only two or three recitations, she was able to recite it from memory herself. He then posted the scripture before the patient’s bed. During the night, the patient saw the characters, each about an inch in size.
The next day, his body felt refreshed and his spirit settled. He continued reciting until midnight, when the ulcer burst open of its own accord.
Pus and blood gushed forth, and he cried out, "My illness is healed! He then asked for water to rinse his mouth and rose to prostrate himself.
The Great Being was restored to his former state. The entire family rejoiced and celebrated, marveling at the compassionate power of the Great Being, exclaiming, "How swift is such a response!
— from the *Record of the Collection on Avalokiteśvara’s Forest of Compassion*.

At the age of nineteen, Zhanfu lost both his parents in quick succession. Every time he recited the "Liao'e" (The Grass by the Pond) poem, he felt a sense of empty shame for failing his filial duties as a bird.

Hearing that observing the fast could provide merit for the deceased, he immediately renounced meat and pungent flavors. Before three years had passed, he read the *Platform Sutra* and suddenly realized the truth of his long-held aspirations.

Knowing that a person capable of such realization can attain Buddhahood, I immediately abandoned my home for the homeless life, hoping to establish myself in the Way and perform deeds to benefit my ancestors’ spirits.

Although I have performed prostrations and earnest prayers on their behalf morning and night, and always offered memorial services whenever I encountered the Ullambana festival, my inner heart remains restless, feeling ashamed that the sincerity of my efforts has not yet been cleansed of its impurities.
Thus, in the spring of the Dingyou year, I used Western white silk to paint the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed [Avalokiteśvara].
The sacred image of Mahākaruṇā was seven feet in height. Its surface was prepared by removing the skin and glue and applying pigments mixed with fragrant liquid.
Furthermore, the painters were required to bathe daily and change their robes. Once the image was completed, he exhausted his resources of robes and alms bowls to invite a great assembly of monks.

First, he expounded upon the essential meaning of the *Mahākaruṇā-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* (The Liturgy of Great Compassion). Subsequently, for twenty-one days, they performed prostrations and worship. Thereupon, he was moved by a vision of the Bodhisattva’s body.
It emitted golden light, and from the two lotus flowers—blue and red—held in its hands, it repeatedly emitted white light that was witnessed by both monastics and laypeople alike;
this was truly rare and brought private joy and consolation, for I was certain that through the power of its compassion, the spirits of my parents would be delivered to the higher realms.
Thereafter, whenever I performed prostrations before the image, white light constantly surged forth from the lotuses, and there was no one who beheld it who did not rejoice and develop pure faith.
I, Xìn, reflect that the Buddha’s benevolence is vast and boundless; though I were to sacrifice my very body, I could never repay it.
For this reason, I have investigated the Tripiṭaka and examined various biographies, compiling this collection based on what I have seen and heard.

It is intended as a mere fraction of a response to his immense grace, so that all who see or hear it may together ascend the precious raft of Prajñā, and all who encounter or revere it may together enter the compassionate grove of fearlessness.
Forever departing from the realms of suffering, one proceeds directly toward the Land of Bliss. This is the record.
Written on a summer day in the Wushen year of the Kangxi era by the monk Hongzan of Dinghu, with prostrations.
